### 64. Hardening ideas from the burnside-project review (2026-07-15) — *(a) SHIPPED v0.99.246 (ADR-0059 implementation note); (b) SHIPPED IN TWO PARTS — v0.99.246 (ADR-0160, lineage CAS) + v0.104.7 (the chain-tip guard the CAS framing missed; read (b) below before assuming CAS covered this); (c) remains demand-gated*

Cross-checks against `pg-cdc`'s reliability catalog found sluice already covers most of it (TOAST `'u'` preserve-semantics; ADR-0059 slot-pressure thresholds; 10s idle keepalive — verified 2026-07-15, see the research addendum). Two genuine gaps + one demand-gated idea:

- **(a) Slot-health notifications (S).** ADR-0059's pre-emptive slot WARNs (70%/85% of `max_slot_wal_keep_size`, 30m inactivity) are **slog-only** — an unattended sync's operator never gets paged before the slot invalidates. Wire the WARN/CRITICAL crossings into the ADR-0157 notification sinks (webhook/Slack/email), same edge-once + failure-isolated posture as schema-drift alerts. The signal (`slot_health_reporter.go`) and the sink plumbing both exist; this is wiring + pins.
- **(b) Backup-store concurrent-writer guard — SHIPPED IN TWO PARTS, and the second part is the one that mattered.** The original filing proposed CAS manifest writes (S3 `If-Match`; filesystem `O_EXCL`) against "two `backup incremental` crons", and that is what ADR-0160 built and shipped in v0.99.246: generation-claim markers (`lineage.gen/g-<N>`, create-only CAS) around every `lineage.json` read-modify-write, coded `SLUICE-E-BACKUP-CHAIN-CONFLICT`, real-cloud-verified on S3/GCS/Azure. **That framing was incomplete, and live testing on 2026-07-28 proved it** — the exact "two overlapping `backup incremental` crons" scenario this entry named still produced a permanently unrestorable chain, on real AWS S3 *and* on a local directory, with **both runs exiting rc=0**. The CAS worked perfectly throughout: the `lineage.gen/` markers advanced 1→2→3, neither manifest was clobbered, nothing was lost. **CAS serialises the WRITES; it never asked whether the LINK belonged at the end of the chain.** Both runs resolved the same parent (the parent is resolved *before* the CDC window opens — that is where the window's StartPosition comes from), so the loser appended a SIBLING beside the winner: two incrementals under one parent, committed as if sequential, and `backup verify`/`restore` refusing it from then on — while the forked chain kept ACCEPTING further incrementals off whichever sibling won the tail, so an operator with overlapping crons banks weeks of green backups on a chain that died at the fork. Postgres slot exclusivity does not prevent it either: the loser blocks on the slot, waits it out, re-reads the same changes from the slot restart position, and commits its sibling reporting the same change count. **The missing guard was a precondition on the link, not more CAS: refuse an incremental whose parent is no longer the chain's tip.** Shipped v0.104.7 (`internal/pipeline/lineage/chain_tip.go`) — checked before the manifest write so the loser writes nothing durable, and again inside `UpdateLineageForManifest` as the durable gate every chain writer funnels through; same `SLUICE-E-BACKUP-CHAIN-CONFLICT` code; gated by the `concurrent-incremental-fork` cell in the chain-shaping × encryption matrix (all three modes, verify + restore row-exact) plus unit pins in `internal/pipeline/backup_chain_fork_guard_test.go`. Operator repair for a chain that already forked is documented at `docs/operator/error-codes.md` → *Repairing a forked chain* (lossless: the siblings captured the same window). **Residual, stated honestly:** ADR-0160's claim→Put window survives — two writers landing inside it can both observe the old tip, and the generation claim does not arbitrate them either (a writer that observes the other's marker claims the generation *after* it and also wins). The outcome there is a LOST UPDATE (one link is orphaned, the chain stays linear and contiguous because both siblings start at the same parent position), never a fork. Closing it needs a compare-and-swap keyed on the catalog's own recorded generation, which reintroduces the stale-lock liveness problem ADR-0160 deliberately rejected — filed here rather than fixed. The pg-cdc "dual-writer circuit breaker after N conflicts" idea remains unbuilt and is now lower value: the conflict is already loud, coded, and self-remedying on re-run.
- **(c) RDS/Aurora IAM-token auth (demand-gated).** Short-lived IAM tokens minted per connect (`BeforeConnect` re-resolution) instead of static DSN passwords. New credential surface — file only; build on operator demand.

### 65. Control-table schema hygiene (operator-flagged 2026-07-15, from a full 11-table inventory) — ✅ BOTH S ITEMS SHIPPED v0.99.249 (`8177c70c`: LONGTEXT widening via detect-then-ALTER + the shared control-table roster in `appliershared/control_table_roster.go`) — *originally: the wider review found the design sound (PK-served hot paths everywhere, deliberate LONGTEXT where it matters, ADR-0082 already fixed the one genuinely dangerous TEXT sizing)*

- **(a) Widen `sluice_cdc_state.source_position` (and `sluice_shard_consolidation_lease.anchor_position`) from MySQL `TEXT` to `LONGTEXT` (S).** The same engine-opaque position token is deliberately `LONGTEXT` in `sluice_cdc_schema_history.anchor_position` ("GTID sets can be long", `mysql/schema_history.go:61-64`) but `TEXT` (64 KB) in these two — a >64 KB GTID/VGTID set (≈1000 server-UUID entries or a very heavily sharded VGTID) would fail the position write loudly (sluice pins `STRICT_TRANS_TABLES`, so never silent) mid-stream. Fix via the existing detect-then-ALTER column-migration pattern; NOTE the ALTER on a safe-migrations PlanetScale target hits the direct-DDL block (the ADR-0162 finding-2 class) — needs the detect-first + skip-or-refuse treatment, or shipping via the expand-DR channel where applicable. PG unaffected (unbounded TEXT).
- **(b) Align the schema-reader control-table exclusion list with the full roster (S).** The target-side schema readers exclude only 5 of the 11 sluice control tables from user-table enumeration (`postgres/schema_reader.go:553-557` and the mysql sibling); `sluice_cdc_schema_history`, `sluice_shard_consolidation_lease`, `sluice_target_metrics_history`, and `sluice_keysets` are missing. Realistic bite: the cutover flow — a promoted ex-target used later as a migration source carries those sluice internals along as user tables (loud/visible, not silent). One shared roster constant + pins on both engines.
- **Reviewed and deliberately NOT filed:** the PK-only indexing on every control table (all hot-path queries are PK/index-served; pgtrigger even drops two legacy secondary indexes as pure write amplification); `sluice_cdc_schema_history`'s natural-key full scan (compaction-bounded to dozens of rows; its SHA-256 surrogate PK exists because a natural-key index would exceed InnoDB's 3072-byte cap); the unindexed age-window prunes on the tiny `sluice_heartbeat`/`sluice_target_metrics_history` tables; `sluice_keysets.bytes BLOB` (key material, far under 64 KB); `sluice_migrate_table_progress.progress TEXT` (per-table cursor JSON, the ADR-0082 fix itself — bounded small by design).

### 66. `sluice deploy-ddl` — ship one verbatim DDL to a PlanetScale production branch safely, as one command (operator demand 2026-07-15) — *S/M; extraction of the ADR-0162 expand leg; NOT raw deploy-request CRUD (pscale CLI owns that)* — **✅ SHIPPED v0.99.254 ([ADR-0165](../adr/adr-0165-deploy-ddl-and-control-table-bootstrap.md)): `sluice deploy-ddl` (shared `legRunner` extraction, freshness gate + safe-migrations preflight + tolerant poller reused, `--dry-run` zero-calls pinned) + `sluice control-tables ddl` (five-table bootstrap set via `ir.ControlTableDDLProvider`, single-sourced byte-identical with the engine's Ensure DDL) + Error-1105 classified at EVERY mysql control-table DDL site into the new coded `SLUICE-E-PS-DIRECT-DDL-BLOCKED` refusal, with the CDC applier's three ensures made detect-then-create so a bootstrapped `sync` actually starts**

**Why.** The ADR-0162 "Future scope" demand signal arrived: the differentiated piece is the SAFETY wrapper, not DR management. One command = dev branch → **the stale-base freshness gate** (the 2026-07-15 live finding: a fresh PS branch can silently propose REVERTING recent production schema; nothing in PlanetScale's own tooling guards this — sluice's gate is currently the only implementation anywhere) → apply verbatim DDL → deploy request → deploy → skip-revert finalize → cleanup. Replaces five hand-driven pscale commands plus a hazard the operator can't see.

**Consumers (the operator-named one is load-bearing):** (a) **one-time control-table bootstrap on a safe-migrations production branch** — with safe migrations ON, plain `backfill`/`sync`/`migrate` cannot create `sluice_migrate_state`/`sluice_cdc_state`/etc. via direct DDL (Error 1105; expand-contract ships its tables inside the expand DR, but the OTHER commands have no DR channel). `deploy-ddl` makes the bootstrap a documented one-liner; consider a companion `--emit-control-table-ddl` (or a `sluice control-tables ddl` printer) so the operator has the exact statements to ship. (b) Ad-hoc schema changes with the freshness guard. **Also in scope:** classify the Error-1105 "direct DDL is disabled" failure at every `EnsureControlTable` site into a coded, remedy-bearing refusal naming safe migrations + the deploy-ddl bootstrap path (today it surfaces as a raw driver error — the v248 detect-then-create means it only fires when the tables genuinely don't exist yet).

**How.** Extraction: `runDeployLeg` + `provisionFreshBranch` + the poller are shipped and generic; the command is CLI wiring + the DDL-printer + tests. Reuses `SLUICE-E-PS-{SAFE-MIGRATIONS-DISABLED,DEPLOY-REQUEST-FAILED,BRANCH-STALE-BASE}` unchanged.

### 83. Is a `rows.Scan` failure on the bulk-copy path a Bug-207 sibling? (raised 2026-07-26 by the new setErr gate) — **RESOLVED 2026-07-26: no. Answered empirically, and the answer is now a pin.**

**The question.** `row_reader.go`'s streaming loop has two error exits and only one classifies: `rows.Scan` parks `fmt.Errorf("mysql: scan: %w", err)` raw, while the trailing `rows.Err()` routes through `classifyApplierError`. Since an unclassified error is terminal to the pipeline, a mid-copy connection drop arriving at the Scan exit would make ADR-0109's per-table reconnect-and-resume unreachable — a routine blip aborting a multi-hour cold copy, which is the bulk-path shape of the Bug 207 class.

**How it was answered.** Not by reading. `TestRowReader_MidStreamConnectionDrop_IsClassifiedRetriable` (integration) seeds 262,144 rows, starts a real full-scan read, and `KILL`s the reader's own connection mid-stream from an admin session, identified by its query text. Ground truth on real MySQL 8.0: the drop surfaced after 2,498 rows at the **`rows.Err()` exit**, classified, as `mysql: rows iteration: invalid connection`, and satisfied `errors.As(err, &ir.RetriableError)`. ADR-0109's load-bearing header claim — that a mid-table drop "surfaces here as the rows-iteration error" — is therefore true against a real server, not merely by construction.

**Why the Scan exit is not on that path.** `database/sql` records a driver failure in `lasterr`; `Next()` then returns false and the loop exits, so `Scan` is never re-entered after a drop. The scan destinations are `*any`, which `convertAssign` cannot fail on. Classifying that exit would be unreachable code, so it stays as-is with the reason recorded in the gate's allowlist rather than left as an open exception.

**What the answer left behind.** The probe is kept as a permanent pin, not deleted after answering: ADR-0109's premise had no test, and the existing source-timeout test only pins that the session timeouts are *raised*. It carries the anti-vacuity checks the other Tier-1 gates do — it fails if the kill never lands, if the stream was fully drained before the kill (proving nothing), and if `Err()` is nil after a truncated read (a truncated copy reported as success is silent loss). Mutation-verified: stripping `classifyApplierError` from the `rows.Err()` exit turns it red with the exact diagnosis.

### 82. A DROPPED table permanently poisons a VStream resume position — warm resume is UNRECOVERABLE, not merely delayed (observed 2026-07-26) — *✅ SHIPPED v0.102.1 (`b9277738`). The terminal disposition was the fix named below: an unreplayable VStream window that exhausts its budget is now classified position-invalid rather than a generic give-up, so the streamer routes to the ADR-0093 cold-start re-snapshot (or refuses loudly under `--no-auto-resnapshot`). `isUnreplayableWindowError` (`internal/pipeline/streamer_retry.go:606`), pinned by `TestIsUnreplayableWindowError`.*

**Status note (2026-08-07):** this entry read OPEN for **thirteen releases** after it shipped — the worst stale-status instance found by the reconciliation sweep. It is worth naming because the entry is long and argues carefully for a fix that then landed almost verbatim, which is exactly the shape that makes a reader trust the header. The rest of this entry is preserved as the reasoning that produced the fix.

**⚠️ CORRECTION 2026-07-26 (the first filing above overstated the gap).** Reading the full log rather than the fatal line alone shows sluice **already recognises this shape and already prints the remedy**. The condition is caught by `isVStreamSchemaResolutionError` and classified RETRIABLE, and every retry logs:

```
source vstream could not resolve a table's schema for the replay position (likely a DDL
cutover, or the Vitess schema historian / track_schema_versions is off) — retrying from
the last position; if it persists, resume from current (cold-start) to skip the
unresolvable window
```

So "tells an operator neither the cause nor the way out" — as first filed — is **wrong**: the INFO lines state both, including the exact recovery. What actually happens is narrower:

1. The shape is classified retriable, which is CORRECT — the same wording covers a genuinely transient DDL-cutover window where the Vitess schema historian is catching up and the next attempt succeeds.
2. It retries the configured 8 attempts with backoff, each logging the remedy.
3. On exhaustion it exits with a **generic** `apply retry budget exhausted after N consecutive failures at position …`, which carries the underlying Vitess text but NOT the remedy the retry lines were printing. The operator's last message before exit is the least useful one.

**Revised finding, and the fix that follows.** The retry-then-exit behaviour is right for the transient case and wrong only for the permanent one, and the two are indistinguishable at first failure — which is exactly why retrying first is correct. What is missing is the *terminal* disposition: once this specific shape has exhausted its budget, the window is demonstrably unreplayable, which is semantically identical to a purged GTID. sluice already has machinery for that: classify as [ir.ErrPositionInvalid] and the streamer routes to the ADR-0093 cold-start re-snapshot (or, under `--no-auto-resnapshot`, refuses loudly with the recovery commands instead of re-copying). That would have auto-recovered the affected soak with no operator intervention, and it reuses a documented, already-shipped recovery path rather than inventing one.

The cheaper half — carry the remedy text into the terminal error so the last line an operator reads names the two exits — is worth doing regardless and is nearly free.

**What this does NOT change:** the underlying replay really is impossible (the Vitess-side plan cannot be built for a window referencing a dropped relation), the exposure is still ordinary (`DROP TABLE` on a keyspace-wide sync, the default shape), and the stream is still permanently down until someone acts. Only the characterisation of sluice's handling was overstated.

**What happened.** A table was created on a PlanetScale (Vitess 22) keyspace with a live keyspace-wide sync attached, written to, and then dropped. Every subsequent warm resume of that stream fails identically and exhausts its retry budget:

```
sluice: error: pipeline: apply retry budget exhausted after 8 consecutive failures
  at position "[{\"keyspace\":\"soak-mysql231\",\"shard\":\"-\",\"gtid\":\"MySQL56/…\"}]"
    failed to build table replication plan for table item80_regions
    failed to parse transaction payload's internal event
```

Reproduced three times across separate relaunches, hours apart: the stream starts, logs `warm resume from persisted position`, engages the apply lanes, then fails the same way and exits. **It is not a transient and it does not age out** — the persisted position points into a GTID window whose events reference a relation that no longer exists, so the plan can never be built for that window.

**Distinct from item 81, and worse.** Item 81 (a `CREATE TABLE` blanket-clearing the FIELD cache) is recoverable: a reconnect re-learns the shapes and the stream continues, which is why the fix there was to make the miss retriable. This one is **not recoverable by reconnect at all** — retrying is exactly what fails, eight times, before the budget gives up. The only exits are resume-from-current (skipping the window, and whatever real changes it contained) or a full cold start.

**Ownership is NOT established and must not be assumed.** The wording (`failed to build table replication plan`, `failed to parse transaction payload's internal event`) reads like Vitess/vstreamer text rather than sluice's own, which would make this a vtgate limitation that sluice merely surfaces. If so, the sluice-side work is classification and remedy rather than a fix: today it presents as a generic exhausted retry budget, which tells an operator nothing about the cause or the way out. A coded refusal naming the dropped table and the two recovery paths would be a large improvement even if the underlying replay is genuinely impossible.

**Severity, stated carefully.** Loud and zero-loss in the sense that nothing is silently mis-applied and the position is intact — but the stream is **permanently down** until an operator intervenes, and the intervention is either data-skipping or a full re-copy. `DROP TABLE` on a keyspace with a live sync is an ordinary operation, and keyspace-wide is the default stream shape (`--include-table` is opt-in), so exposure is not exotic. This is a worse operational outcome than either item 79 or item 81, both of which self-heal once classified correctly.

**How it was found (and the caveat that comes with it).** As collateral from the item-80 verification: a test table was created on a live soak's source, used, and dropped. So the trigger is confirmed, but the surrounding conditions were not controlled — a second stream was reading the same keyspace at the time, and the DDL sequence was CREATE → INSERT → DROP in close succession. Before designing a fix, reproduce deliberately on a disposable Vitess source: single stream, plain CREATE → INSERT → DROP, and establish whether the poison requires the writes, the drop, or both.

**Interim operator guidance worth documenting regardless of the fix:** if a table is dropped on a source with a live sync and the stream then refuses to resume, the position is unrecoverable for that window — resume from current if the gap is acceptable, otherwise cold start. Do not simply keep restarting; the retry budget will exhaust every time.

### 81. A mid-stream `CREATE TABLE` killed a keyspace-wide VStream with "row event without preceding FIELD event" (observed 2026-07-26) — *✅ ROOT-CAUSED + FIXED 2026-07-26: blanket FIELD-cache clear vs per-table FIELD re-emit; the miss is now retriable*

**✅ ROOT-CAUSED AND FIXED 2026-07-26 — the mechanism explains the one detail that looked wrong.** No cluster boot was needed: the production error itself is the proof. `dispatchDDL` (`internal/engines/mysql/cdc_vstream.go`) invalidates the FIELD cache with a **blanket `clear(r.fields)`** across every `(shard, table)` pair — deliberately conservative, and correct as a safety measure, because decoding rows against a stale column list after an `ALTER` is silent corruption. But **vtgate only re-emits a FIELD event for the table whose shape actually changed.** An unrelated table in the same keyspace has no reason to be re-announced, so its next ROW event finds an empty cache entry and trips the loud floor in `dispatchRow`.

That is exactly why the fatal named **`soak_events`** — a long-established table — rather than the table the DDL created. Any explanation that did not predict the wrong-table-in-the-error detail would have been the wrong explanation, which is what made this diagnosable by reading rather than by re-running.

**It also retires the uncontrolled variables.** The concurrent second stream and the `CREATE`+`INSERT` pairing were both noted as possibly load-bearing; neither is. A blanket cache clear plus continued writes to *any other* table in the keyspace is sufficient, and a keyspace-wide stream (the default — `--include-table` is opt-in) with a continuously-written table makes it near-certain rather than rare.

**Fix: classify the cache miss as RETRIABLE rather than terminal** (`isVStreamMissingFieldEventError` → `classifyReaderError`), matching the item-79 pattern. This is deliberately **not** a weakening of the floor: nothing decodes a row with guessed or stale metadata. A reconnect re-opens the stream at the last position, where the VStream protocol emits a FIELD event ahead of the first ROW event for every table in the filter, so the reader re-learns the *current* shape and resumes correctly. If a FIELD genuinely never arrives, the retry budget still exhausts loudly instead of looping forever. Pinned RED-before-GREEN on the verbatim production string plus the concurrent-COPY twin, with two near-misses (an unrelated "field event" mention, a generic row-event decode failure) asserted to stay terminal so the carve-out cannot widen, and an assertion that the miss is never routed to `ErrPositionInvalid` — that would turn a free reconnect into a full cold-start re-copy.

**Deliberately NOT done: narrowing the blanket clear.** Invalidating only the DDL's own table would avoid the miss entirely, but it requires attributing a DDL statement to a table, and the existing parser handles only the canonical `TRUNCATE` shapes — everything else already falls through to generic handling. Guessing wrong there means keeping a *stale* FIELD entry for an altered table, which is the silent-corruption outcome the blanket clear exists to prevent. Trading a loud, self-healing reconnect for a silent-corruption risk is the wrong direction, so the conservative clear stays and the recovery is what changed.

**What happened.** While verifying item 80, a new table was created on `soak-mysql231` — a PlanetScale (Vitess 22) source with a **live, keyspace-wide** sluice sync attached (`soak231`, no `--include-table`). The running stream first logged, correctly and harmlessly:

```
WARN postgres: applier: skipping CDC event for unknown target table op=insert schema=public table=item80_regions
```

and then **died**:

```
sluice: error: pipeline: source cdc reader:
mysql/vstream: row event for "-/soak-mysql231.soak_events" without preceding FIELD event
```

Note the table named in the fatal error is **`soak_events` — the pre-existing table the soak has been replicating for days**, not the newly created one. So the DDL did not merely introduce an unknown table; it disturbed FIELD-event sequencing for an **established** table in the same keyspace.

**Why this is worth fixing rather than filing as operator error.** "Someone creates a table while a continuous sync is running" is an ordinary thing to happen in production, not a contrived test condition. A keyspace-wide stream is also the DEFAULT shape — `--include-table` is opt-in — so most streams are exposed. The failure is **loud and zero-loss** (the position is intact and a warm resume recovers, as it did here), which puts it in the same family as item 79: a transient, recoverable protocol condition classified as terminal, taking down an unattended stream that a reconnect would have healed.

**Severity + exposure.** Loud, zero-loss, recoverable by restart. Exposure is broad (default stream shape, ordinary DDL) but the trigger is a schema event rather than a data event, so a stream on a static schema never meets it. The soak that hit this had been up cleanly for a day.

**Do NOT fix from this description alone.** The observation was a by-product of an unrelated experiment, so several variables were uncontrolled: a SECOND sluice stream (the item-80 test stream) was reading the same keyspace concurrently, and the DDL was `CREATE TABLE` + `INSERT` in quick succession. Any of those could be load-bearing. This is a three-phase-protocol candidate: reproduce deliberately on a disposable Vitess source (single stream, CREATE TABLE alone, then CREATE+INSERT, then with a concurrent second consumer) and establish which variable actually produces the missing FIELD event before writing a classifier change.

**Likely shape of the fix, once ground truth exists.** If a row event for a table whose FIELD event has not yet been seen is a *transient* sequencing artifact around a DDL boundary — the VStream will re-send a FIELD event — then the reader should treat it as retriable (the item-79 pattern: reconnect from the last position rather than exiting) or resynchronize the table's field cache, rather than failing the stream. If instead it indicates genuine decode ambiguity, the current loud refusal is right and the fix belongs in documentation plus a clearer error naming the DDL as the probable cause. The distinction matters: retrying a genuine decode ambiguity would risk misdecoding rows, which is exactly the silent-loss class the loud refusal exists to prevent.

**Related.** Item 79 (graceful GOAWAY classified terminal) is the same *class* — a recoverable source-side condition ending an unattended stream — and its fix landed in `internal/nettransient` with a per-call-site delegation, which is the shape a fix here would likely reuse.

### 80. The filtered move-IN/move-OUT crux family was RED on Vitess 21 & 22 — ✅ RESOLVED 2026-07-26: TEST-ONLY; the product is VERIFIED correct on Vitess 22 against a real PlanetScale database

**✅ PRODUCT VERIFIED CORRECT ON VITESS 22 (2026-07-26) — the convergence check the suite never had.** The reasoning above said the data outcome was *likely* fine but unverified, because these tests assert event SHAPES and nothing checked that the target actually converges. That gap is now closed by measurement, not inference. A scoped filtered sync (`--include-table` + `--where region='EU'`) was run from **`soak-mysql231`, a live PlanetScale database on Vitess 22**, into a throwaway local-rig Postgres target. Cold start landed exactly the in-scope rows {1,3}. Then a move-IN (id=2 US→EU), a move-OUT (id=1 EU→US), an out-of-scope INSERT (id=4 US) and an in-scope INSERT (id=5 EU) were applied together. **Source EU set {2,3,5}; target {2,3,5} — exact convergence.** The move-IN appeared, the move-OUT was removed, the out-of-scope row never arrived. sluice's filtered sync is correct on Vitess 22; the CI failures were the tests encoding v23+'s wire shape as the contract.

**Fixed in the tests, not the product.** `assertMoveIn` / `assertMoveOut` now accept EITHER shape — an `ir.Update` carrying both images (v23+) or the pre-classified `ir.Insert` / `ir.Delete` (v21/v22) — while the stronger both-images assertions stay gated behind `expectedScopeTransitionShape()` to the majors that can satisfy them, so the F-P1 before-image guarantee remains pinned where it applies. The warm-resume collector also terminated only on an `ir.Update`, so on ≤22 it drained past a correctly-delivered move-OUT and timed out; it now terminates on the DELETE form too. The pre-classified move-IN is still checked for an IN-SCOPE after-image, so a genuine out-of-scope leak would still fail the test.

**⚠️ Cost of the verification, recorded honestly.** Creating the test table in `soak-mysql231` disturbed the live soak. That stream is keyspace-wide (no `--include-table`), so it saw the new table's events (`skipping CDC event for unknown target table`) and then **died** on `mysql/vstream: row event for "-/soak-mysql231.soak_events" without preceding FIELD event` — a mid-stream `CREATE TABLE` breaking FIELD-event sequencing for an EXISTING table. The soak was relaunched and warm-resumed from its persisted position; all test artifacts were removed. The blast radius was mis-predicted (the stream's scope was assumed to be its cold-start table set; it is not), which is the process lesson. That crash shape is filed as **item 81** — it is a plausible real-world event and it was reached by accident rather than by design.

**What.** `TestVitessClusterFilteredSync` and `TestVitessClusterFilteredSyncWarmResume` fail on **Vitess v21.0.6 and v22.0.4** and pass on **v23.0.4, v24.0.1, and latest**. The weekly `vitess-version-matrix.yml` schedule run is where this surfaces.

**Timeline — it is a regression, not a permanent gap.** Scheduled runs: 2026-06-21 ✅, 06-28 ✅, 07-05 ✅, **07-12 ✅**, **07-19 ❌**, 07-26 ❌. So it broke in the **07-12 → 07-19** window, whose delta is the v0.99.279–283 collation / filtered-sync arc (PAD-SPACE `--where` evaluation A1/A2, the float-ordering B1 fix, the A0 client-side COPY fallback, and the F-P1 VStream **warm-resume server-side filter push-down**). F-P1 is the most suspicious single change, because the warm-resume test is one of the two failing and the push-down is exactly the thing whose server-side support could differ by Vitess major.

**Observed shapes (v21.0.6, 2026-07-26).** Not a boot or infra failure — the cluster comes up and the *cold* filtered COPY passes:
- `filtered COPY PASS: only in-scope EU rows {1,3} landed; out-of-scope US row 2 excluded` — the copy leg is fine.
- then `out-of-scope INSERT id=11 (US) leaked into the filtered stream: ir.Row{"id":11, "payload":"moved-in-11", "region":"EU"}` and `no ir.Update on regions for id=11 among 3 changes (ir.Insert,ir.Insert,ir.Delete)` — the CDC leg delivers a **different event shape** than the crux expects for a move-IN.
- Warm-resume fails differently: `timed out after 1m30s waiting for the move-OUT update id=20`, preceded by the alive-but-idle WARN (`heartbeats flowing … NO change events for 30s`). A connected, healthy-looking stream delivering nothing.

**✅ DIAGNOSED 2026-07-26 — both failures are ONE root cause, and it is an event-SHAPE difference by Vitess major, not a data defect.** On Vitess >=23 a row crossing the filter boundary is delivered as an `ir.Update` carrying BOTH images (before out-of-scope, after in-scope, or the reverse). On **v21/v22 the same transition arrives pre-classified as a plain `ir.Insert` (move-IN) or `ir.Delete` (move-OUT)** — vtgate appears to resolve the scope change server-side rather than handing the client both images. That single difference explains every symptom:

- The `out-of-scope INSERT id=11 (US) leaked` assertion fires on a row whose payload is `region: EU` — i.e. it is NOT a US row leaking, it is the move-IN arriving as an INSERT of the AFTER image. Assertion (B) rejects any `ir.Insert` for id=11, so the correctly-scoped move-IN trips it.
- The very next assertion, `no ir.Update on regions for id=11`, is the same event seen from the other side.
- Warm resume is the same thing again: `collectResumedRegionChanges` drains *until it observes an `ir.Update`* for id=20, and on <=22 the move-OUT is an `ir.Delete`, so it never returns and times out at 90s. The `alive … NO change events for 30s` WARN is the idle window AFTER the three events already arrived, not a stalled stream.

**Product-correctness assessment — reasoned, NOT yet verified, and the distinction matters.** If vtgate <=22 delivers move-IN as INSERT and move-OUT as DELETE, sluice applies them verbatim and the target converges to the same state `route()` would have computed from an Update pair; the before-image guard (`SLUICE-E-WHERE-CDC-BEFORE-IMAGE`) simply never engages because there is no Update to be missing an image. So the data outcome is very likely correct on both majors. **But that is an inference from event shapes, not a measurement:** these tests assert SHAPES, so nothing in the suite actually checks that the target converges on <=22. Do not close this as test-only until convergence is observed.

**Note the client/server skew.** The suite runs sluice's vendored `vitess.io/vitess v0.24.1` client against v21/v22 servers, so this may be new-client-against-old-server skew rather than a pure server behavior change. Worth distinguishing, because it decides whether the fix belongs in the test or in a documented version floor.

**Recommended fix — assert convergence, not shape.** The durable repair is to make the crux assert the TARGET STATE after the transition (row present after move-IN, absent after move-OUT) rather than the event kind that produced it. That is what the guarantee actually is, it is what an operator cares about, and it would be robust across both vtgate behaviors instead of encoding one major's shape as the contract. Keep a shape assertion if desired, but as a version-gated sub-check rather than the load-bearing one.

**Why nobody noticed for a week.** `vitess-version-matrix.yml` is **not** one of the six required checks; its only blocking incarnation is the `filtered-tag-gate` job, which runs on tag pushes **pinned to `VITESS_TAG: v24.0.1`** — a version that passes. So the tag-time gate is structurally blind to a regression that only affects 21/22, and the weekly run that does see it blocks nothing. **Gate proposal:** either promote the older-version cells to something that blocks (at minimum, a loud failure notification on the weekly), or state explicitly in `docs/production-readiness.md` which Vitess majors are supported so a red cell on an unsupported version is a documented non-event rather than an ambiguous one. Today it is ambiguous, which is the worst of both.

**Not release-blocking by the documented gates** — the six required checks are green on `3f510cfa`, and the tag gate's pinned v24.0.1 passes — but that is a statement about the gates, not about the behavior.

### 79. A graceful server-side GOAWAY kills a VStream CDC stream instead of reconnecting (observed live 2026-07-24) — *✅ FIXED 2026-07-25: `nettransient.IsGracefulGoAway` (conjunction: GOAWAY + `ErrCode=NO_ERROR`) consulted by the VStream reader classifier before its terminal-on-InvalidArgument arm; RED-before-GREEN pinned on the verbatim production string, with every error-carrying GOAWAY pinned terminal*

**What happened.** The `soak231` soak (PS-MySQL → PS-Postgres, running v0.100.0) exited on:

```
sluice: error: pipeline: source cdc reader: mysql/vstream: recv: rpc error:
code = InvalidArgument desc = protocol error: incomplete envelope:
http2: server sent GOAWAY and closed the connection;
LastStreamID=1, ErrCode=NO_ERROR, debug="graceful_stop"
```

**Why this is a defect, not a legitimate refusal.** `GOAWAY` with **`ErrCode=NO_ERROR`** and **`debug="graceful_stop"`** is HTTP/2's *polite drain*: the server is telling the client "this connection is going away, reconnect" — the textbook retriable condition. It is almost certainly the same PlanetScale edge-pod rotation documented in item 75(a) (connector series churning within hours), i.e. routine platform maintenance, not an error at all. But the transport failure surfaces wrapped in gRPC **`InvalidArgument`**, and `classifyReaderError` (`internal/engines/mysql/reader_errors.go`) deliberately treats `InvalidArgument` as TERMINAL on the stated reasoning that "the operator's request is wrong, and retrying would mask it". That reasoning is right for a genuine `InvalidArgument` and wrong here: the code describes the *envelope-parse* failure, not the operator's request.

**Confirmed absent:** `grep -ri "goaway"` over the whole tree returns nothing — no GOAWAY handling exists anywhere, and `internal/nettransient`'s matcher set does not cover it either. So every VStream consumer is exposed, and the exposure scales with how often the platform rotates edge pods.

**Severity.** LOUD and ZERO-LOSS — the stream exits with a clear error and the persisted position is intact, so a warm resume loses nothing. But an unattended continuous sync **stays down** until someone restarts it, which is precisely the failure mode continuous replication exists to avoid. Two of this session's soak outages trace to it.

**Fix shape.** Classify the graceful-GOAWAY signature as transient and let the existing reactive-resume path reconnect. Match on the *conjunction* — a GOAWAY carrying `ErrCode=NO_ERROR` (and/or `debug="graceful_stop"`) — never on the bare word `GOAWAY`, because a GOAWAY with a real error code (`PROTOCOL_ERROR`, `ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM`) is a different animal and must stay terminal. Home it in `internal/nettransient` beside the existing shapes rather than in the MySQL reader, since the same drain can hit any gRPC/HTTP2 consumer (the ADR-0111/Bug-203 precedent of one shared matcher with per-engine delegation). Pin RED-before-GREEN with the verbatim error string above, plus a negative control proving a non-NO_ERROR GOAWAY still exits terminal.

**Gotcha.** `debug="graceful_stop"` is a *vtgate*-chosen debug string, not a protocol constant — do not make it load-bearing on its own. `ErrCode=NO_ERROR` is the standards-defined part and should carry the decision; treat the debug text as corroborating evidence only.

### 78. Peer-tool review follow-ups — one pre-registered landmine, one unverified sibling, one gate (filed 2026-07-24) — *not started; three small independent items*

Three residuals from reviewing a peer Postgres-migration tool's recent fixes and a third-party Vitess CDC connector's known-issue list against sluice. Most of both lists was already closed in sluice or structurally inapplicable (sluice binds parameters rather than building SQL literal text, so the float-precision-in-WHERE class cannot arise; the shard-list `FailedPrecondition` and the retry-forever-on-a-dead-cursor pathologies are already fixed and pinned; sequence priming at cutover is already more thorough). These three are what survived.

- **(a) ✅ DONE 2026-07-25 — the predicate is in, version-gated.** The FK read now excludes Postgres internal per-partition FK clones via a new pure helper fkParentOnlyExpr(version) (schema_reader.go) keyed on pgVersionConstraintParentID = PG 11. **A compatibility trap surfaced while landing it and is worth recording:** conparentid exists only on PG 11+, sluice floor is PG 10 (pgoutput CDC), and populateForeignKeys runs against EVERY PG source — the Bug 100 refusal covers partitioned tables, not partition-free ones — so the obvious unconditional AND con.conparentid = 0 would have 42703-ed the entire foreign-key read on a live supported version. Gated exactly like the C3 UNIQUE-attribute reads (constant true below PG 11, which is exact rather than degraded since no such server can produce clones), with a unit version matrix. Still unreachable-by-design today (partitions are refused), so this remains pre-registered insurance for when partition support ships — but it is now insurance that cannot itself break anything.
- **(b) ✅ VERIFIED 2026-07-25 — the answer SPLITS BY FLAVOR, which is exactly why it could not be inherited from the Postgres one. MySQL binlog: NO BUG. VStream (PlanetScale/Vitess): CONFIRMED SILENT DIVERGENCE on pre-existing rows.** Adding a column with a default emits **no row-level events for existing rows** — the engine backfills logically without writing per-row changes — so the only thing that can keep the target consistent is the forwarded DDL carrying the DEFAULT. Whether it does depends entirely on which CDC flavor built the IR:
  - **MySQL binlog source — consistent, no action.** The binlog flavor re-reads `information_schema` at a DDL boundary via `loadTableSchema` (`internal/engines/mysql/schema_reader.go`), whose SELECT list includes **`column_default`**. So the CDC IR column carries `Default`, `SchemaWriter.AlterAddColumn` renders it through `emitColumnDef` → `emitDefault`, and the target's own `ADD COLUMN … DEFAULT 5` backfills its pre-existing rows to 5 exactly as the source did. (Note `AlterAddColumn` force-sets `Nullable=true` per Bug 83, but deliberately leaves `Default` untouched — so the nullability wart does not defeat this.)
  - **VStream source — DIVERGES.** The VStream flavor projects its IR from the vtgate `FieldEvent` via `projectVStreamFields` (`internal/engines/mysql/field_to_ir.go`), which populates **only `Name`, `Type`, and `Nullable` — there is no `Default`, because the FIELD wire never carries one.** The forwarded statement therefore lands as `ADD COLUMN c … NULL` with no DEFAULT: **source pre-existing rows hold the default, target pre-existing rows hold NULL, and no row event will ever reconcile them.** Newly-changed rows are unaffected (CDC carries explicit values), so the divergence is confined to rows that existed at the moment of the ALTER — and is invisible to a row-count check, surfacing only under a value-comparing `verify`.
  - **This is the same defect class a third-party Vitess CDC connector documents as its "ADD COLUMN backfill gap"** — arrived at independently from sluice's own code. The shared root cause is that Vitess's FieldEvent is a *decode* contract, not a *catalog* contract; it carries what is needed to interpret bytes, not what is needed to reproduce DDL. This is the same lesson as ADR-0179's Postgres finding stated for a different transport: **a shape classifier can only classify what the change stream carries.**

  **✅ (i) LOUD-NOT-SILENT SHIPPED 2026-07-25.** refuseComputedDefaults now WARNs when the in-band CDC IR carried no DEFAULT but a source probe finds one — naming the table, the column, the source default text, and two remedies (SET DEFAULT + backfill UPDATE, or re-run with --backfill-added-column). Gated so it fires only when something is genuinely lost: a column with no source default, or one whose default the projection DID carry (the MySQL binlog case), stays quiet — pinned in all three directions, because a WARN on every forwarded ADD COLUMN would be noise and stop being read.

  **What landing it revealed — the faithful carry is much cheaper than estimated.** sluice ALREADY probes the source for the canonical DEFAULT text (defaultProber, built from the source SchemaReader by newSourceDefaultProber; Bug 90 added it because neither pgoutput nor the binlog TableMapEvent carries the field). refuseComputedDefaults reads that probe into a LOCAL variable, uses it for the ADR-0058 §2a volatility classification, and then DISCARDS it — the resolved default is never written back onto the column, so AlterAddColumn still emits without it. Option (ii) is therefore not "re-read information_schema at the boundary" (that already happens, on demand, once per ADD COLUMN) but merely "stop throwing the answer away". **Residual risk that kept it out of this change:** the raw-probe path returns ir.DefaultExpression carrying VERBATIM source text (PG raw column_default), and emitting that against a different target dialect is exactly ADR-0179 territory. A safe first cut would carry only ir.DefaultLiteral values — constants translate trivially — and keep WARNing for expression-shaped defaults. Also note the volatility classifier already REFUSES computed defaults, so everything reaching this point is non-volatile, which materially bounds the risk.

  **Prior analysis, retained.** Option (iii) do-nothing was and remains not recommended: the silence is what violated the loud-failure tenet, not the missing default itself — which is why (i) shipped first and independently of whether (ii) ever does.
- **(c) Gate — pin the evaluator-facing doc against its source of truth.** Bug 206 (found by the v0.100.0 regression cycle) was `docs/production-readiness.md` still claiming in-scope `oid`/`lo` columns "copy as plain integers" when the binary refuses — the exact claim v0.100.0's own release notes corrected, while `docs/type-mapping.md` already carried the corrected wording. Two shipped docs contradicted each other and the **wrong one was the front door evaluators are pointed at**. Independently, the peer tool shipped a fix for a diagnostic command that had drifted from the real code path and reported "0 parts" for every table — the same class: a surface whose only job is to describe behavior, drifting from the behavior. Extend the existing doc-sync test family (the `TestMetricsDocSync` pattern) to pin `production-readiness.md`'s Known-Limitation claims against the authoritative doc/code, so this class goes stale-loud instead of needing a regression cycle to notice.

### 77. Within-table chunking is blind to row WIDTH — a wide-row/TOAST-heavy table below `--bulk-parallel-min-rows` copies single-stream (filed 2026-07-24) — *not started; perf + CDC-lag class, no data-correctness impact*

**Why.** sluice decides within-table chunking on **estimated ROW COUNT alone**: `shouldParallelChunk` (`internal/pipeline/migrate_parallel.go`) compares `migcore.ApproximateRowCount` (PG: `pg_class.reltuples`, with the exact-`COUNT(*)` fallback on the never-analyzed sentinel) against `--bulk-parallel-min-rows` (auto default **80,000**, dialled down to a 10,000 floor on many-table schemas). The ADR-0123 finer-chunk-count derivation is likewise row-count-driven. **Row count is a proxy for copy work, and the proxy breaks when rows are wide** — Postgres TOAST is the extreme case, but a MySQL source with large `BLOB`/`JSON`/`TEXT` columns has the same shape. A table of 50k rows × 20 MB of out-of-line data is ~1 TB of actual transfer and sits *below* the 80k threshold, so it copies with a **single reader** while the parallel budget goes unused. The failure is invisible: the copy simply takes hours, and nothing in the log says "this table declined chunking because it looked small."

**Prior art, same class from the opposite direction.** pgcopydb sizes its split decision on **heap `relpages`** and ignores TOAST entirely, so a small-heap/huge-TOAST table never trips its `--split-tables-larger-than` threshold and runs as a single unsplit part. Different proxy (bytes-of-heap vs rows), identical outcome (`[1/1]` on the largest table in the migration), and their reported real-world impact was multi-hour-to-multi-day single-stream copies. Worth stating plainly because it is the argument for fixing the *class*: **any single scalar proxy for "how much work is this table" has a shape that defeats it.**

**Second-order effect — this is not purely a throughput knob.** A cold copy that runs long delays the snapshot→CDC handoff, so the CDC start position is further back and the stream begins its life with a correspondingly larger backlog to burn down. On a source with tight binlog/WAL retention that widens the window where a slow copy can push the resume position out of reach — the retention-window hazard already documented for DigitalOcean (~13–16 min) and Vultr MySQL (~10 min, no knob). So a chunking miss on a wide-row table is a *reachability* risk on those platforms, not just a slow migration.

**What.** Make the chunk decision width-aware rather than replacing the row-count signal:
- **Cheapest correct signal (PG):** `pg_table_size(oid)` (heap **+** TOAST, excludes indexes) — or `pg_total_relation_size` if index build is to be considered — divided by `reltuples` gives an average row width with one extra catalog lookup and no scan. Note sluice currently reads **no** size catalog function anywhere; this would be the first. MySQL's sibling is `information_schema.TABLES.AVG_ROW_LENGTH` (+ `DATA_LENGTH`), with the usual InnoDB-estimate caveat, and it does **not** account for off-page LOB storage faithfully — so treat it as a floor, not a truth.
- **Decision shape:** chunk when `rows ≥ minRows` **OR** `estimated_bytes ≥ minBytes` (a new sibling threshold), so the existing row-count path is unchanged and the byte path only ever *adds* chunking. That ordering matters — it cannot regress a schema that chunks correctly today.
- **Loud when it matters:** the existing "parallel copy not applicable; using single-reader path" INFO already names its reason. A table that declines chunking on row count while carrying a large byte estimate should say so explicitly, so the operator can see the one table that will dominate the run.
- **Per-table override** as the escape hatch for the shape no heuristic catches.

**Gotchas.** (1) `reltuples`/`AVG_ROW_LENGTH` are estimates; a never-analyzed PG table yields the sentinel and the exact-count fallback already handles rows but not bytes — decide what `pg_table_size` on a never-analyzed table means (it is real on-disk size, so it is actually the *more* reliable of the two). (2) Backup's within-table sweep (ADR-0149) shares this threshold via `--bulk-parallel-min-rows`, so a fix should reach both modes or explicitly declare the gap per `docs/dev/perf-parity-matrix.md`. (3) Don't lower the global row threshold as a workaround — it over-splits ordinary narrow tables, which is the tradeoff the peer tool's own thread rejected.

**Two refinements from the peer tool's follow-up fix (their PR #50, open at time of writing) — both change how this should be built.**

- **Make the DECISION metric and the COUNT metric move together, or this bug reappears in a subtler form.** Their actual defect was not "ignores TOAST" but a *mismatch between two size metrics inside one feature*: the split **decision** compared `pg_table_size()` (heap **+** TOAST, correctly width-aware), while the part-**count** calculation used `relpages` (heap only). A TOAST-heavy table therefore **passed the split gate and then computed one part** — still a serialized copy, now with the gate falsely reporting it had been handled. sluice does **not** have this mismatch today: the decision (`shouldParallelChunk` vs `minRows`) and the count (ADR-0123's `clamp(ceil(estRows/within-threshold), …)`) are *both* row-count-based, so they are at least consistent. That consistency is the thing to preserve — when the byte-aware signal is added it must reach **both** call sites, or sluice recreates their exact bug with a table that clears the new byte gate and is then split into one chunk by the untouched row-based count.
- **Splitting by heap-page range parallelizes TOAST reads for free — so chunks do not need to be byte-uniform.** Their stated mechanism: a CTID range scan reads heap rows and *detoasts each row on the fly*, so dividing the heap page range divides the TOAST fetch work with it. This dissolves what looked like the hard part of this item (that row-count-equal ranges over a 20 MB-per-row table are not byte-equal): the out-of-line bytes follow their heap row, so an even heap-page split is already an even work split. Their caps are worth copying wholesale — cap parts at an explicit max, **cap parts at `relpages`** (never create more ranges than there are heap pages), and distribute heap pages evenly.

**Related gap this surfaced — keyless / non-chunkable-PK tables get NO within-table parallelism at all.** `CanParallelChunkTable` refuses outright when `table.PrimaryKey == nil || len(table.PrimaryKey.Columns) == 0` ("table has no primary key"), and both shipped strategies need an orderable PK: `StrategyMinMaxDivide` (single integer PK) and `StrategyKeysetSample` (other orderable / composite PK). So a large **keyless** table — or one whose PK is non-orderable, or sluice-injected — always copies single-stream on every engine. The peer tool's CTID path exists for exactly this case: `ctid` is a *physical* row locator that needs no key at all, so a keyless heap still splits into page ranges. This is PG-only (MySQL/SQLite have no ctid analogue; MySQL's hidden `DB_ROW_ID` is not exposed), which makes it a per-engine optional surface rather than an IR-level concept — the same shape as the existing optional reader capabilities (`RangeBoundsQuerier`, `KeysetSampler`). Worth sizing separately from the width fix above; it is the difference between "wide tables under-parallelize" and "keyless tables do not parallelize."

### 76. PS-PG walsender-reap measurement — the v0.100.0 55006-budget rationale was a MISDIAGNOSIS; two doc corrections owed (measured 2026-07-24) — *✅ CLOSED 2026-07-24: findings recorded; BOTH follow-ups done — (a) doc corrections, (b) `wal_sender_timeout` confirmed 60s across every PS-PG tier, so the 5-min budget stands unchanged*

**What was measured.** After v0.100.0 shipped the 55006 slot-active retry as a 5-minute wall-clock budget "because PS-PG on Postgres 18 holds a closed reader's walsender active 10+ minutes," a controlled measurement (PS-PG PG17 [17.10] vs PG18 [18.4], both PS_10; raw pgconn/pglogrepl harness whose clean close is byte-identical to sluice's `closeReplConnGraceful` → PG `Terminate`) **disproved that causal story.** Full report: `workspace/pg17-pg18-walsender-reap-2026-07-24.md`. Reap latency by disconnect mode (PG17 and PG18 **identical**): clean graceful close (= sluice's real path) = **sub-2s**; abrupt socket/TCP-FIN close = sub-second; truly silent vanish (no Terminate, no FIN — network partition / host death) = **60s (= `wal_sender_timeout`, which is 60s on both tiers)**.

**Conclusions (accurate record):** (1) **NOT PG18-specific** — PG17 and PG18 are indistinguishable; the reap is governed by disconnect observability + `wal_sender_timeout`, not the major version. (2) **A real user essentially never hits a loud 55006 on restart** — sluice's clean close reaps sub-2s, so a normal stop→restart is clear; even a crash with a TCP FIN is sub-second; only a truly silent client vanish waits the 60s timeout, comfortably inside the 5-min budget. So the answer to "how easily could a user encounter this" is: **they can't, at default settings.** (3) The **5-minute budget is still correct** and the raise from the old ~31.5s was still justified — the 60s silent-vanish case alone would have marginally exceeded 31.5s — but the *justification is the 60s `wal_sender_timeout` case, not a mythical 10-min PG18 hold.* (4) **The >12-min hold observed in psverify was NOT reproduced and is NOT the walsender-reap path** (12 min ≫ the 60s ceiling at default timeout); its true cause is unexplained — most likely an artifact of the psverify suite's shared-slot concurrent structure (which the unique-name test fix independently resolved), NOT reap latency a user would see.

**Two cheap follow-ups owed:**
- **(a) Doc corrections — ✅ DONE (2026-07-24).** The measured story now lives in the code: `ir.SlotActiveReapBudget`'s doc comment states disconnect-observability (not the PG major version) as what governs the reap, names the three measured modes, and explicitly flags that it corrects the story the const shipped with in v0.100.0; the two consumers that repeated ">90s on PG18" — `internal/pipeline/decommission.go` and both `planetscale_verify_test.go` timeout consts — now cite the 60s `wal_sender_timeout` ceiling and label the one unreproduced >90s CI observation as insurance, not a measured floor. The forward correction for operators is staged in `CHANGELOG.md` under `[Unreleased] → Corrected` and rides the next release's notes. The published v0.100.0 CHANGELOG entry and `docs/releases/release-notes-v0.100.0.md` are deliberately left as shipped — a forward correction, not a retroactive banner, because nothing about the behavior was wrong.
- **(b) `wal_sender_timeout` across PS tiers — ✅ DONE (measured 2026-07-24). Verdict: `wal_sender_timeout` is 60s on EVERY PS-PG shape measured, and PlanetScale does not set it at all — so the 5-minute budget stays adequate with ~5× headroom. NO change owed; it does not need raising and does not need to become operator-configurable.** Five throwaway PS-PG databases spanning the axes that could plausibly carry a different config — `PS-10-AWS-X86` (smallest), `PS-160-AWS-X86` (largest **non-metal** tier, 16× the vCPU/RAM; everything larger is a metal SKU), `M1-10-AWS-ARM-D-METAL-10` (**metal** = different storage architecture, **HA `--replicas 2`**, aarch64), a **GCP**-region DB (different cloud), and `PS-160-AWS-X86` on **PG 17.10** (large tier × older major — the earlier report only had PG 17 on the smallest tier). All five: `SHOW wal_sender_timeout` = **`1min`** / `pg_settings.setting` = `60000` ms; `wal_receiver_timeout` 60000 ms; `max_replication_slots` 20; `max_wal_senders` 10; `wal_level` logical; `idle_replication_slot_timeout` 0 (PG 18 only, i.e. disabled); `max_slot_wal_keep_size` -1. **The decisive evidence is `pg_settings.source`: for `wal_sender_timeout` it is `default` on all five** — i.e. Postgres's compiled-in `boot_val`, set by PlanetScale *nowhere*. That generalizes past the five shapes sampled, because PlanetScale demonstrably manages the replication GUCs it *does* care about through the two channels that would show up here (`command line` for `wal_level`/`max_wal_senders`/`max_replication_slots`, `configuration file` for `hot_standby_feedback`/`max_slot_wal_keep_size`/`synchronous_commit`) — a tier-dependent override would have had to appear as one of those. Nothing was near 5 min and nothing was disabled (`0` = infinite). Only cross-tier difference in the whole sweep: **OS-level** TCP keepalives on GCP (`tcp_keepalives_idle` 300s / interval 60s / count 5) vs AWS (7200 / 75 / 9) — host-kernel defaults, not PG config, and if anything they make a dead peer *more* likely to be noticed before the walsender timeout fires. Consequence for the record: the silent-vanish reap ceiling is 60s **fleet-wide**, so the >12-min psverify observation is even more firmly *not* the reap path — strengthening conclusion (4) above. Full data (per-tier matrix, verbatim `pg_settings` rows, teardown record) appended to `workspace/pg17-pg18-walsender-reap-2026-07-24.md` § "wal_sender_timeout across PS-PG tiers (item 76b)". All five databases were deleted immediately after their values were read; the org listing was verified back to its exact 6-database pre-state (zero `sluice-wst-*` orphans).

### 75. `metrics-watch` fleet/informational observability — egress metric + org-wide auto-discovery + a persistent-storage sink (operator-flagged 2026-07-24) — *(b) + (c) IMPLEMENTED 2026-07-24 ([ADR-0180](../adr/adr-0180-metrics-watch-fleet-and-sample-sink.md), SHIPPED v0.102.0); (a) still BLOCKED on a question to PlanetScale*

**Status of the three parts.**
- **(a) egress metric — NOT built, still blocked.** See the ⚠️ preamble below: live measurement falsified the filed plan and the family choice is unresolved. (b)/(c) were shaped so an egress field lands later as further nullable record fields + one more gauge family, without reshaping either.
- **(b) org-wide auto-discovery — IMPLEMENTED.** Omitting `--planetscale-metrics-db` watches the whole org; `--include-database`/`--exclude-database`/`--fleet-concurrency` scope and pace the fan-out. **The filed `ListDatabases`/`ListBranches` route was NOT taken** — probed live, the existing per-org metrics SD call already returns one element per database+branch WITH its signed scrape URL, so discovery is one control-plane call regardless of org size and needs no wider credential (rationale in ADR-0180 §Decision 1). The SD document carries **no engine label** and a real org is mixed, so each target's metric-name table is resolved from marker-metric presence in its own exposition.
- **(c) persistent-storage sink — IMPLEMENTED.** `--sink-file` (rotating JSONL) and `--sink-http` (generic JSON push) in the new `internal/telemetrysink`, advisory + failure-isolated like the `--notify-*` sinks, with the record treated as a codec (null-not-zero, loud UTF-8 / non-finite refusal, exact >2^53 integers, a reflection ratchet over the schema). Parquet was considered per the note below and rejected — it wants schema declaration + file finalisation, which fits an export, not an append-per-minute stream.

**Two follow-ups the live fleet pin surfaced (both PRE-EXISTING, neither introduced by (b)/(c)):**
1. **PG storage reads `n/a` on the live endpoint — in single-database mode too.** `planetscale_volume_*` is emitted per-pod labelled `planetscale_role="primary"|"replica"` (NOT `planetscale_tablet_type`, no `planetscale_container`), so `selectPrimaryValue`'s cascade sees three indistinguishable series and honestly refuses. No wrong number, but `--notify-storage-util` can never fire on a PG target. Fixing it means teaching the cascade the `planetscale_role` label AND deciding the reduction (the primary pod's volume vs the fullest volume across pods) — an (a)-shaped semantics question, so it is filed, not guessed.
2. **`postgresMetricNames`' "no PG replica-lag series" comment (probed 2026-06-23) is now FALSIFIED.** The live PG exposition carries `planetscale_postgres_replica_lag_seconds` (per-replica, 2 series), `planetscale_postgres_settings_max_connections` (3 series incl. one `role="primary"`), and `planetscale_edge_postgres_active_connections` (1 series). Wiring them needs the same per-series reduction decision as (1); do the two together.

**Why.** Today `metrics-watch` is shaped as a per-database ALERTER: it requires `--planetscale-metrics-db` (one database) + optional `--planetscale-metrics-branch` (defaults `main`), collects CPU/mem/storage/lag, and its only durable outputs are edge-triggered `--notify-*` alerts (Slack/webhook/SMTP) or a live Prometheus `/metrics` scrape endpoint (`--metrics-listen`). It opens no data-plane connection — only the PlanetScale control-plane metrics API. An operator surfaced a distinct use case (2026-07-24): general *informational* fleet telemetry — collect CPU/mem/storage/lag **and egress** for **every database (and branch) in a PlanetScale org**, on the regular polling cadence, and store it **persistently outside PlanetScale** so the operator can build their own portal/dashboard. Three gaps block that.

**What (three parts, each independently shippable):**
- **(a) Egress metric — ✅ RESOLVED 2026-07-24 by a billing-export cross-check: the metrics endpoint is NOT a usable egress source, and the invoice line items ARE. Build (a) against billing, not `/metrics` — but read the catch below first.** Ground truth came from an operator-supplied CSV export of the July invoice (532 rows) joined by `Public ID` against the JSON API's 225. Findings: **(1) Egress IS metered per database** — `Egress for branch 'main'`, with real units, on exactly the two PlanetScale **Postgres** databases and no Vitess/MySQL one (matching PlanetScale's pricing, which lists egress as a Postgres dimension only). **(2) The `planetscale_edge_postgres_bytes_*` counters are CORRECT counters that a point-in-time SUM cannot use.** Stated precisely, because an earlier revision of this entry wrongly called them "wrong": they are per-**edge-connector-pod** cumulative counters and they behave exactly as the Prometheus counter contract specifies — monotonically increasing, reset to zero on restart. Each surviving series is monotonic across scrapes (`p2cxl` 97,073 → 97,851; `b2v9f` 2,156 → 90,445). **The defect is in the reduction, not the metric.** The connector fleet ROTATES: across ~2 h on one branch, two of four public connectors disappeared (taking 163,207 + 33,172 B of counted traffic with them) and a new one appeared at zero, so the series count went 8 → 6 while the SUM crept 295,608 → 301,327. A sum of instantaneous counter values across an ephemeral series set is therefore not cumulative egress — it is "bytes accumulated by whichever pods happen to be alive at scrape time", which is why it sits a consistent ~70× under billed egress on two independent databases (`soak-pg231`: 819,162 B vs **62.6 MB** billed; `d1cdc-pg`: 295,608 B vs **20.8 MB**) and why it can appear frozen when departures offset gains. This is the ordinary counter-reset/series-churn problem that `rate()`/`increase()` exist to solve: a Prometheus *server* tracks each series independently and sums per-series increases, so it gets the right answer. sluice's distill is a point-in-time scraper and cannot — it would have to accumulate per-`connector_id` deltas across polls itself, detect series disappearance, and would *still* miss any pod that both appeared and vanished between two polls. So: do not wire these into a scalar egress gauge; billing remains the correct source. **(3) THE CATCH — the JSON API silently omits every `$0.00` line item.** The join is exact and unambiguous: 307 of 532 CSV rows are absent from the API, **100% of them `$0.00`**, while **0%** of the 225 returned rows are `$0.00` (0 rows appear in the API but not the CSV). The dropped categories are precisely the usage-based ones — `Pro storage (per byte)` ×165, `Development branch usage (per second)` ×75, `Storage (IOPS)` ×29, `Storage (Throughput)` ×29, `Storage (Volume)` ×6, **`Egress` ×2**, `backup` ×1. Egress is currently rated `$0.00 per 1 GB` on this account, so **the authoritative egress source is hidden by the API for exactly as long as egress is free** — and would silently start appearing if it ever becomes chargeable. A build that reads egress from the invoices API must therefore treat "no egress row" as *unknown*, never as *zero*, or it reports a confident 0 GB while the CSV shows tens of MB. That asymmetry is the whole design constraint for (a). (This also retires three successive wrong claims made during this investigation — that PlanetScale does not bill egress, that the metrics families merely needed the right reduction, and that the API response was complete evidence of anything. The API's silent `$0.00` filtering is what made all three look supported.) The original filing and the falsified plan follow, retained for the metric names and doc links.

  **✅ RECONSTRUCTION VALIDATED 2026-07-26 — egress IS derivable from the metrics endpoint, but ONLY with skew-tolerant accumulation; the textbook rule over-counts by up to 2.2x.** A ~34h collection (8,024 samples, 60s poll, 4 databases) bracketed by three invoice exports settled it. Over a CLEAN 24h billing window with no soak downtime, per-series accumulation reconstructs billed Egress to **0.98x (soak-pg231)** and **1.09x (d1cdc-pg)** — accurate enough to be useful. But the SAME data under the textbook Prometheus increase() rule (any decrease is a counter reset, add the new value) gives **1.39x and 2.24x**. The difference is not resets: this endpoint dips CONSTANTLY — 350 and 1,255 small decreases in that window — with the embedded sample timestamp still ADVANCING and several series dipping in the same scrape, i.e. backend-view skew, not counter restarts. A representative event is 901,858 -> 900,640, a 0.1% dip that the naive rule scores as a reset and credits with the ENTIRE 900,640 bytes. **What a build must therefore do:** accumulate against a per-series high-water mark (a dip contributes zero and does not lower the mark), and treat a decrease as a genuine reset only when it falls below a RELATIVE threshold of the previous high (50% worked here; 1 real reset per database per day survived that gate). The earlier 2.2x on soak-pg231 in the FIRST window is unrelated and already explained — that database was down 7.5h of an 18h billing window, so the metrics window covered only its active time. **Bottom line for the feature: the metrics endpoint is now a viable egress source, with the invoice Units remaining the authority; anyone implementing this must not reach for a stock increase() and assume it is right.**

  ⚠️ THE PLAN BELOW WAS FALSIFIED BY LIVE MEASUREMENT (2026-07-24) — see `workspace/ps-egress-metric-semantics-2026-07-24.md`. A Phase-A probe against the live `sluicesync` metrics endpoint (SD + signed scrape on the running `d1cdc-pg` / `d1cdc-mysql` soaks; read-only, nothing provisioned) found three things that invalidate the plan as written: **(1)** the counter-vs-gauge "open question" is answered trivially by the endpoint's own `# TYPE … counter` and was never the hard part; **(2)** the metric names below cross two different measurement layers — the filed pairing puts Postgres's *edge* counter against MySQL's *mysqld-side* counter, and the live MySQL surface carries **three** byte families (`planetscale_edge_mysql_*`, `planetscale_edge_mysql_http_*`, `planetscale_mysql_*`), not one; **(3)** decisively, **every `planetscale_edge_*` byte counter sat frozen across both a 180 s and a 900 s window on a database whose mysqld-side counter advanced +17.2 MB at a steady ~19 KB/s** — so the edge families are not a live-traffic signal on these branches at any cadence tested, and building on them would ship a metric that reads flat zero for a busy database. Two further findings for whoever builds this: the correct reduction is **family-dependent** (edge counters fan out across connectors/instances where each series is a disjoint slice → **sum**; the mysqld family is per-tablet with replicas moving *more* than the primary → **select primary**, since summing would roughly triple it), and the counter-reset hazard is **routine, not theoretical** — the HTTP family produced a real −8.7 MB decrease inside one 15-minute observation when a series dropped out of the set. **Recommended next step is a question to PlanetScale** (what the `planetscale_edge_*` byte counters meter, and why they can sit flat on an active branch) rather than more probing, because the answer decides both the family choice and whether PG has any per-branch egress source at all — PG exposes *no* mysqld-side equivalent, so if edge is unusable the honest outcome is the `metricNames` empty-field degrade (`*Known` stays false), never a wrong number. **Parts (b) and (c) below carry none of this uncertainty and can proceed independently.** The original filing follows, retained for its doc links: `metrics-watch` collects no network/egress series. The per-engine metric-name table (`metricNames` in `internal/planetscale/telemetry/distill.go` — `cpuUtilPct`/`memUtilPct`/volume/`replicaLagSec`) is built for exactly this: add sent/received fields + distill logic + a `sluice_target_{egress,ingress}_*` gauge/counter + an optional `--notify-egress-*` threshold. **Metric names** (from PlanetScale's Prometheus-metrics docs — Postgres: <https://planetscale.com/docs/postgres/monitoring/prometheus-metrics-postgres>, MySQL/Vitess: <https://planetscale.com/docs/vitess/integrations/prometheus-metrics>): Postgres = `planetscale_edge_postgres_bytes_sent_total` / `planetscale_edge_postgres_bytes_received_total` (the `planetscale_edge_postgres_*` family — note the per-engine table already keys MySQL off `planetscale_mysql_*` and PG off `planetscale_pods_*`/`planetscale_volume_*`, so this adds a new PG name-source); MySQL = `planetscale_mysql_bytes_sent_total` / `planetscale_mysql_bytes_received_total`. **The open question is VALUE SEMANTICS, and it must be confirmed against the live metrics API (we hold a `read_metrics_endpoints` token) before wiring distill:** the `_total` suffix is the Prometheus convention for a monotonic CUMULATIVE COUNTER, so "egress over an interval" needs `rate()`/`increase()` or successive-sample diffing in distill — UNLIKE the existing point-in-time util gauges — and whether the counter is instance-lifetime (resets on pod restart, so a diff can go negative and must be handled) or billing-aligned "month-so-far" (likely only in PlanetScale's BILLING API, not the metrics endpoint) determines whether this answers a "usage/cost" portal directly or only via a computed rate. So the distill for egress is counter-shaped (keep the raw total + expose a computed delta/rate), not a gauge copy — don't mislabel a counter as a gauge.
- **(b) Org-wide auto-discovery.** Relax the `--planetscale-metrics-db`-required model: with `--planetscale-org` alone, enumerate all databases + branches via the PS API (`ListDatabases(org)` / `ListBranches(org, db)` — small additions over the existing `internal/planetscale/api.Client.Get` + `/v1/organizations/{org}/databases/...` path helpers already used by ADR-0148), then fan-out the poll with **bounded concurrency** + `--include`/`--exclude` filters (a large org × branches is many metrics-API calls per interval — respect PS rate limits) and per-DB/branch labeling. Pairs naturally with the exporter mode: a `database`/`branch` gauge label → one Grafana dashboard for the whole org.
- **(c) Persistent-storage sink.** Today the only durable path is an EXTERNAL Prometheus scraping `--metrics-listen`; there is no built-in store, so "collect it and keep it for my own portal" requires standing up Prometheus. Add an opt-in persistent sink for the polled samples — a rotating local file (JSONL/CSV, or Parquet reusing the existing writer) and/or a generic HTTP push to a user endpoint/TSDB — advisory + failure-isolated like the `--notify-*` sinks (a dead sink is logged-and-swallowed, never stalls the poll). This is the piece that turns `metrics-watch` from an alerter (its `--quiet` + `--notify-*` shape) into a general fleet-telemetry collector.

**Gotchas.** (1) Egress: the metric NAMES are known (see (a)); the open item is VALUE SEMANTICS — cumulative counter (needs rate/diff, handle counter-reset-on-restart) vs point-in-time, and instance-lifetime vs billing "month-so-far" — confirm against the live API before choosing the distill + gauge/counter shape. (2) Org fan-out: bound concurrency + honor PS metrics-API rate limits; keep the 60s cadence default (the PS granularity). (3) The live stdout line gets noisy across dozens of DBs — org-wide mode should lead with the exporter + persistent-sink paths, not the single live line. (4) Persistent-sink format + rotation choice; keep it engine-neutral and failure-isolated. (5) This generalizes the feature's framing (alerter → collector); the CLI help + a sluicesync.com guide should reflect both use cases once (a)–(c) land. **The guide follows the capability, not before it.**
