Cell 3 was verified to produce the real mixed chain (`root=7 segments=[5 9]`). The backward-refusal cell also asserts the refusal does NOT blame the passphrase, key or decryption — a v0.103.x binary once told an operator holding the correct passphrase that it was wrong, and an operator handed the wrong cause rotates keys instead of upgrading. Weekly + dispatch, and the leg comment says to dispatch it by hand before tagging any release that bumps `BackupFormatVersion`.

**One caveat on that gate.** It has been run locally end to end (all four cells, real Postgres, 78s) but has never executed on Linux CI; the first scheduled or dispatched run is its real proof.

### 91. `schema add-table` reports the deferrable-key refusal under the wrong code and exit status (Bug 213, v0.104.0 regression cycle) — *✅ SHIPPED v0.104.1*

The deferrable-key preflight refusal reaches `schema add-table` with its full prose and remedy, but arrived wrapped as `SLUICE-E-BULKCOPY-TABLE-FAILED` with exit 1, where `sync start` and chain restore report the documented `SLUICE-E-TARGET-DEFERRABLE-KEY` with exit 3. An operator matching on the documented code — which is what the error-codes table tells them to do — would not have matched this one. The refusal was correct and the guidance intact; only the machine-readable half was wrong.

**Root cause, and why the fix is the class not the instance.** `migcore.WrapWithHint` matched on message SUBSTRINGS and then *unconditionally* built a fresh `sluicecode.CodedError`, discarding whatever code the error already carried. The bulk-copy catch-all matches `"pipeline: copy table"`, which is the prefix every copy caller wraps with — so ANY precisely-coded refusal travelling up through that path was re-coded, and because `CodedError.ExitCode()` derives from the code's class, the exit status changed with it. A more specific substring entry for the deferrable case would have fixed the one report and left the class open; instead `WrapWithHint` now returns an already-coded error untouched. Confirmed by mutation: disabling the guard reproduces `SLUICE-E-BULKCOPY-TABLE-FAILED` / exit 1 exactly.

The generic hint was not merely redundant in these cases but wrong — the bulk-copy catch-all tells the operator earlier tables are missing their secondary indexes, and a refusal by definition copied nothing. Pinned both directions in `hints_coded_passthrough_test.go`: a coded refusal survives intact, and a bare engine error still gets the phase code and remedy (the hint layer's actual job).
### 146. A cold copy whose target connection dies mid-`LOAD DATA` HANGS FOREVER — Bug 229 — *✅ SHIPPED v0.114.0. It was a CONCURRENCY CHUNK (the watchdog is a new goroutine over shared progress state), so CI's `-race` Integration job was required green before the tag — and was.*

**Implementation notes.**

**Both halves shipped, and the second one is why.** (1) A per-socket-WRITE deadline on every database connection, default 10 minutes, in the new `internal/netdeadline`. (2) An idle-progress copy WATCHDOG in `internal/pipeline` that warns, loudly and by name, when a copy lane has made no forward progress for 5 minutes.

**Why a write deadline and not a statement deadline.** The deadline bounds ONE socket write — how long the peer may go without draining a single packet — never how long a statement may take. That is the distinction that makes it safe: a legitimately slow-but-live target keeps its receive window opening, so every packet completes and the next one is re-armed fresh, and a four-hour `LOAD DATA` against a loaded server is untouched. A per-statement context deadline would have to exceed the slowest legitimate statement, which is unbounded; a write deadline only has to exceed the longest legitimate PAUSE.

**The value is 10 minutes, and it was chosen against the false-positive side.** ADR-0109's premise is that a PlanetScale storage auto-grow blocks the target's writes for seconds-to-MINUTES; during one the target stops consuming the socket, so an in-flight write parks on a perfectly healthy connection. A 15s deadline — the value the entry's own experiment used — would convert every storage grow into a copy abort, which is strictly worse than the hang it replaces. 10 minutes is ~10× the documented worst case and is deliberately the SAME number as `sourceReadSessionTimeoutSeconds`, so the source-read and target-write halves of one stall are bounded on one clock (`TestWriteDeadline_ExceedsTheLongestLegitimateStall` fails if they drift apart).

**Sibling sweep — every connection funnel, fixed-or-exempt.** `mysql` **FIXED** via `mysql.Config.WriteTimeout` in `finishParseDSN`, which covers all four DSN parse entry points (`parseDSN`, `parseServerDSN`, and both `…ForFlavor` variants), TCP and unix sockets alike, and every write path the driver owns — LOAD DATA, batched insert, applier, DDL. `mysql` binlog syncer **FIXED** separately via `netdeadline.Dialer()` (it does not read that cfg). `postgres` **FIXED** at all three pgx funnels — `openPgxDBAs`, `openPgxDBDescribeExec`, the CDC replication conn. `planetscale`/`vitess`/`mariadb` **COVERED** (Flavors of the mysql engine, not separate connection paths). `postgres-trigger` **COVERED** transitively (every pool comes from `postgres.OpenPgxDB`). `sqlite`/`sqlite-trigger` **EXEMPT** — a local file has no receive window. `d1`/`d1-trigger` **EXEMPT** — HTTP, already bounded whole-request by `http.Client.Timeout`. `csv`/`tsv`/`ndjson`/`mydumper` **EXEMPT** — filesystem sources. The MySQL `keepaliveNet` dial registration is the one dial site that deliberately does NOT compose `netdeadline.Dialer` (the driver field already covers those sockets, and wrapping would arm the same deadline twice); it says so where it is defined. Enforced rather than promised by `TestEverySocketEngineArmsAWriteDeadline` (registry-derived, fail-by-default, stale entries fail) plus `TestEveryEngineDialSiteComposesTheFullTransportPolicy` (an AST walker over every `DialFunc`/`Dialer` assignment in `internal/engines`, anti-vacuity floor 4). The roster gate immediately earned itself: it caught `mariadb`, a registered engine the hand-written list had missed.

**The READ side deliberately gets no deadline, and that is a decision with a named residual.** A read deadline is a whole-query timeout in disguise — the client blocks in `Read` from the moment it sends a query until the first result packet, so any bound tight enough to catch a dead peer also kills a legitimate long `COUNT(*)`, `ALTER`, or index build. What covers the read side instead: the ADR-0109 server-side source session timeouts, TCP keep-alive on a genuinely idle socket, and the watchdog. **This is not hypothetical — the integration test found the residual directly.** With a proxy-wide blackhole the first flush failed on the write deadline in 5s and the run then hung in the retry's fresh-connection HANDSHAKE READ. The test's proxy was made per-CONNECTION so it measures the write hang it is about, and the observation is recorded in the test file's header rather than discarded. That residual is the sharpest argument for having built the watchdog and not only the deadline.

**The premise this argument rests on, named.** `netkeepalive` advertises a ~60s dead-peer bound, which reads like it should already have covered this. It does not: **TCP keep-alive probes are only sent on an IDLE connection**, and a connection with unacknowledged data in the send queue is governed by the retransmission timer instead. A blocked write is exactly the state keep-alive cannot see. Bound to a test rather than asserted: `TestWrapConn_RealSocketWriteToANonDrainingPeerTimesOut` requires the surfaced error to be a `net.Error` **timeout** on a real socket, so a transport whose behaviour changed would change the test's shape rather than silently invalidate the argument.

**The watchdog's three design decisions.** *Progress is rows handed to the writer* (bytes on the raw byte-pipe lane) — not chunks completed and not durable checkpoints, because those advance at whole-chunk granularity and a stall INSIDE one chunk is every one of the three incidents. The row counter already exists, is already atomic, and freezes for the right reason: rows reach it through the tee that feeds the writer. *It warns, it does not abort* — a stalled copy and one merely slower than the threshold are indistinguishable from here, which is the whole premise, so aborting would eventually kill a legitimate copy on a guess; the layers that CAN tell (the deadline, the retry budgets) keep the loud-failure duty. *It is silent during a deliberate quiesce* — an ADR-0110 window parks every lane on purpose for up to `GrowGateMaxHold` (20 min), so the gate is asked directly via a new `ir.GrowGateQuiesceObserver` / `GrowGate.QuiescedSince`, and quiesced time never accumulates toward the threshold. A watchdog that cried wolf on every storage grow would be suppressed, and a suppressed watchdog catches nothing. The re-warn interval WIDENS (5m, 15m, 35m, 75m, then hourly) for the same reason: a line every five minutes overnight is the same suppression failure by a different route.

**5 minutes, and NOT an operator flag — recorded as a decision.** The threshold sits above the plausible range of legitimate no-row gaps (a large segment draining to a slow target, a chunk-boundary query, a first row that has not arrived), with the escalation rather than a tighter value doing the work for a genuine stall. It is not a CLI knob because it cannot break anything — the watchdog only warns — and a knob whose only effect is when a log line appears is one nobody can be advised about; the `netkeepalive` constants make the same call. If a real need appears it lifts into the copy-phase flag surface, and then it owes `TestCopyPhaseFlagParityMigratorStreamer` an entry like every other copy-phase knob.

**Watchdog sibling sweep — every copy lane.** It rides inside `newProgressTicker` / `newProgressTickerForChunk`, so all eight ticker-building lanes are covered by construction. The exception, and the one that would have been the hole: `copyChunkRaw` → `runRawCopyChunk` (the ADR-0078 raw byte-pipe) has **no ticker at all**, because it has no rows to observe — so it now starts its own watchdog over BYTES that completed a pipe write. `TestCopyStallWatchdog_ReachesEveryCopyLane` walks the package by call site (floor: 8 ticker lanes) and names the raw lane explicitly, because that one cannot be inferred. The quiesce source reaches the tickers through the context, bound at the two drivers that reach the copy graph: `runBulkCopyPhases` (migrate + the ADR-0079 fast cold-start, from `parallel.growGate`) and `runBulkCopyWithOpts` (both sync cold-starts, from a new `bulkCopyOpts.GrowGate` knob that the existing fail-by-default `TestBulkCopyOptsProductionSitesSetEveryKnob` roster now enforces at every production site).

**What this does NOT reach, stated rather than implied.** The watchdog observes the COPY. A stall in a phase with no row flow — index build, constraint add, schema apply, CDC apply — is outside it. Those have their own bounded-retry ladders and are not the class the three incidents came from, but the gap is real and is recorded at the watchdog's definition.

**Gates.** `internal/netdeadline` unit pins (arm-per-write; never-lengthen-an-owner-deadline ×4 shapes, which is the property that keeps the wrapper from un-cancelling a pgconn cancellation; zero-owner-deadline-means-none; real-socket timeout). `TestParseDSN_EveryEntryPointArmsAWriteDeadline` (4 parse entry points × {tcp, tcp+params, unix}) and `TestParseDSN_OperatorWriteTimeoutWins`. The registry roster + dial-site walker above. Watchdog: reports-a-stall, silent-on-slow-but-progressing, silent-during-a-quiesce (driven through the REAL `migcore.GrowGate`, plus the other direction — a stall AFTER the window reopens IS reported, so the exclusion cannot become a permanent mute), widening re-warn, live-through-the-real-ticker-constructor, and the lane roster. **The crux gate is `TestLoadDataWriteDeadline_DeadSocketFailsLoudly`** (integration): a real MySQL behind a blackholing TCP proxy that forwards the handshake and 64 KiB of the LOAD DATA stream and then stops reading without closing. Both shapes the entry names: KEYLESS returns in **5.05s** with the documented `SLUICE-E-COPY-RETRY-AMBIGUOUS-KEYLESS` (checked through `sluicecode.FromError`, not by substring — the code lives in the envelope, not the message), KEYED rides the retry budget and fails loudly naming the window in **26.6s**. Both carry their own timeout, because a test that reproduces a hang by hanging is not a test. The keyless case's wall time is asserted against the write deadline on BOTH sides, which is what binds the surfaced failure to the deadline rather than to some other route.

**Mutation runs, each confirmed APPLIED (grep for the marker) before the result was trusted** — the 2026-08-05 rule, which cost a destroyed working file to relearn: M1 drop the MySQL default → the parse-entry-point pin FAILS; M2 revert one PG dial site to keep-alive only → the dial-site walker FAILS naming the file and line; M3 drop `postgres` from the roster → the registry gate FAILS in both directions (missing engine AND stale entry); M4 never warn → the stall pin and the live-ticker pin FAIL; M5 drop the quiesce exclusion → the grow-gate pin FAILS; M6 never reset on progress → the slow-but-progressing pin FAILS; M7 remove the watchdog from the chunk ticker → the lane roster and the live-ticker pin FAIL; M8 remove it from the raw lane → the lane roster FAILS naming that lane; M9 drop `GrowGate` at the multi-database site → the `bulkCopyOpts` roster FAILS; M10 make `QuiescedSince` always true → the QuiescedSince pin FAILS; M11 ignore the owner deadline → never-lengthens FAILS in three shapes; M12 no wrapper at all → arm-per-write and the real-socket pin FAIL; M13 fixed re-warn interval → the widening pin FAILS (9 warnings where ≤6 is the bound).

### 162. A server-side `max_error_count=0` silences SHOW WARNINGS, so the MySQL silent-clamp refusal never fired and a truncating LOAD DATA exited 0 — *✅ SHIPPED v0.121.0. Audit 2026-08-11 finding COLD-1 (CONFIRMED HIGH, observed). NOT a concurrency chunk (a write-path warning-count read), so the `-race` Integration job is the ordinary gate.*

v0.121.0 closed the two bulk write cores; the sweep missed the third `readShowWarnings` consumer — the CDC-apply clamp WARN (`reportApplyClampWarnings`), found by the post-release learnings sweep the same day and SHIPPED v0.122.0 with the full three-consumer enumeration written into the commit.

**The gap.** sluice's silent-clamp detection (Bugs 102/103 Vector B) and the item-114 replay accounting trigger off the SHOW WARNINGS row count, which the server TRUNCATES at `@@max_error_count`. `max_error_count = 0` is a legal, documented bulk-load memory tuning ("to disable message storage") that leaves `@@warning_count` accurate but makes SHOW WARNINGS return zero rows — so `reportLoadDataWarnings`/`reportBulkWriteWarnings` hit their `Visible == 0` early return and never refused. Observed on mysql:8.0: `SET SESSION max_error_count=0; SET SESSION sql_mode=''` → an over-long value's LOAD DATA commits the truncated row, `@@warning_count=1`, SHOW WARNINGS empty. sluice pins `sql_mode`/`time_zone`/charset per session precisely because it distrusts server settings here, but never pinned `max_error_count`.

**The fix (and the approach that did NOT survive CI).** The first cut pinned `max_error_count = 1024` on every connection via `cfg.Params` — and CI caught it: `SET max_error_count` requires `SESSION_VARIABLES_ADMIN` on MySQL 8.0 (measured on a real server; `time_zone`/`sql_mode` do not), so injecting it on every connection broke every lower-privilege user's connect at ping — six restricted-user integration tests (backup-snapshot no-RELOAD, connection-budget probe, heartbeat permission-denied) failed with `Error 1227` before their scenario even began. The pin was also wrong SCOPE: those read-only probes do no silent-clamp detection and had no business carrying it. The shipped fix instead READS the uncapped `@@warning_count` — which needs no privilege — as the detection trigger in the write path: `reportLoadDataWarnings` and `reportBulkWriteWarnings` (both write cores' warning readers, swept together) gate on the true count rather than the SHOW WARNINGS row count, degrading to the visible count only if the read itself fails. On the replay path, a visible list truncated below the true count (`Visible < total`) means the hidden warnings cannot be classified as duplicate-key skips, so it refuses conservatively rather than tolerating blind.

**Gates.** The integration pin `TestLoadData_MaxErrorCountZero_StillRefusesSilentClamp` sets `GLOBAL max_error_count=0`, opens the WRITE pool AFTER the flip so its fresh sessions inherit the suppressed buffer (SHOW WARNINGS empty, `@@warning_count` accurate), and asserts the truncating LOAD DATA still refuses off the `@@warning_count` read. Mutation (verified locally against real MySQL 8.0.46): reverting the trigger to the visible count lands the clamped value silently and the pin flips red. The six restricted-user tests that caught the privilege regression are the standing guard against re-introducing a session-var SET on the shared connection path.

### 161. `schema diff`'s CHECK canonicalizer dropped backslashes as MySQL escapes, so a weakened regex CHECK canonicalized onto the original and reported IN SYNC — *✅ SHIPPED v0.121.0. Audit 2026-08-11 finding DIFF-1 (CONFIRMED HIGH, observed). NOT a concurrency chunk (a pure-function contract fix), so the `-race` Integration job is the ordinary gate.*

**The gap.** `decodeLiteral`/`rawLiteralEnd` treated `\X` inside a string literal as a MySQL escape and dropped the backslash. But since the escaping-scanner chunk (`74299e34`) both diff inputs reach the canonicalizer in SQL-STANDARD spelling: the IR keeps expression literals apostrophe-doubled with backslashes BARE, and each engine re-escapes only at its own DDL emit boundary (`mysql.escapeExprLiteralBackslashes`; PG is standard-conforming). So a backslash inside a CHECK literal is a VALUE character. Dropping it made two genuinely different literals differing only by an interior backslash — a weakened regex `'^a\d+$'` (digits required) vs `'^ad+$'` (accepts `add`) — canonicalize EQUAL, so `schema diff` certified a weakened/tampered CHECK as in sync; and it mis-scanned a value ENDING in a backslash, consuming the closing quote and folding following expression text into the value (the phantom-drift mirror). This falsified the file-header injectivity claim.

**The fix.** Treat backslash as an ordinary value byte in both `decodeLiteral` and `rawLiteralEnd`, keeping only the SQL-standard `''` doubling escape — matching the contract the readers and emitters already hold. The removed test case (`'o\'brien'` "agrees with" `'o''brien'`) pinned an input shape that cannot occur at the IR/diff layer and asserted exactly the buggy fold.

**Gates.** Backslash rows in `TestCanonicalCheckExpr_TamperIsStillVisible` (`'^a\d+$'`≠`'^ad+$'`, both the `~` and the emitted-`REGEXP_LIKE` carrier) and `TestCanonicalCheckExpr_LiteralScanning` (backslash-as-value; trailing-`\` does not swallow the close), plus `TestSchemaDiff_BackslashWeakenedCheckIsReportedAsDrift` at the Schemas() level. Mutation confirmed: reintroducing the escape arm flips all three RED.

### 160. The pre-create shape gate looks pre-existing target tables up case-SENSITIVELY, so on a folding target a source table differing only in case silently merges into an unrelated pre-existing one — *✅ SHIPPED v0.121.0. Audit 2026-08-11 finding PRF-2 (CONFIRMED HIGH, observed live). NOT a concurrency chunk (a new optional interface plus pure fold-keyed lookups), so the `-race` Integration job is the ordinary gate rather than a pre-tag requirement.*

**The gap (observed on the HEAD binary, two SQLite files).** `existingTablesGate` (ADR-0166) reads the target catalog and shape-compares, but keyed `actual` by the exact stored spelling and looked it up with the source's exact spelling (`actual[t.Name]`). On a folding target — SQLite always, MySQL under `lower_case_table_names != 0` — a source `Orders` misses a stored `orders` entirely, so it reads as ABSENT: `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` no-ops against the existing `orders`, and the bulk copy lands the `Orders` rows in it. Reproduced live: source `Orders`(2 rows) + target `orders`(1 row) → "migration complete", exit 0, zero WARNs, one `orders` with all 3 rows merged. The item-148/149 fold refusals do not reach it — they claim SOURCE tables against each other, never against the target catalog.

**The fix.** A third fold surface, `ir.TargetTableNameFolder`, returns the function the target compares TABLE identifiers under (MySQL reads `lower_case_table_names` once; SQLite is the unconditional ASCII fold; a case-sensitive target returns nil = identity). The gate resolves it with the one catalog read, keys `actual` by the fold, and folds every lookup — the shape compare, the tolerated-table WARN, and the pre-existing-FK check — so the whole gate agrees on one rule. A differing-shape fold-hit now takes the existing `SLUICE-E-TARGET-TABLE-SHAPE-MISMATCH` refusal instead of merging; a matching-shape fold-hit PROCEEDS (a folding MySQL stores sluice's own `Orders` as `orders`, so this is the resume/bootstrap case the gate must not false-refuse — the documented `--resume` trap) but WARNs when the spellings differ, so the merge is never silent. A case-sensitive target (nil fold) is byte-exact and behaviourally unchanged.

**Why not refuse every fold-hit.** On a folding target sluice cannot create two tables that fold together, and its own resumed/bootstrapped table reads back case-differing (lct=1 stores `orders`), so refusing a case-differing fold-hit outright would refuse a run for having worked — the exact `--resume` false-refusal `PreflightTableNameFold` documents. Shape-match → skip-create + WARN is the resume-safe resolution; the residual (a shape-COMPATIBLE unrelated pre-existing table still merges, now with a WARN naming both spellings) is the same ambiguity the gate cannot resolve without a resume marker, and is filed rather than papered over.

**Gates.** `TestMigrateShapeGate_FoldingTarget_PRF2` (differing-shape refuses; matching-shape proceeds+WARNs; identity-fold stays byte-exact; fold-read failure WARNs and falls back to exact) and `TestMigrate_FoldingTargetMergeRefusedEndToEnd` (full Run refuses before any DDL/copy). Anti-vacuity: the pipeline test uses a stub that implements the interface, so `var _ ir.TargetTableNameFolder = Engine{}` compile-pins in BOTH the sqlite and mysql engines guard against the production engines silently NOT implementing it, and `TestTargetTableNameFold_UsesSQLitesOwnFold` pins that SQLite returns its ASCII rule and not `strings.ToLower` (the item-150 over-refusal). Mutation confirmed: reverting the shape-compare lookup to exact-case flips the differing-shape and end-to-end pins RED.

### 159. "Can the target hold this column type?" is answered for ONE engine pair, by a hand-coded name-keyed check — every other pair finds out from CREATE TABLE — *✅ SHIPPED v0.119.0. NOT a concurrency chunk (no goroutine / channel / FSM / shared-state change; the change is pure functions over the IR plus five call sites), so the `-race` Integration job is the ordinary gate rather than a pre-tag requirement.*

**Implementation notes (2026-08-10).**

**The shape of the gap.** `migcore.CheckCrossEngineSupportable` opens with `pgToMySQL := isPGSourceEngine(src) && IsMySQLFamilyEngine(dst); if !pgToMySQL { return nil }`. That is the only early door for column types, and it covers one direction of one pair. PG → SQLite, MySQL → SQLite, SQLite → anything, and MySQL → Postgres all fall straight through it, so the refusal comes from the target's own `emitColumnType` at CREATE TABLE — after the dry-run plan is printed, after the writers are open, and table-by-table, so a schema whose last table carries the offending column leaves every table ahead of it created on the target. That last part is measured, not argued: with the new call removed, the integration test reports `table "a_orders" EXISTS on the target after the refusal` on BOTH a SQLite and a Postgres target.

**Derive, do not declare — this is the positive half of the `SupportedTypes` deletion (`a7306627`).** The seven capability fields were deleted for being a second copy of a truth the engines hold structurally; the replacement cannot be another table. So the new optional surface `ir.ColumnTypeEmitPreflighter` asks the target ENGINE, and each engine answers by running its OWN `emitColumnType` — the same function its `emitColumnDef` calls on the create path. Early verdict and late verdict are one function, and a pair nobody wrote down is covered because the engine is doing the deciding.

**Why a FIFTH interface rather than one more question inside `PreflightTables`.** `ir.TableEmitPreflighter` already means something narrower than its name — the connection-free half of the `IF NOT EXISTS` silent-merge class — and `TestEveryTargetRefusesACollidingTableNamespace` records `postgres`/`postgres-trigger` as EXEMPT from it with a safety argument about identifier comparison, **failing an engine that both implements it and is exempt**. Folding column types in would make Postgres an implementor for an unrelated reason and leave that roster reading as coverage of a question it does not ask. One question per name; the sharing is at the call sites, and `preflightHelpers` took a fifth string with one line per entry point and no new list — the third consecutive member to arrive that way.

**Over-refusal was the whole risk, and two of the three engines needed a carve-out to avoid it.** Postgres has TWO configuration-dependent refusals (`GEOMETRY requires PostGIS`, probed when the writer opens; `--enable-pg-extension`, a flag this surface does not carry) and ONE arm that is not a refusal at all (`Enum` returns "use emitColumnDef" — an internal wrong-entry-point guard). A naive walk would refuse every enum, geometry and extension column on every PG target. The fix is `preflightEmitOpts`: run the emitter under the MOST PERMISSIVE configuration the run could have (PostGIS present; every extension the schema NAMES enabled, derived from the schema rather than the catalog so an uncatalogued extension is still refused), so what survives is refusable under every configuration. The Enum skip is TOP-LEVEL ONLY, mirroring `emitColumnDef`'s branch exactly — an `Array` of enum has no such branch and IS refused. Both halves are pinned in both directions, and the configuration-dependent GAP is pinned by asserting the EMITTER still refuses what the preflight lets through, so the relocation cannot be mistaken for a hole.

**The retarget premise, named and checked.** Both restore lanes preflight the manifest's SOURCE-shaped schema and run `translate.RetargetForEngine` afterwards. That is safe only because the sole emit-lane rule table (`retargetPGtoMySQL`) mirrors the MySQL emitter's own auto-emit arms — every type it rewrites, `emitColumnType` already accepts unrewritten. Rather than write that down, `TestPreflightColumnTypes_IsRetargetInvariant` drives the REAL retarget over the whole matrix and fails if the two verdicts ever diverge (anti-vacuity floor: ≥5 shapes must actually be rewritten). Confirmed by mutation: adding an `ir.Interval` arm to the rule table fails it immediately.

**Gates.** `internal/typematrix` is the shared family × shape matrix (~72 cells) held to `ir.AllTypes()` by `TestCases_CoverEveryIRTypeFamily` — one list for three consumers, because three copies of a shape list is the Bug-74 rot one level up. Each engine runs `TestPreflightColumnTypesAgreesWithTheTableEmitter` over it against its REAL table emitter, failing in both directions (preflight-refuses/emitter-accepts = over-refusal; the reverse = coverage gap), MySQL across all four flavors. `TestEveryTargetCapableEngineAnswersTheColumnTypePreflight` (docsync) holds the implementor set to the registry, fail-by-default with stale-exemption detection. `internal/pipeline/migrate_column_type_preflight_cross_integration_test.go` covers PG→SQLite (`inet`), MySQL→PG (`VARCHAR(0)`, catalog Bug 107) and the PG→MySQL auto-emit control, each with its own non-refusing control, each asserting the refusal names table+column+type AND that no table reached the target.

**Mutation runs, each confirmed APPLIED (grep for the marker) before the result was trusted, each reverted by a targeted edit:** M1 delete pgtrigger's delegation → the docsync roster FAILS naming `postgres-trigger`; M2 drop the call from `add-table` → the entry-point roster FAILS; M3 make PG's enum skip recursive → the agreement matrix and the carve-out pin FAIL on `array/of enum`; M4 remove the enum skip → three PG pins FAIL with over-refusals; M5 use non-permissive `emitOpts` → six over-refusals (geometry ×3, extensions ×3) plus the GAP pin FAIL; M6 use `stdEmitter` instead of the flavor emitter → **NOTHING FAILS, recorded as UNGATED at the code** (no flavor changes the verdict today, only the rendered bytes); M7 make SQLite's walk never refuse → the agreement matrix FAILS on 15 shapes; M8 drop the `inet` family from the matrix → the completeness gate FAILS in both of its arms; M9 add a rule table arm for `ir.Interval` → the retarget-invariance gate FAILS; M10 drop `migrate`'s call → the cross-engine integration test FAILS on real containers with `a_orders` present on the target after the refusal, on both pairs.

**What it does NOT reach, stated rather than implied.** Refusals that come from a column's NAME (PG's 63-byte identifier limit) or its DEFAULT rather than its type; the two configuration-dependent PG refusals above; and `CheckCrossEngineSupportable`, which is deliberately LEFT IN FRONT and untouched — it still owns the PG → MySQL messages, whose `--exclude-table` / exact-`--type-override` recovery guidance this surface cannot derive. **Follow-up worth its own chunk:** several `unsupportablePGtoMySQL` arms (`ir.Interval`, the negative-scale decimal, the uncatalogued extension type) are now double-covered — the same column refused by both, with the hand-coded message winning on ordering. Folding those into the derived door and keeping only the recovery-guidance wrapper would shrink the name-keyed check to the shapes that are genuinely not column types (sequences, EXCLUDE constraints, opclass indexes). Not done here: it changes operator-visible messages on the one pair that already worked, which deserves its own diff.

### 158. `schema diff` mysql→postgres reports phantom column-TYPE drift on a target `migrate` itself created — the reverse-direction rule table Bug 234 filed rather than hid — *✅ SHIPPED v0.118.0. NOT a concurrency chunk (no goroutine / channel / FSM / shared-state change; the change is pure functions over the IR plus one comparison option), so the `-race` Integration job is the ordinary gate rather than a pre-tag requirement.*

**Implementation notes (2026-08-08).**

**The rule table was MEASURED, and the measurement is now the gate.** The mirror of `retargetPGtoMySQL` is the wrong derivation — "what does a PG `text` become on MySQL" is a different question from "what does a MySQL `TEXT` read back as on PG" — so the table came from migrating a fixture carrying every arm of `internal/engines/mysql.translateType` onto a real PostgreSQL 16 and diffing the read-back against the source IR. **Sixteen of thirty-seven columns moved, in exactly four families:** integers (PG has no unsigned and three widths — `Int8`/`UInt8`→`Int16`, `UInt16`/`Int24`/`UInt24`→`Int32`, `UInt32`/`UInt64`→`Int64`), the TEXT tiers (all → `Text[long]`), the whole binary family (`Binary(N)`, `Varbinary(N)`, every BLOB tier → `Blob[long]`), and `Set{…}` → `Array<Text[long]>`. Everything else round-tripped identically — Boolean, Decimal, Float, Bit, Char, Varchar, Date, Time, DateTime, Timestamp, Enum, JSON, the MariaDB-native UUID/INET families — **as did NOT NULL, DEFAULT, and STORED generated columns**, which the filing did not claim either way. That fixture is now `TestSchemaDiffAfterMigrate_MySQLToPostgres_TypeFamilyMatrix`, so the derivation re-runs on every CI Integration job instead of being trusted.

**The mirror direction has item 153's trap, and it is sharper — so the table is COMPARE-ONLY.** `retargetRuleFor`'s table is shared between both entry points, and for postgres→mysql that sharing is correct. Two of the four mysql→postgres rewrites DESTROY what the Postgres DDL emitter dispatches on. `ir.Set` is the live one: `postgres.emitTableDef` reads it to emit `CONSTRAINT "<t>_<c>_set" CHECK (<c> <@ ARRAY[…])`, the only thing carrying the source's member list onto the target, and the flattened `Array<Text>` leaves it nothing to match — a **silent constraint drop on `restore` / `chain restore` / the broker's schema-delta replay / schema-forward**, traded for a loud phantom line, which is the worse side. `ir.Integer.Unsigned` is the latent one: `ScanUnsignedBigintNotices` dispatches on it for the Bug 11 (2^63, 2^64) narrowing warning. So `compareOnlyRuleFor` is a second table only `RetargetForShapeCompare` consults, and the claim is a gate rather than prose: `TestEmitTableDef_CompareOnlyRewriteWouldDropTheSetCheck` asserts the emit-lane pass emits the CHECK **and** that the compare-lane pass does not, with `TestRetargetForEngine_MySQLToPostgresIsStillIdentity` stating the wider class.

**The integer arithmetic is now ONE statement, not two.** Predicting PG's read-back width means restating `effectiveWidth` + `postgresIntName`'s two-stage widen-then-collapse, which is exactly the shape that drifts. Following Bug 234's `PGIndexName` precedent, the policy moved to `translate.PGStorageIntegerWidth` and `postgres.emitIntegerType` now NAMES its column from it (`effectiveWidth` deleted; `postgresIntName` reduced to the three widths PG has). Output is byte-identical for every input a reader produces. The premise it rests on — "a PG catalog reads SMALLINT back as `Int16`" — is a claim about `postgres.translateScalarType`, which `translate` cannot see, so it is bound by the integration matrix rather than asserted; mutation M6 is the proof (breaking the shared function moves the emitter and the prediction TOGETHER, leaving the integration matrix green and failing only the unit pins — which is what "bound" means).

**Direction coverage, enumerated rather than implied.** Bug 234 closed the index-NAME axis in all six ordered directions at once because a primary key is matched by ROLE. The TYPE axis has no such shortcut. `TestRetargetPairRosterCoversEveryOrderedFamilyPair` derives the storage families from the registry and classifies all nine ordered pairs: three identity (same-family), two rule (postgres→mysql, mysql→postgres), **four filed GAPS — every SQLite pair** (`postgres→sqlite`, `sqlite→postgres`, `mysql→sqlite`, `sqlite→mysql`), whose read-back is affinity-resolved and needs its own measured matrix. Each gap carries a stated reason; an unclassified direction, a stale entry, and a classification that disagrees with behaviour all fail, with anti-vacuity floors on all three classes.

**`HasStorageShapeMapping` deliberately WITHHOLDS the new pair, and says so at its definition.** It gates the ADR-0166 migrate pre-create gate, which REFUSES; the bar for arming a refusal is higher than for improving a report, and `ir.Geometry` (PostGIS target) is the one family the matrix could not measure. So `schema diff` gets the mapping and `migrate` keeps its WARN-and-proceed posture, unchanged. `TestHasStorageShapeMapping_WithholdsTheCompareOnlyPair` pins the divergence in both directions with a control, so it cannot be read as a missing case. **Follow-up chunk:** a postgis-tagged family matrix, then flip the predicate to `shapeCompareRuleFor`.

**Bug 234's deferred PG-only-object list, swept — one live, two not.** **RLS/policies: FIXED.** Only the PG reader populates `RLSEnabled`/`RLSForced`/`Policies`; MySQL's SchemaWriter WARNs once and drops them (`maybeWarnRLSDrop`) and its reader can never report them back, so every PG→MySQL diff of a target `migrate` succeeded on reported `RLSMismatched` + every policy missing, permanently, with no target-side action able to close it. New `irdiff.Options.TargetCannotHoldRowLevelSecurity`, keyed on the already-declared `ir.Capabilities.PostgresBackend` rather than an engine name. **Standalone SEQUENCES and EXCLUDE constraints: deliberately still compared.** The line, stated where the option is defined: *suppress where sluice's own migrate WARNs and DROPS; keep reporting where migrate REFUSES.* `migcore.CheckCrossEngineSupportable` refuses both outright for a MySQL or SQLite target, so `migrate` can never have produced that pair — a "missing on target" line there is the diff telling an operator with a hand-built target exactly why a migration would refuse.

**Residual, stated rather than left to be found (item 156's mirror).** A `SET` column's membership CHECK still reports as `ChecksExtra` on every mysql→postgres diff. The TYPE axis is closed; the CHECK axis is not, and item 156's measured obstacle applies here only halfway — the constraint NAME is deterministic (`<table>_<column>_set`, unlike MySQL's positional `<table>_chk_N`), but PostgreSQL does not return the expression it was given (`("c" <@ ARRAY['x','y']::TEXT[])` reads back as `(c <@ ARRAY['x'::text, 'y'::text])`), so matching still needs a normalizer and a name-only match would accept a TAMPERED predicate as in sync. `TestSchemaDiffAfterMigrate_MySQLToPostgres_SetCheckIsPhantomDrift` is a CHARACTERIZATION pin that says so in its name and instructs its own inversion, including for the dangerous partial-fix state.

**The over-refusal half is the one that matters, and it is paired everywhere.** Every rule makes `schema diff` say LESS, so each rewritten family carries a genuine-drift row: `TestRetargetMySQLtoPGShapeCompare_GenuineDriftIsStillReported` (10 shapes) at the unit layer, and four real `ALTER`s on the live Postgres target in the integration matrix (integer re-widened, unsigned narrowed back, TEXT gaining a length constraint, a binary column becoming text) — each reported. The RLS suppression gets the same treatment at the WIRING layer, which the unit pins structurally cannot reach: `TestSchemaDiffAfterMigrate_PostgresToPostgres_RowLevelSecurityStillCompared` migrates an RLS table PG→PG and then strips the policy and the flag on the real target, binding the capability to the comparison rather than leaving two facts adjacent.

**Mutation runs, each confirmed APPLIED (`grep` for the `MUTANT158_*` marker) before the result was trusted; checkpoint-committed first so every revert was a targeted `git checkout` against a confirmed-clean path.** M1 `ir.Text` arm removed → 3 unit cells FAIL **and** the integration matrix FAILS with `3 type mismatches`. M2 `ir.Integer` arm removed → 9 unit cells FAIL. M3 the three binary arms removed → 5 unit cells FAIL. M4 `ir.Set` arm removed → the unit cell FAILS and the SET characterization pin FAILS on real containers, naming `expected=Set{email,sms} actual=Array<Text[long]>`. M5 the compare-only table leaked onto the emit lane (**the opposite direction**) → the SET-CHECK evidence gate FAILS printing the constraint restore would have lost, the emit-lane identity gate FAILS naming three columns, the both-tables exclusivity pin FAILS for four engine pairs, and the withholding pin FAILS. M6 `PGStorageIntegerWidth` collapsed 8/16 onto 32 → the width pin and 4 matrix cells FAIL while the integration matrix stays GREEN — the binding, demonstrated. M7A the RLS wiring hardcoded false → the PG→MySQL round trip FAILS with `1 row-level-security mismatch, 1 missing policy`. M7B hardcoded true (**the over-suppression direction**) → the PG→PG binding gate FAILS naming the unreported dropped policy. M8 a filed gap re-classified as `rule` → the pair roster FAILS on the behaviour disagreement AND on the gap-count floor.

### 156. A DOMAIN's CHECKs land on a MySQL target as table-level CHECKs the shape-compare expected side cannot carry, so `schema diff` reports PHANTOM drift on a table sluice itself created — *FIXED 2026-08-10, SHIPPED v0.119.0, together with Bug 237, which is the same shape with a different constraint source. NOT a concurrency chunk. Filed grading (MEDIUM, advisory-surface only) was CORRECT for this item and WRONG for Bug 237(a) — see the re-grading note at the end.*

**How it closed (2026-08-10).** Fix shape (ii) of the three weighed below, which is the one that needs no DDL behaviour change. A new optional engine surface, `ir.EmittedCheckPredictor`, lets a SchemaWriter state which CHECK constraints it SYNTHESIZES for a table beyond the ones the source declares; `internal/pipeline`'s differ attaches them to the expected side marked `ir.CheckConstraint.SluiceEmitted`, and `diffChecks` pairs them off against the target's by CANONICALIZED EXPRESSION before its ordinary name-keyed pass runs.

**Expression matching, not name matching, and not suppression.** Obstacle (a) — the unpredictable `<table>_chk_N` — is dissolved rather than solved: the name is never the key. Obstacle (b) — the catalog not returning what it was given — is met by `internal/ir/diff/check_expr_norm.go`, which is applied ONLY to `SluiceEmitted` entries; source-declared CHECKs keep their byte-exact, name-keyed comparison. The predicted body comes from the SAME function the emitter calls (`domainCheckBodyForMySQL`), so the prediction cannot drift from the DDL. A DROPPED domain CHECK still reports missing and a TAMPERED one reports missing + extra, both pinned on real containers, which is what makes this a fix rather than a blindfold.

**Both siblings closed in the same pass, enumerated.** The Postgres writer synthesizes TWO such constraints, not one: the SET-membership CHECK item 158's residual note named, and the Bug-25 generated-enum CHECK it did not. Both are predicted. The generated-enum column additionally carried a phantom TYPE line (`Enum{…}` expected against the `Text[long]` PG reads back), which is a COLUMN-level emitter effect rather than a type-level one and therefore could not be an arm of any pair rule table — it went into the new compare-lane `translate.targetEmitShapeRuleFor` pass, which is keyed on the TARGET alone and so also reaches same-engine postgres→postgres, where no rule table exists at all. The MySQL target's only synthesized kind is the DOMAIN CHECK; SQLite's writer synthesizes none.

**Named wart.** The canonicalizer removes every parenthesis rather than balancing them (balancing needs an expression parser), so two predicates differing ONLY in grouping compare equal. Sound here and stated where it lives: three of the four emitted shapes are single operators with no boolean structure, and the fourth is a pure conjunction where regrouping cannot change meaning. Pinned in both directions by `TestCanonicalCheckExpr_GroupingOnlyDifferencesAreTheOnlyCollision`.

**Two findings the fixture surfaced, which is what a comparison surface is for.** (1) **FIXED in the same commit:** the PG→MySQL DOMAIN regex translator did not un-double the apostrophe PG's `pg_get_constraintdef` hands out inside a string literal, so it re-escaped on top and a DOMAIN over `^o'brien$` landed on MySQL as a regex requiring TWO apostrophes — the target REFUSED a row the source accepts, shipped since v0.97.0. That is the Bug 113 shape the translator exists to prevent, arriving through the escaping rather than through the grammar. Pinned against the server's own enforcement by `TestDomainRegexApostrophePredicateIsEnforcedAsWritten` (an INSERT, deliberately: the read-back path cannot be the evidence — see (2)). (2) **FILED, not fixed:** MySQL's SchemaReader `convertMySQLEscapedApostrophes` is a blind `\'`→`'` replace, and `information_schema` renders such a literal DOUBLE-escaped, so any CHECK clause — or generated-column body — containing an apostrophe reads back malformed. Wider blast radius than this chunk (the same normalization serves `GENERATION_EXPRESSION`), needs its own escaping matrix including `NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES`, and its effect on this comparison is loud and safe (missing + extra rather than a silent match).

**Re-grading, recorded because it was wrong in the backlog and the cost is the reason.** Bug 237's temporal arm was filed LOW/advisory. It is not: the ADR-0166 migrate pre-create gate compares the same `RetargetForShapeCompare` rendering, so a SECOND `sluice migrate` over a target the first one created REFUSED — measured, `1 pre-existing target table(s) differ … column "ts_bare": want DateTime(unspecified), target has DateTime(6)` — for any PG schema carrying a bare `TIME`/`TIMESTAMP`/`TIMESTAMPTZ`, which is the ordinary shape. `TestMigrateTwice_PostgresToMySQL_BareTemporalDoesNotRefuse` is the pin, and it drives `Migrator.Run` rather than the diff because the diff assertions alone would not have caught it.

**Original filing below, retained: the obstacles it measured are exactly what the fix had to route around.**

**The shape.** `schema diff`'s expected side is built by `translate.RetargetForShapeCompare`, which flattens an `ir.Domain` to its base type — correct for storage, and the whole point of item 153. But a domain's CHECKs ride the WRAPPER (`ir.Domain.Checks`), and MySQL's `emitTableDefWithDomainChecks` turns the translatable ones into inline table-level CHECK clauses at migrate time. `diffChecks` only ever looks at `ir.Table.CheckConstraints`, so the target holds constraints the expected side has nowhere to put, and every one is reported as `ChecksExtra`.

**PRE-EXISTING, not an item-153 regression.** The un-flattened wrapper never matched the table-level constraint either — the CHECK was inside `ir.Domain.Checks` and never in `Table.CheckConstraints` on either side of item 153's change.

**Evidence (real PG 16 + MySQL 8.0, not reasoning).** A `dcheck` table with a regex domain, a range domain, and an un-translatable one migrates cleanly; `information_schema` confirms exactly 2 CHECK constraints landed (the emitter drops the un-translatable one, as designed); `schema diff` then reports `[dcheck_chk_1 dcheck_chk_2]` as extra-on-target. Pinned by `TestDiff_PGToMySQL_DomainChecksAreReportedAsPhantomDrift_Item156` (`internal/pipeline/diff_domain_check_mysql_integration_test.go`).

**Why item 153's fixture could not have caught it, and why that is worth recording.** `retargetShapeSeedDDL`'s domains are deliberately CHECK-FREE, for an unrelated reason its own comment gives (`ir.Domain.String()` prints the check count, so a checked wrapper would change the expected rendering). A check-free domain emits no inline CHECK, so that fixture's target had nothing extra to report — the fixture was constructed so it could not compare the easy case, and the case it excluded is where the defect lives.

**Why it is FILED rather than fixed, with both obstacles measured.** (a) **Names** — `diffChecks` matches by name, and MySQL auto-names the emitter's unnamed inline clause `<table>_chk_N` by position, which the expected side cannot predict. Making it predictable means naming the constraint in the emitter, a DDL BEHAVIOUR change that re-partitions every already-migrated target (the old auto-name reads as extra AND the new name as missing on the first diff after upgrade). (b) **Expressions** — even with matching names, `diffChecks` compares `Expr` byte-exactly after `TrimSpace`, and MySQL does not return what it was given: `CHECK (REGEXP_LIKE(email, '^[a-z]+$'))` reads back as ``regexp_like(`email`,_latin1\'^[a-z]+$\')``. Closing this needs a MySQL check-expression normalizer. Together that is a chunk with a compatibility decision in it, not a hunk.

**Fix shapes to weigh when it is taken up.** (i) name the emitted domain CHECKs deterministically + a MySQL check-expression normalizer for `diffChecks` (complete, but the compatibility break above needs a release note); (ii) have the shape-compare retarget record, per table, the checks the target emitter WOULD inline, and have `diffChecks` suppress an unmatched target-side check that matches one — narrower, no DDL change, but it needs the same normalizer to do the matching; (iii) suppress target-side CHECK extras entirely for cross-engine pairs where the target cannot round-trip the expression — cheapest and loses real drift detection, so it needs an argued reason rather than being the default.

**The pin was a CHARACTERIZATION test and said so in its own name.** It asserted the defect WAS present (`…AreReportedAsPhantomDrift_Item156`), with an anti-vacuity floor that asks MySQL's catalog — not sluice — whether the constraints landed at all, and it instructed its own inversion. INVERTED 2026-08-10 to `TestDiff_PGToMySQL_DomainChecksAreReconciled_Item156`, keeping the catalog-sourced anti-vacuity floor and adding the two DIRTY halves; the SET-check mirror `TestSchemaDiffAfterMigrate_MySQLToPostgres_SetCheckIsPhantomDrift` was inverted in the same pass to `…_EmittedChecksAreReconciled`.

### 155. `internal/domaingate` did not walk `internal/translate`, and its walker was blind to package-level registries — two live Bug-233 instances behind a gate that read as complete — *✅ SHIPPED v0.117.0. NOT a concurrency chunk (no goroutine / channel / FSM / shared-state change), so the `-race` Integration job is the ordinary gate rather than a pre-tag requirement.*

**Two independent scope defects, and the gate's own doc is what hid both.**

**(a) `internal/translate` was outside the gate.** The package doc scoped it to "every engine that can be a TARGET for a Postgres-family source; an engine without a gate file is itself a finding" — drawn around WHO OWNS THE CODE, not around where the class lives. Item 153 put `ir.Domain` dispatch in `translate`, and instantiating the gate there surfaced **two live instances of the exact Bug 233 class**: `ScanWideVarcharNotices` and `ScanUnconstrainedNumericNotices` both dispatch on `col.Type` behind a `sourceEngine == "postgres"` guard, so a `CREATE DOMAIN … AS varchar(70000)` / `AS numeric` column matched no arm and its advisory never fired — while MySQL's `emitColumnType` recurses `ir.Domain` into the base type and down-maps the column to TEXT / DECIMAL(65,30) regardless. The operator got the rewrite with no notice. `TestRetargetRuleArmsAreAllProbed` does not cover this and is named in the new gate file so it is not mistaken for coverage: it grades the retarget RULE TABLE's arms, one function in one file, and both instances were elsewhere.

**(b) The walker only visited `*ast.FuncDecl` bodies.** A registry-shaped package — `var rules = []rule{{match: func(...) …}}` — was entirely invisible to it. `internal/translate/notes.go` declares its note and hint predicates exactly that way, so 7 dispatch sites (including three PG-sourced hints: `uuid`, unbounded `text`, unconstrained `numeric`) were never graded. **The `MinSites` floor could not catch this**, because the floor counts what the walk reached; a package whose FuncDecl sites are all clean clears it while its registry rots. Fixed by `dispatchScopes`, which returns function bodies AND var/const initialisers; existing rosters are unaffected because function scopes keep their existing key.

**Dispositions, enumerated (the sibling-sweep step).** FIXED by unwrapping: `ScanWideVarcharNotices`, `ScanUnconstrainedNumericNotices`, and all 7 sites in `noteEntries`/`hintEntries`. EXEMPT with a written SOURCE-SIDE reason: `ScanMySQLTimeRangeNotices` and `ScanUnsignedBigintNotices` — both return nil unless `IsMySQLFamily(sourceEngine)`, and MySQL has no `CREATE DOMAIN`. The notes registries were unwrapped rather than exempted deliberately: a domaingate key is `(file, scope, operand)` and a `var`'s scope is the whole registry, so an exemption there would have silently shielded the next PG-sourced entry anyone adds. `internal/engines/postgres` remains deliberately un-instantiated, and the reason is now written at the gate rather than implied — PG is the engine that HAS domains, its emitter creates the DOMAIN type (`emitCreateDomainType`) instead of flattening, so "what does this column land as" is answered by the wrapper.

**Gates + premises.** `TestDomainTransparency_TranslateDispatchRoster` (floor 8; the package has 11 sites, and dropping the GenDecl scope takes it to 4 — so the floor is what catches a re-narrowed walker). `TestMySQLFamilySourceCannotCarryADomain` is the premise pin for the SOURCE-SIDE exemptions, and states its own scope: it grades `targetTypeRegistry` (the `--type-override` route, live because the scanners run POST-override) and explicitly does NOT reach the "a MySQL reader starts synthesising an ir.Domain" route, which cannot be pinned from `translate` since the dependency only runs the other way. `TestScanWideVarcharNotices_SeesThroughADomain`, `TestScanUnconstrainedNumericNotices_SeesThroughADomain` and `TestHintsFor_SeeThroughADomain` are the behavioural half, shaped as bare/wrapped PAIRS asserting the two produce the SAME advisory — a pin on the domain case alone would pass a scanner that fired on everything — with a negative column in each so the unwrap cannot have made them fire indiscriminately.

**Mutation runs, each confirmed APPLIED (grep for the `MUTANT155*` marker) before the result was trusted.** M-COUNT `MinSites` raised to 999 → reports the true site count (11), which is how the floor was chosen rather than guessed. M-WALK the GenDecl scope removed → the floor FAILS at 4 sites, and the mysql/sqlite rosters stay green (so the widening is additive, not a re-point). M-WV the wide-varchar unwrap reverted → the behavioural pin FAILS naming the missing notice AND the roster FAILS naming the file and line. M-UUID the `hintEntries` uuid unwrap reverted → the hint pin FAILS for that family only, and the roster names `notes.go:hintEntries:src.Type` — which is also the proof that (b)'s widening is load-bearing, since that site is invisible to the old walker.

### 154. A PG array or `jsonb` PRIMARY KEY PANICS the concurrent apply path — `valuesEqualForKey` compares two `any` with `==` — *✅ SHIPPED v0.117.0. CONCURRENCY-ADJACENT: the fix is a pure function, but its callers are the lane-routing decision of the concurrent appliers, so read the `-race` Integration job before the tag.*

**The crash.** `laneapply.valuesEqualForKey` did `a == b`, which panics at runtime whenever the interface's dynamic type is uncomparable. Its caller `PKChangedUpdate` is reached from all three concurrent-apply routing sites (`postgres/change_applier_concurrent.go:258`, `mysql/change_applier_concurrent.go:220`, `mysql/change_applier_multirow.go:293`). The existing `[]byte` special case shows the author stopped one type short of the general problem — and `[]byte` is itself uncomparable, so the special case was load-bearing for exactly one of the four kinds that reach a key.

**Reachability — VERIFIED, not argued, and it is a supported configuration.** Postgres permits a PRIMARY KEY on an array column (btree `array_ops`) and on `jsonb` (`jsonb_ops`); confirmed against a real PG 16 (`CREATE TABLE a (k text[] PRIMARY KEY …)` and the `jsonb` sibling both succeed). Both PG readers produce an uncomparable Go value for one: the native reader's `decodeArray` returns `[]any` (the documented IR contract for `ir.Array`), and pgtrigger's `to_jsonb` payload decodes to `[]any` / `map[string]any` — and pgtrigger's setup explicitly ACCEPTS `text[]` columns (only `json[]`/`jsonb[]` are refused, pinned by `TestSetup_RefusesJSONArrayColumn`'s negative half). PG's Update always carries a Before image (a real OldTuple, or the key-only one `synthesizeKeyOnlyBefore` copies out of After), so EVERY update on such a table reached the comparison. Note the shape of the crash: interface comparison panics on an uncomparable dynamic type unconditionally, so even the identity-copied Before image panics.

**The fix, and why structural equality rather than the key encoder.** `reflect.DeepEqual`. The alternative considered and REJECTED was comparing `WriteCanonicalKeyValue`'s bytes, for consistency with the router's own notion of identity: that encoder's `default` arm renders unknown kinds with `%v`, so `[]any{"a b"}` and `[]any{"a","b"}` encode identically. For the lane-routing caller a collision is harmless (colliding keys hash to the SAME lane, so nothing can commit out of order) — but `change_applier_multirow.go` uses the same predicate to decide whether upserting the after-image would ORPHAN the old-PK row, and there a false "unchanged" is silent data loss. One notion of equality that is exact beats one that is consistent-but-lossy on a path where lossiness corrupts.

**The binding property, pinned rather than asserted.** Equality here must IMPLY same lane, because both callers use a false result to skip the barrier. `TestValuesEqualForKey_ImpliesSameLane` binds `valuesEqualForKey` to `WriteCanonicalKeyValue` over the full corpus, so a change to EITHER side fails the build; the converse is deliberately not asserted and the doc says why.

**Named wart.** `bytes.Equal` called a nil and an empty `[]byte` equal; structural equality calls them different. That is the conservative direction (both callers treat "changed" as barrier / don't-coalesce), a PK column is NOT NULL so no live reader produces the pair, and `TestValuesEqualForKey_NilVersusEmptyByteSlice` pins it so the divergence is a test rather than a sentence.

**Sibling sweep — the tree has exactly ONE `any == any` site and this was it.** Swept by four independent passes: direct `any == any` (only `== nil`, which never panics, and interface-vs-concrete comparisons which cannot); `map[any]` keys (3 hits, all in one test stub); value `switch` scrutinees (13, all string/byte/enum); and indirect routes (`comparable`-constrained generics, `slices.Contains/Equal` over `[]any`, `sync.Map` with non-string keys, `==` on an `any`-returning decoder call) — zero hits each. The two NEAREST neighbours are exempt for the same structural reason and it is worth recording: smart compaction's PK-change barrier (`chain_compact_smart.go:1024`) keys on `pkValueKey`'s `%T\x1f%v` rendering, and the lane router (`router.go:185`) type-switches with a `%v` fallback. **Both stringify before comparing, which is precisely why the defect was unique to `valuesEqualForKey`.**

**Gates.** `TestValuesEqualForKey_FamilyMatrix` — every Go value kind `docs/value-types.md` permits in a Row that can also sit in a PK, at every shape: the comparable scalars, plus `[]byte` (incl. empty), `[]any` (1-D, 2-D, NULL-element, empty), `[]string` (`ir.Set` — a MySQL SET is indexable, a family the original report did not name), and `map[string]any` (flat and nested). It carries an anti-vacuity floor on BOTH axes: `eqPanics` asserts each row's declared comparability still matches reality, so a later edit cannot quietly replace the uncomparable corpus with comparable values, and the matrix requires ≥5 uncomparable families. `TestCDCReader_UncomparablePrimaryKeyReachesTheLaneRouter` (integration, pgtrigger) is the REACHABILITY pin and is deliberately BINDING rather than two adjacent facts: it creates the table on a real PG, runs the real Setup, reads the real captured UPDATEs, asserts the decoded key is genuinely `[]any` / `map[string]any`, and then feeds that exact value to the exact function the appliers call — for both families × {non-key UPDATE, key-MIGRATING UPDATE}.

**Mutation runs, each confirmed APPLIED (grep for the `MUTANT154*` marker) before the result was trusted.** M-A the original body restored → the family matrix PANICS with `comparing uncomparable type []interface {}`. M-B equality by `%v` → the lane-binding pin FAILS naming `int64(1)` vs `uint64(1)` (canonical bytes `i1` vs `u1`, lanes 2 vs 6) and the nil-vs-empty wart pin FAILS. M-C always-equal → the matrix FAILS on every family's changed-key half, and the pre-existing `TestPKChangedUpdate` FAILS too. M-D the bare pre-fix `a == b` → **the INTEGRATION pin panics on real reader output**, which is the evidence that the reachability claim is about the product and not about a hand-built value.
### 157. The grow gate escalates on evidence-free trouble, so a chronic transport-drop storm livelocks the cold copy while the retry machinery reports perfect health — *✅ SHIPPED v0.117.0. CONCURRENCY CHUNK — the change alters lane coordination in the shared gate; the `-race` Integration job MUST be green before the tag.*

**Reported by a real user, and their summary line is the finding:** "`audits`, which `migrate` handles as part of a 45-minute whole-database copy, never finished." A 2.64 GB / 16 M-row / 197-table MariaDB → PlanetScale move. `migrate` copied everything in 45 minutes with no errors; `sync` failed five times, always in cold-start bulk copy, always on `audits` (1.7 M rows, ~890 MB, ~520-byte rows — a `text` column of Psych YAML). Run 3 was killed after 91 minutes having absorbed **2,687 vtgate drops with zero unhandled**, tolerated 9 duplicate-key collisions, reached retry attempt 36, and copied **four chunks in its last sixty minutes**. Drops per bucket were flat throughout (176, 354, 336, 247, 290, 292, 255, 303, 313). Every individual mechanism behaved exactly as designed.

**Phase A, measured from the field log rather than reasoned about.** The gate was **CLOSED 81.1% of the run** — 4,369 s of 5,385 s across 246 windows — and **92–97% of every ten-minute bucket after 14:00**, which is the hour the four chunks landed in. The correlation is direct and is the whole diagnosis: the one bucket that ran at 42% duty completed 62 tables; the buckets at 92–97% completed three. 165 of the run's 170 table completions happened before 14:05. Mean hold across all 246 windows was **17.8 s** (4,369 s / 246); the ladder SATURATES at `GrowGateBackoffCap` = 30 s in the sustained stretches, which is where the 92–97% buckets come from, and the run-wide mean is lower because the early minutes had short holds. An earlier draft of this entry said "mean hold sat at ~30 s", which its own totals contradict — recorded because a figure that disagrees with the numbers beside it is exactly what this queue exists to catch. All 2,687 drops classify `no-grow-evidence`: they are `vtgate connection error: {no endpoints, unexpected EOF}`, and that literal is in the transport half of the item-143 partition by construction.

**Both confounds, named rather than assumed, because the user's own comparison is not clean.**

- **`migrate` vs `sync` is mostly `migrate` vs the TARGET.** `migrate` ran against a **PS-160 production branch**; every failing `sync` ran against a **dev branch**, which the log confirms independently (`innodb_buffer_pool_size=33554432` — 32 MiB, the dev-branch signature, and the run also logs the dev-branch parallelism warning). A dev branch is by far the more likely source of a chronic drop storm. Structurally the two entry points construct the *same* gate with the *same* envelope (`migrate_phases.go:647` vs `streamer_coldstart.go:1099` / `streamer_coldstart_parallel.go:310` / `streamer_multidb.go:808` — re-derived 2026-08-11; the originals drifted with the item's own commit); the only difference is migrate's nil recovery probe, which affects early release, not hold length. So the honest answer to "why does `migrate` survive" is **the target, not the code path** — and the defect is real anyway, because the gate is what converts a degraded-but-progressing copy into a stalled one on *any* target that drops at this rate.
- **The user's binary predates the ceiling.** v0.111.1 is before item 138's run-level share ceiling (v0.113.0), which on current `main` bounds this at 50%. That is why the log reads 81% — it is literally the population item 138 was filed from.

**Why 50% was not good enough, which is the part that makes this a fresh item rather than a duplicate of 138.** A fraction of wall clock is the wrong unit. Half the clock spent in **30-second units** quantises a lane to one chunk per hold: a lane that finishes a chunk one millisecond after the gate closes waits a full cap-length hold before it may start the next, so throughput collapses independently of the average. And by ADR-0110's own scope correction, a healthy sibling's hold is not alignment at all — `Await` runs before *every* attempt, so one lane's drop parks fifteen lanes that were copying fine.

**The fix: `GrowGateEvidenceFreeHoldCap` (250 ms)** bounds a single window's hold during an episode in which no trip has yet carried grow evidence. An evidenced episode keeps the full 30 s ladder. The flag accumulates per episode — one evidenced trip restores the deep ladder for the rest of it, the conservative direction — and resets with the ladder.

**What this deliberately does NOT do, because these are the parts of item 143's refusal that still stand:** the **trip set is unchanged** (every classified transient still trips and still quiesces — this is not the "narrow the trip on absence of evidence" change 143 declined); the **early rungs stay evidence-independent**, so the first hold, which is what the shield rides on, is bit-identical for every evidence value. What is rejected is only the deep escalation on an episode that has produced no evidence across many armed-held-reopened-refuted windows — at which point "this is a bounded serving transition needing quiet" is not unfalsified but *refuted by the gate's own measurements*, since a grow window resolves and that is what makes it a window.

**Why the discriminator has to be the evidence.** The tempting evidence-free fix — de-escalate on immediate re-trip, since that hold demonstrably bought nothing — is wrong in the dangerous direction: a real multi-minute grow produces immediate re-trips too, so de-escalating on them would hammer the target during exactly the window ADR-0110 exists for. Prompt re-trip is ambiguous between the two populations; the evidence is the only available signal that is not, which is what makes item 143's derived-but-unused verdict the right lever.

**Duty cycle, before and after.** Worst case before coalescing is `H/(H+I)` against a drop interval `I` of ~2 s: **81.1% measured → ~11%** at a 250 ms cap, versus the ~50% the share ceiling alone still permits. The number is anchored, not picked: 250 ms covers the tripping lane's own first two backoff rungs (both engines' ladders start at 100 ms and double), which is exactly the overlap "alignment" names. A first cut used 1 s and the throughput gate **caught it at 49.7%** — 1 s against a 2 s drop interval is 50%, i.e. exactly what the ceiling already gave.

**MEASURED post-release (v0.117.0 regression cycle, annotated 2026-08-11 — the ~11% above is a FLOOR, not the observed value).** The cycle replicated the field shape (chronic evidence-free drop storm, 1.8 M rows): v0.116.1 was killed at 105 s having landed 309,212 rows at 2,379 rows/s; v0.117.0 completed all 1,800,000 in 95 s at **14,173 rows/s — 5.96×, 86% of the no-storm reference — with gate duty (from its own `hold=` field) 92.6% → 36.4%**. The projection under-predicts duty because `H/(H+I)` assumes one gate window per drop, and a fleet-wide sever trips many lanes at once, each opening its own window; 36.4% is still comfortably under the 50% ceiling, and throughput — the unit the gates are stated in — is what the fix restored. Full run tables in `sluice-testing/session-reports/v0.117.0.md`; celled in `docs/dev/perf-parity-matrix.md` row 17 (2026-08-11, with the mode-dependent-trigger parity note: `ir.GrowEvidenceTelemetry` has one producer, the streamer's headroom watch, so the cap binds more readily on migrate/restore, which construct the gate with no telemetry seam).

**Gates, stated in the user's units.** `TestGrowGate_EvidenceFreeDropStormLeavesTheCopyMostOfItsThroughput` scores **chunks landed against the same lanes, against the same target, with no gate at all**, measured in the same run — an independent expected value that no change to the gate's self-reporting can move. Requires ≥50% of ungated throughput (pre-fix: **9.1%**), with an anti-vacuity half requiring an *evidenced* storm to still be quiesced to ≤25% so the cap cannot leak onto the evidenced path. `TestGrowGate_EvidenceGovernsTheDeepEscalationAndNotTheEarlyHolds` pins both halves of the scope; `TestGrowGate_EvidenceAccumulatesPerEpisodeAndResetsWithTheLadder` pins stickiness and reset. The old `TestGrowGate_SustainedDropStormLeavesTheCopyMostOfTheWallClock` is renamed `...SustainedStormIsStillBoundedByTheShareCeiling` — its old name read broader than the truth, since "the declared share" is half and half is not "most".

**Mutation runs, each confirmed applied before the result was trusted:** M1 disable the cap (`if false &&`) → the throughput gate FAILS at 9.1% and the scope gate FAILS; M2 apply the cap to ALL evidence (drop the `!episodeSawGrowEvidence` conjunct) → three gates FAIL including both anti-vacuity halves; M3 make the evidence non-sticky (`= evidence != None` instead of `|=`) → the accumulation gate FAILS; M4 delete the episode-boundary reset → **PASSED, which was the finding**: the ladder resets to rung 1 independently, so the first window after a healthy stretch holds `base` whether or not the flag reset, and the cap is not observable at rung 1. The gate was rewritten to drive four windows after the reset and now FAILS on M4. That mutant is the reason the "verify the mutant applied" rule has a fourth step: the mutant *had* applied (`grep -c` of the reset line returned 0), so a green run there was a genuine coverage gap and not a no-op edit.

**The `withScaledGrowGate` trap, worth recording.** The first implementation passed the entire existing suite untouched — because the helper scales the ladder to milliseconds while `GrowGateEvidenceFreeHoldCap` sat at its 1 s production default, two orders of magnitude above any hold the tests produce. The cap was unreachable and every pin was blind to it. It is now an explicit parameter of the helper, so a new test cannot silently omit the dimension. A suite that goes green on a behaviour change it cannot reach is indistinguishable from one that covers it.

### 153. Re-running `migrate` PG→MySQL over an existing target FALSE-REFUSES on every `json` column, and on every DOMAIN column — *✅ SHIPPED v0.117.0. NOT a concurrency chunk (no goroutine / channel / FSM / shared-state change), so the `-race` Integration job is the ordinary gate rather than a pre-tag requirement. Impl notes below; ADR-0166 carries the full amendment.*

**Implementation notes (2026-08-07).**

**A third bare-column family the filing did not name.** Ground-truthing every retargeting family against a real MySQL turned up `bit varying(N)` alongside `json`: PG reads it as `Varbit(8)`, MySQL has no varying-bit type and lands a fixed `BIT(8)`, and the un-normalised expected side false-refuses exactly as `json` does. The report's fixture had no such column. Two rule-table arms close both — `ir.JSON{Binary:false}` → `ir.JSON{Binary:true}` and `ir.Bit{Varying:true}` → `ir.Bit{}` — and both are inert on the emit lanes (MySQL's emitter reads neither field).

**The DOMAIN half is a second ENTRY POINT, not a rule arm, and the reason is a silent-loss trap.** `translate.RetargetForShapeCompare` is `RetargetForEngine` plus one thing: `ir.UnwrapDomain` before the rule table. Flattening inside `RetargetForEngine` was **rejected on evidence** — `restore`, `chain restore`, the broker's schema-delta replay and schema-forward hand its output to a SchemaWriter, and MySQL's emitter translates a domain's CHECKs into inline table CHECKs through `ir.DomainOf`, which reads `Column.Type`. Flattening there would trade this item's LOUD false-refusal for a SILENT constraint drop on the restore lane. The claim is a gate, not prose: `TestEmitTableDef_FlatteningTheRetargetWouldDropTheDomainCheck` asserts the wrapper-keeping pass emits the CHECK **and** that the flattening pass does not. `schema diff` accordingly builds two schemas — flattened for the comparison, wrapper-carrying for its `CREATE TABLE` suggestions.

**The premise pin was re-derived, not deleted.** `TestRetargetRules_NeverProduceABinaryType` ("no rule produces a binary type") is FALSE once `Domain{d AS Blob}` → `Blob`. Its replacement `TestRetargetRules_BinaryOutputOnlyFromABinarySource` pins what `columnIsNativelyBinary` actually needs — **the retarget never MANUFACTURES binariness**, so recorded provenance can only confirm the verdict the un-retargeted column would have given, never invert it — and its doc states plainly what it no longer guarantees. It carries an anti-vacuity floor on BOTH axes (≥8 probes rewritten, and the shape-compare lane must produce at least one binary output, which is the `Domain{d AS Blob}` cell).

**The entanglement is pinned rather than remembered.** Flattening without Bug 233's `arrayElementType` / `columnIsArrayLike` domain unwrap re-opens Bug 232 through domains, silently. `TestRetargetedDomainColumn_KeepsItsArrayElementFamily` drives the real retarget over EVERY element family the PG reader decodes × four shapes and fails if either unwrap is removed while the flattening stands (confirmed by mutation, both functions independently).

**Gates.** `TestRetargetCallSitesDeclareTheirLane` — an AST divergence map over `internal/pipeline`, `…/backup`, `…/migcore` making every retarget call site declare EMIT or COMPARE with a reason; fails on an undeclared site, a stale entry, and a lane/code disagreement in **both** directions. `TestRetargetRuleArmsAreAllProbed` — the rule table's arms derived from its own source, failing on an arm no probe reaches (the gap that let the missing `ir.JSON` arm go unnoticed for two years). `TestMigrate_PGToMySQL_RetargetedShapeMatchesTheCatalogReadBack` — every retargeting family × {bare, DOMAIN} on a real MySQL, with the postgis-tagged sibling carrying geometry.

**Mutation runs, each confirmed APPLIED (`grep` for the `MUTANT_Mn` marker) before the result was trusted.** M1 `ir.JSON` arm removed → the plain-`json` unit cell + all three integration sub-tests FAIL with the reported refusal text. M2 `ir.Bit` arm removed → same for `c_varbit`. M3 the DOMAIN unwrap removed → 13 unit cells, the binary premise's anti-vacuity floor, and the mysql binding pin all FAIL. M4 `ir.UnwrapDomain` removed from `columnIsNativelyBinary` → the binding pin FAILS naming the inversion. M5 / M6 the same removal from `arrayElementType` / `columnIsArrayLike` → the element-family matrix FAILS per family. M7 a rule that manufactures binariness (`ir.Text` → `ir.Blob`) → the re-derived premise FAILS on both lanes — the OPPOSITE direction. M8 two unprobed arms added → the arm roster FAILS naming both. M9 / M10 a COMPARE site put on the emit pass and an EMIT site on the compare pass → the lane roster FAILS in both directions. M11 the two entry points collapsed → the CHECK-drop evidence gate FAILS, printing the `CHECK` the emit lane would have lost.

<details>
<summary>Original report (kept for provenance)</summary>


`translate.retargetPGtoMySQL` has **no `ir.JSON` arm and no `ir.Domain` arm**, so the existing-tables shape gate — and `sluice schema diff` — compares an **un-retargeted** expected side against what MySQL actually read back. Ground truth, from a re-run over empty existing tables:

```
pipeline: 2 pre-existing target table(s) differ … refusing before any data moves:
  table "dom"   (column "jarr": want Domain{d_jarr AS Array<JSON[text]>}, target has JSON[binary])
  table "plain" (column "jscl": want JSON[text],                          target has JSON[binary])
```

**The `json` half is the wider one and has nothing to do with domains:** any plain PostgreSQL `json`/`jsonb` column makes a second `migrate` run against a populated-or-created target refuse. That is the `--resume`-shaped workflow and the "re-run after fixing one table" workflow, both of which an operator reaches for precisely when something already went wrong.

**Loud, no data loss, and a different lane from Bug 233** — that fix corrected the value/DDL path, which is why it is landed and this is not.

**Why it was deliberately NOT bundled with Bug 233.** The fix flattens `retargetTable`'s output, which invalidates the documented premise pin `TestRetargetRules_NeverProduceABinaryType` — the gate asserting "no rule here produces a binary type", which is load-bearing for `columnIsNativelyBinary`'s safety argument (nil `SourceColumnType` reads as "natively binary"). `Domain{d AS Blob}` → `Blob` would produce exactly that. So closing this means re-deriving that argument, which is a chunk, not a hunk — and bundling it would have been the Phase-B hedge CLAUDE.md warns against.

**The entanglement, stated because the order matters.** Flattening the retarget *without* Bug 233's `arrayElementType` / `columnIsArrayLike` domain unwrap would **reintroduce Bug 232 through domains**. That unwrap is already in (`a44c0fa7`), so this is now safe to do — but it was not before, and a future reader reversing the order would ship a silent-loss regression.

**Gate.** The shape gate's expected side must be built by the same retarget the writer's target-landing decisions use, and the pin should compare *retargeted expected* vs *catalog read-back* for every family that retargets — `json`/`jsonb`, `hstore`, `varchar`/`text`, `bit`, `geometry`, and each of those through a DOMAIN. Re-derive `TestRetargetRules_NeverProduceABinaryType`'s claim rather than deleting it: if flattening makes it false, the honest replacement is a pin on what `columnIsNativelyBinary` actually needs, not the removal of its evidence.

</details>

### 152. A `json[]` / `bytea[]` column reaching a MySQL target silently base64s its elements — *✅ SHIPPED v0.116.0 ( `f67dd126` + the review follow-up below). NOT a concurrency chunk, so the `-race` Integration job is the ordinary gate rather than a pre-tag requirement.*

`convertArrayLikeToJSON` (`internal/engines/mysql/row_writer.go:1433`) hands the array to `encoding/json` in its `[]any` arm (`:1453-1458`), and `encoding/json` renders a `[]byte` element as **base64**. So a Postgres `json[]` holding `{"{\"a\":1}"}` lands on a MySQL JSON column as `["eyJhIjoxfQ=="]` — a document replaced by an opaque string — at **exit 0**. `bytea[]` is the same shape on the same arm.

**Why it is silent rather than loud.** `json.Marshal` succeeds; every layer reports success; the target holds a syntactically valid JSON array of the right length. Nothing downstream can tell a base64 string from a string the source actually contained, which is what puts it above the loud unwritable-family failures (items 141/145) rather than beside them.

**It is item 145's unenumerated sibling, and that is the generalisable part.** Item 145 swept the `json[]` family across the PG target and the pgtrigger door and closed both; it did not look at the MySQL target. The two doors were fixed and their third was not — the sibling-sweep shape CLAUDE.md calls the project's most expensive recurring failure. No pin exists in any shape on the MySQL side of this family.

**Fix shape, and the ambiguity that constrains it.** The leaf has to be decided rather than marshalled: `[]byte` elements need an explicit arm that renders the document (or the `\x`-hex bytes) rather than falling through to `json.Marshal`'s default. Note item 145's finding applies here verbatim and is already written down at the pgtrigger refusal — **`json`/`jsonb` is the one array family whose value space collides with the capture format's own encoding**, so a payload-decoded `json[]` cannot distinguish a JSON `null` element from a SQL NULL element, nor an array-valued element from a nested dimension.
