Compaction's default budget as a literal → the binding's consumer half fails alone. Slot roll at 2× budget → the new tight-bound cell fails while the degraded-case cell correctly still passes. Report wiring removed → the integration assertion fails on a real chain. `pushCollapsed` releasing the held commit → all THREE F3 flushers fail (PK-change barrier, DDL barrier, eviction), which is the non-vacuity proof for the invariant this item was warned it could break.

**Original filing follows.**

Item 127 bounded the retained-INPUT term: `s.accumulators` now evicts under a byte ceiling. `s.out` was the OTHER growing structure the audit named, and it is untouched — the compactor appends every emitted event and holds them all until `applySmartCompactionToIncremental` re-encodes them. So peak is now O(cap + output) rather than O(input).

**Why that is a real improvement and still not a bound.** For the collapsing workloads smart compaction exists for, output is small and the cap is the whole win — the audit's 100:1 corpus goes from 248 MiB to roughly the cap. For an incremental with NO collapse opportunity, output ≈ input and the peak is essentially unchanged. Both halves are worth saying: the fix is not cosmetic, and it is not a ceiling.

**Why it was not just another counter.** Three things stack up, and only the first is the compactor's own:

1. `s.out []ir.Change` — would need the compactor to stream into a sink instead of accumulating. Tractable on its own: the only ordering subtlety is `flushCollapsedInsideClosingTx`, which needs the closing `TxCommit` held back, and a one-slot lookahead reproduces that exactly.
2. **Step 2 packs every emitted event into `chunkBuckets[0]`** and leaves the other chunks empty, so the rewritten chunk is one unbounded blob regardless of how many chunks the incremental had. Distributing across the existing chunk slots under a byte budget is the natural fix, and `DefaultBackupChunkBytes` is the obvious budget — output bytes are ≤ input bytes, so for chains written by ≥v0.111.1 (whose chunks are already capped at 64 MiB) the slots always suffice.
3. **The encrypted `ChangeChunkWriter` buffers the whole gzipped chunk in `gzBuf`** and encrypts at Close — one GCM tag per chunk is the format. So bounding (1) without (2) achieves nothing for encrypted chains, which is the shape that would make a gate pass on a plaintext test and be inert where it matters.

**And the reason this cannot be done as a small change:** step 1 READS every staged chunk and step 3 WRITES them. Streaming output during the read phase would overwrite staged input chunks that have not been read yet. The escape routes both have real cost — writing to fresh paths changes the chunk AAD (`ChangeChunkAAD` binds `c.File` and the index, deliberately, as the anti-splice property) and would ripple through every surface that references a chunk path; staging to temp paths and moving costs a full extra read+write of every chunk, on object storage, on a maintenance path.

**Take it with the same gate shape item 127 used:** a measured ceiling with an anti-vacuity control (the same corpus, uncapped, must blow past it), plus a byte-identical control for a corpus that never reaches the ceiling. Note that a peak-memory assertion on `s.out` needs a real accounting hook, not `runtime.MemStats` — the latter is flaky enough to be worse than no gate.

### 129. `backup verify` cannot detect an unreadable chunk, because it never parses a row — *✅ IMPLEMENTED on branch 2026-08-05; shipped in **v0.113.0***

**What landed: `backup verify --depth read`.** A second depth that streams every chunk — data chunks AND change chunks — through the real `ChunkReader`/`ChangeChunkReader` with the exact (CEK, AAD, codec, segment store) quadruple `restore` resolves, and discards the rows. `hash` stays the default and is byte-identical to before; the depth is a `VerifyDepth` whose ZERO VALUE is `hash`, so the CLI is the only thing that can turn the cost on (the v0.99.51 zero-value trap, applied in the safe direction). A byte-intact chunk its own reader cannot decode is the new `SLUICE-E-BACKUP-CHUNK-UNREADABLE`.

**Both chunk kinds from the outset, deliberately.** Item 128's first cut closed two of three WRITE cores and the third was found a day later; repeating that shape on the read side would have left the incremental/CDC lane — the one the residual actually bites on — uncovered. The mutation run confirms the lanes are independently covered: skipping the read for change chunks fails exactly the four change-chunk cells and leaves the four data-chunk cells green.

**What the depth covers, and what no depth covers.** Covered, each verified as passing the hash depth and failing the read depth: an over-long row/change line (Bug 226's shape on pre-v0.112.0 artifacts), a truncated codec stream with a re-stamped SHA, a wrong RECORDED segment codec, a value envelope the decoder rejects, and — on an encrypted chain with key material — a wrong CEK/AAD. NOT covered by any depth, said out loud in the code, in `error-codes.md`, and in the cookbook rather than implied: whether the VALUES are correct (a parse proves the chunk decodes, and a backup cannot be independent evidence about itself — that is `sluice verify`'s job), and whether the rows will APPLY to a target. One more named residual: a CHANGE chunk whose decoded event count disagrees with its recorded `RowCount` is NOT refused, because chain restore does not check it either and verify must never refuse a chain `restore` would accept. Row chunks DO get that cross-check, from the same `checkChunkRowCount` predicate `Restore.streamChunkRows` uses — one predicate, two callers, so they cannot drift the way the manifest-preflight LISTS did (Bug 217/218).

**The acceptance fixture is deliberately not the writer's output.** The artifact under test is one a pre-item-128 binary produced, and the current writers refuse exactly that row on all three cores — so building the fixture with them would be the item-104 trap in its purest form (a fixture of post-change values proving the binary agrees with itself). The over-long chunks are assembled at the BYTE level, and the split is stated where it is built: the header line and every ordinary record line come off the REAL writers, the over-long line is one of those real lines with a marker inflated past the limit (a genuine record whose only defect is length), the gzip framing is stdlib rather than the codec under test, and the recorded SHA is always stamped over the final on-disk bytes so the hash depth has nothing to complain about.

**Gates, and both mutation directions.** The unit matrix asserts a PAIR per cell — the hash depth returns rc=0 AND the read depth refuses — over {data, change} × {plaintext, encrypted} × {over-long line, truncated stream}, plus healthy controls at both depths and a layer-2 row-count cell. Asserting only the refusal would pass on a verify that had merely become stricter; asserting only the rc=0 would pass on a verify that does nothing. Mutations, each confirmed applied before being trusted: read depth made inert → all 8 hostile cells + the layer-2 cell + the zero-value pin fail; change chunks routed back to the hash path → exactly the 4 change-chunk cells fail; hash depth made to read → the rc=0 half fires on every cell, which is what proves that half is not vacuous. The FALSE-REFUSAL direction — the one hand-built fixtures cannot speak to, since a fixture's codec and AAD are whatever the fixture said — is gated by wiring the read depth into `TestChainShaping_EncryptedRoundTripMatrix`'s `verifyChain`, so every rotated/pruned/compacted chain × {plaintext, per-chain, per-chunk} must now pass BOTH depths and the two must agree on chunk and decrypted counts. Green on real Postgres.

**Audit C-4 closed in the same pass** (compaction re-stamping its own verify hashes). `applySmartCompactionToIncremental` stamped `SHA256`/`RowCount` from its own writer's in-memory accounting and never read the object back, so every later consumer checked the store's bytes against a number the writer asserted. It now re-reads each rewritten chunk through the store with the real reader and compares the decoded event count against the recorded one. Sibling sweep, stated at the gate: smart compaction is the ONLY maintenance path that re-encodes chunk bytes and re-stamps a SHA — the non-smart path moves chunks verbatim through `copyFile` carrying their ORIGINAL hash (evidence this run did not produce), and `backup prune` rewrites no bytes at all. Gated by a store whose `Put` silently drops the tail; mutation-confirmed.

**Not done here:** the chunk-header ↔ manifest-schema column cross-check that `Restore.streamChunkRows` performs is still restore-only, so a chunk written against a different schema version stays a verify-green/restore-refuses shape. It is a schema-pairing check rather than a readability one and was left out to keep this diff to one class; filed as its own residual rather than folded in silently.

**Original filing follows.**

Item 128 stopped new backups containing a row larger than `MaxChunkLineBytes`. It did nothing for artifacts ALREADY written, and the reason those were possible is still live: **`backup verify` rehashes chunk BYTES and never parses a row**, so it confirms the bytes are intact while saying nothing about whether they can be read back.

That is the shared-evidence class the 2026-08-01 rule names — a verification whose "all clear" derives from the same artifact as the thing it verifies. Bug 226's exact shape: `backup full` rc=0, **`backup verify` rc=0**, `restore` rc=1 with 0 rows.

**The independent evidence is cheaply available and unused:** whether the chunk's own reader can scan it. A verify depth that streams each chunk through the real `ChunkReader` (decompress, decrypt, scan lines, discard rows) would catch an over-long line, a truncated stream, and a codec/AAD mismatch that a hash alone confirms as "intact". Cost is one full read per chunk, which is why it likely belongs behind a depth flag rather than the default — `verify` today is deliberately hash-only so it can run against object storage cheaply.

**Scope it honestly when taking it:** the point is not only the >64 MiB row. It is that the whole verify surface's evidence is the artifact itself. State which failure modes the new depth actually covers and which it still cannot, rather than implying a parse makes verify complete.

**Where the wider audit backlog lives — now TRACKED: [`audit-backlog.md`](audit-backlog.md).** The full audit reports still live in gitignored `workspace/`, but the open findings they carry no longer exist only there. That file is the durable copy; add to it whenever an audit lands, and promote anything with a confirmed silent-loss consequence to a numbered item here instead.

**Two corrections the 2026-08-05 reconciler made to this paragraph, both of which had been repeated as fact:**

- **The 08-01 gate proposals are NOT "nine of ten open".** Verified against the code: **6 BUILT, 2 PARTIAL, 2 OPEN.** Proposals 2/4/5 were built during the C1/C3 remediation itself (`f9389105`, `7e2a2d94`). Still open: the IR field-classification/DDL property gate, and the goroutine global-read analyzer. The wrong figure also propagated into project memory and was corrected there.
- **The MEDIUMs named here are the 08-04 audit's, not 08-01's** (compaction re-stamping its own verify hashes; `verifySchemaHashes` never running for a bare full; the broker's hand-rolled preflight subset).

This is the doc-lags-code shape the working agreements already name, on a paragraph whose whole purpose was to record what is untracked — worth noting that a note *about* backlog durability rotted the same way anything else does.

### 128. A backup you can take, VERIFY CLEAN, and never restore — a row over 64 MiB (Bug 226) — *✅ SHIPPED in **v0.112.0** (2026-08-05)*

Found by the v0.111.1 regression cycle while BOUNDING item 116's new chunk byte ceiling — pushing on the limit next door is what surfaced it. **Pre-existing**, identical on v0.111.0 and earlier, not a regression from 116.

**The shape, which is the worst one this project has:**

```
backup full    rc=0
backup verify  rc=0        <-- reports the backup fine
restore        rc=1, 0 rows   "chunk reader: scan: bufio.Scanner: token too long"
```

The operator finds out at the moment they need the backup. Measured by the cycle: a 60 MiB row round-trips, a 70 MiB row does not, and `migrate` of the SAME rows is rc=0 — so the data is fine and only the backup format's read path was not.

**Root cause.** `backup_chunk.go` sized the reader's `bufio.Scanner` at 64 MiB with a comment asserting that covered "the wide-row workloads `--max-buffer-bytes` targets" — an unverified premise about row size — and **the writer had no corresponding cap at all**. Two numbers where there should have been one, and one of them did not exist.

**Why `verify` could not see it, and why that is the interesting half.** `backup verify` rehashes the chunk BYTES and never parses a row. Its evidence is the same artifact it is checking, so it confirms the bytes are intact while saying nothing about whether they can be read back — the shared-evidence class the 2026-08-01 rule names ("a verification whose all-clear derives from the same artifact as the thing it verifies"). The independent evidence available and unused: whether the chunk's own reader can scan it.

**Fix.** `MaxChunkLineBytes` is now ONE exported constant; the reader sizes its scanner from it and the writer refuses on it, on BOTH write cores (the fast append encoder and `writeRowLegacy` — a refusal on one leaves the defect reachable through any row the fast path declines to encode). The writer refuses rather than the reader growing: raising the limit moves the wall without removing it and does nothing for backups already written, whereas refusing converts an unrestorable artifact with a green verify into a loud failure while the operator can still act. The message names what would otherwise have happened.

Pinned by a refusal test, a large-but-readable control (1 MiB round-trips — wide rows are what this format is for), a both-cores count, and a SOURCE-level assertion that the scanner is configured from the shared constant rather than a literal. That last one is the durable fix: a value-equality test would pass against two literals that agree today and drift tomorrow, which is precisely the failure being closed. Mutation-confirmed both ways.

**The sibling sweep this fix's own commit did not do — found 2026-08-05, before v0.112.0 published.** "BOTH write cores" meant *both write cores in `backup_chunk.go`*. There is a THIRD: `ChangeChunkWriter.WriteChange` in `backup_change_chunk.go`, which had **no refusal at all**, and whose reader capped a line at a **literal** `64*1024*1024` rather than `MaxChunkLineBytes`. So Bug 226 was still fully live on the incremental/CDC path — a change event carries a whole row image, so a wide `TEXT`/`JSON`/`BLOB` column reaches the limit by exactly the same route, and `backup incremental` rc=0 / `backup verify` rc=0 / `restore` "token too long" reproduced verbatim.

**The gate did worse than miss it: pinned to `== 2` and substring-scoped to one file, it would have FAILED on a correct fix.** That is the "a GATE owes the same enumeration" rule in its sharpest form — a check whose name says *both write cores* and whose reach is *the two in this file*, which stops the next reader from looking. Replaced with an AST-derived roster over the whole package: every function writing a marshalled record (the `bufW.Write(b)` shape) must call `checkChunkLineLength`, and every `bufio.Scanner` over a chunk stream must be sized from `MaxChunkLineBytes` — each with an anti-vacuity floor (≥3 cores, ≥2 readers) so a walker that stops matching the code fails loudly instead of passing on zero findings. Mutation-confirmed three ways: refusal removed → both the behavioural test and the roster fail and the roster names the function; scanner reverted to the literal → the roster fails; walker's match string broken → the floor fires.

**One interaction the sweep surfaced.** Collapsing merges after-images as a UNION of their columns, so `backup compact --smart-compaction` can now refuse a *collapsed* event that is larger than any of the events it replaced — a chain the source backup wrote happily. Refusing is correct (the rewritten chunk would not restore), so the compaction path recognises the refusal via the new `blobcodec.ErrChunkLineTooLong` sentinel and adds the remedy the codec cannot know: re-run with `--smart-compaction-off`.

**Residual, stated rather than implied:** `backup verify` still cannot detect this class on backups written by OLDER binaries — it does not parse rows. A verify that scans each chunk with the real reader would be the independent check; that is its own item (129), not folded in here. Note that item 129 now covers strictly more than it did when filed: change chunks are in its scope too.

### 127. `--smart-compaction` buffers an ENTIRE incremental in RAM — no row cap, no byte cap (audit 2026-08-04 HIGH, measured) — *✅ RETAINED-INPUT HALF FIXED in **v0.113.0**. The emitted-output half is item 130.*

**What landed.** A byte ceiling on retained accumulator state (`defaultMaxRetainedBytes`, 32 MiB of ESTIMATED SERIALIZED bytes) with early eviction, so an incremental carrying no TRUNCATE and no DDL can no longer retain itself entirely.

**The eviction ORDER is the design, not the ceiling.** A cap on a collapsing transform must sacrifice something, and the roadmap's original suggestion — largest-first — is only half right. The policy is: single-event chains first in INSERTION order, then largest-first among the rest. Single-event chains cost *nothing* to evict (a one-event accumulator's flush emits that event verbatim, which is exactly what finalize would have emitted, in the order `flushAll` would have used). That matters more than it looks: **an incremental with no collapse opportunity is all single-event chains, so the workload with the worst retention is also the one where the cap changes nothing observable.** Hysteresis (drain to cap/2) stops a corpus sitting at the ceiling from re-sorting its accumulator set on every event. Reservation happens BEFORE the append, so the ceiling is one the compactor stays under rather than overshoots by an event.

**Correctness under eviction** rests on one property: a chain evicted at time T is emitted at T, and any later event for the same PK starts a fresh accumulator emitted after it — so per-PK source order holds, which is what ADR-0064 §2's policy table is defined over. A chain collapses in two groups instead of one: always a superset of the events full collapse emits, never a different end state. Pinned by replaying both streams and asserting identical final row state.

**Gates, and what the mutation runs caught.** Peak-under-cap with an anti-vacuity control (same corpus uncapped must blow past it — measured 19.3×); a byte-identical control for a corpus below the ceiling; the no-collapse corpus asserted unreordered. Mutating the policy to largest-first-only initially PASSED, because every row in that corpus had the same width and `sort.SliceStable` left equal elements in insertion order — the test could not tell the two policies apart. Widths now vary, and the mutation fails. Worth recording as its own small lesson: **a gate over an ordering policy needs inputs whose natural order and policy order differ, or it pins nothing.**

**The cap is enforced on an ESTIMATE**, so `TestEstimateChangeBytes_TracksRealMarshalledSize` binds `estimateChangeBytes` to real `json.Marshal` output across the value families the format carries. Without it the cap would be checked against its own arithmetic — the shared-evidence shape the 2026-08-01 rule names.

**The F3 invariant broke, exactly where the filing said it would.** The entry warned "the F3 position invariant must still hold — see `flushCollapsedInsideClosingTx` and item 101 for how easy that is to break", and the first cut broke it. `flushCollapsedInsideClosingTx` holds the closing TxCommit back AT FINALIZE; eviction appended straight to `s.out`. On an incremental whose window ends mid-transaction — row events after the last TxCommit — eviction appended after the commit, finalize then saw a non-TxCommit tail, took the plain `flushAll` path, and the stream ended on a collapsed row event carrying its chain's FIRST position: a chain below its own recorded EndPosition, which F1 refuses as truncated. `evict` now splices before a trailing TxCommit so the closing position is last at EVERY point in the pass. **The generalisable half: the finalize-time check was a LOCATION, not the invariant** — and a second writer to the same stream is all it took to get out from under it. Caught by re-reading the filing after implementing, not by a test; the test came after and is mutation-confirmed.

**Two things the constant's doc says out loud** because a reader would otherwise get them wrong: the number is wire bytes, not Go heap bytes (heap is a multiple — the audit's 261 MiB for 100k events implies ~2.6 KiB apiece for far smaller events), and a single event larger than the cap is still retained because there is nothing left to evict, bounded in turn by the chunk format's 64 MiB per-row limit.

**Not fixed here: the emitted-output term.** Filed as item 130 with the reasons it is not a small change.

**Original filing follows.**

**Confirmed at HEAD (2026-08-05):** `chain_compact_smart.go` has no `maxEvents` / `maxBytes` / byte-cap of any kind. The compactor holds two growing structures for the whole pass — `s.out` (every emitted event, appended at three sites) and `s.accumulators` (every per-PK chain, retained until a flush barrier) — and the only barriers are TRUNCATE, `SchemaSnapshot` and end-of-incremental. An incremental with none of those retains everything.

*Measured by the audit:* 100k events → **261 MiB**; a 100:1-collapsing corpus → **248 MiB**, i.e. **no relief from collapsing**, because the inputs are retained until flush regardless of how well they collapse. ~2.6 GiB extrapolated at 1M events.

**This is NOT roadmap 116, and the audit says so explicitly.** Item 116 P3 capped the backup CHUNK WRITER's buffer (shipped v0.111.1, 64 MiB). This is the compaction transform's own accumulator, a different buffer on a different path — and fixing the neighbour is exactly the kind of near-miss that makes a reader assume the class is closed. It is not.

**Why it is harder than 116 P3.** The chunk writer could roll at any row boundary; the compactor cannot flush an accumulator mid-chain without giving up the collapse it exists to perform, and flushing early changes WHICH events collapse — an observable output change, not just a memory one. So a cap has to decide what to sacrifice: likely flush the LARGEST accumulators first (bounded memory, partial collapse, correct output) rather than refusing. Whatever is chosen, the output must remain correct under ADR-0064 §2's policy table, and the F3 position invariant must still hold — see `flushCollapsedInsideClosingTx` and item 101 for how easy that is to break.

**Gate it with a measured ceiling**, in the shape item 116 P3 used: a test that drives the real compactor with wide events and asserts peak retention stays under the cap, plus a control asserting a narrow corpus still collapses exactly as it does today (byte-identical output).

### 126. Copy-parallelism AIMD burns its whole retry budget on the first wave, so a transient slot shortage aborts the run (audit 2026-08-04 HIGH) — *✅ SHIPPED in **v0.112.0** (2026-08-05)*

**Implementation notes.** `attempts` / `totalWait` became `attemptsByChunk` / `waitByChunk`, keyed on the `chunkIndex` the API already carried. Justified at the time by "the gate is constructed PER TABLE over that table's chunk set (`NewCopyParallelismGate(len(chunks), …)`), so the index is unique within a gate — checked, not assumed." **That sentence is now WRONG and is left here as the exhibit:** ADR-0123's run-wide gate falsified it without touching it, and the check it claimed was a reading, not a test. Item 137 keys on `(table, chunk)` and pins the uniqueness with a test that fails when the table is dropped from the key.

**The SHRINK deliberately stays run-wide.** Many concurrent 53300s SHOULD collapse parallelism hard and fast; that is the AIMD working. Only the give-up bound and the backoff exponent are properties of one chunk's own progress. The new test asserts both halves — sixteen concurrent first attempts all proceed AND the effective parallelism still collapses to the floor of 1.

**The existing test asserted the DEFECT as the contract.** `TestCopyParallelismGate_ConcurrentShrinkBackoffBound` pinned "many chunks hammering concurrently produce exactly MaxRetries successes and the rest give up" — sixteen distinct chunks, each on its FIRST attempt, eleven aborted. That is the bug written down as an expectation, and it is why the audit had to find this by reading rather than by a red test. Replaced with `_ConcurrentFirstAttemptsAllProceed`, plus `_OneChunkStillGivesUp` for the other half: a per-chunk budget must still be BOUNDED, and one chunk exhausting its budget must not pre-abort its peers. Mutation-confirmed by re-sharing the counter across chunks.

**Confirmed at HEAD (2026-08-05):** `CopyParallelismGate.attempts` (`copy_parallelism_gate.go:69`) is documented as "the total slot-exhaustion retries across all chunks of this table" and `ShrinkAndBackoff` increments it once per FAILING WORKER (`:143`), then feeds that run-wide count straight into `NextCopyBackoff`'s give-up bound.

So the counter conflates two different things: how many times ONE chunk has retried, and how many workers have hit 53300 at all. At the shipped 4×4 = 16 concurrent, sixteen workers hitting a slot shortage at nearly the same moment consume the entire budget (`MaxRetries` 6) between them — **the 7th aborts the whole run while workers 1–6 are still parked in their first backoff, having executed ZERO retries.** The gate's stated purpose — "a transient slot shortage degrades to slower-but-correct" — does not hold at any parallelism ≥ 7, which is every default multi-core run.

**The shrink half still works**, which is what hides it: parallelism does come down, so an operator sees the AIMD "working" right up until the abort.

**Fix shape.** Separate the two quantities: a PER-CHUNK attempt count feeding the give-up bound, and a run-wide tally for the shrink signal (which is what the AIMD genuinely wants — many concurrent 53300s SHOULD shrink hard). `totalWait` has the same shape and deserves the same look. **Gotcha:** the give-up bound is also what stops an infinite retry against a genuinely full target, so the per-chunk budget must still terminate; the goal is that 16 workers get 16 chunks' worth of retries, not that any one chunk retries forever.

**Gate it at parallelism ≥ 7 specifically** — the audit's finding is that the property holds at low parallelism and fails at the default, so a test at 1–4 workers is green and vacuous.

### 125. `sluice schema diff` is structurally blind to the constraint drift the S8 work exists to prevent (audit 2026-08-04 HIGH, S9) — *✅ SHIPPED in **v0.112.0** (2026-08-05, both halves)*

**Index half — DONE.** `TableDiff.IndexesMismatched []IndexDiff` compares indexes present on both sides under one name, on the attributes that decide WHICH ROWS ARE LEGAL: the column list rendered INCLUDING per-column prefix length (so `email(10)` vs `email` is visible — the S8 class), `Unique`, and the partial `Predicate`. The PRIMARY KEY participates, matching `indexNames`' set. Deliberately NOT compared: index kind/method (a performance property no cross-engine pair agrees on; would make every MySQL↔PG diff noisy) and column ORDERING (ADR-0029 v1 scope). Wired through `HasChanges`, `Summary`, the JSON counts and the text renderer — the renderer leads with the CONSEQUENCE (`the target ACCEPTS ROWS THE SOURCE REJECTS`) rather than the attribute, because that is what decides urgency. Pinned by a matrix derived from the defect family (prefix dropped/differs, uniqueness dropped, predicate dropped, column set) plus two clean controls; mutation-confirmed twice — removing the comparison, and dropping the prefix from the renderer, each fail exactly the rows they should.

**FK half — DONE.** `ForeignKeysMissing/Extra/Mismatched` by constraint name, comparing what the constraint ENFORCES: the referencing and referenced column lists and parent table (a re-pointed FK constrains something else entirely), `OnDelete`/`OnUpdate` (a source CASCADE against a target RESTRICT changes what a parent delete DOES), `Match` (MATCH FULL rejects a partially-NULL composite key MATCH SIMPLE accepts — audit 2026-07-26 SL-7), and deferrability (reported as a unit, since the two flags are only meaningful together and `false` is both a real value and the zero value).

**UNNAMED foreign keys are counted, not silently skipped.** They have no stable identity to match on across two schema reads, so they cannot be compared — and `ForeignKeysUnnamed` says how many were skipped rather than letting a clean report imply coverage it does not have. MySQL always names FK constraints, so it is normally zero.

Mutation-confirmed: removing the comparison fails the drift matrix and the dropped-FK test.

**Confirmed at HEAD (2026-08-05):** `TableDiff` (`internal/ir/diff/schema_diff.go:153`) carries `IndexesMissing []string` and `IndexesExtra []string` — **name-only** — with no `IndexesMismatched` and **no foreign-key fields at all**. A source `UNIQUE(email(10))` against a target `UNIQUE(email)` therefore compares **EQUAL**: same name, present on both sides. So does a dropped partial predicate, a changed column list, and any FK difference whatsoever.

That is the operator-facing surface someone would reach for to CHECK for exactly the silent constraint weakening items 118 and 120 were built to refuse. It cannot see it.

**Read the mis-mapping before starting, because it is the instructive part.** The 08-01 audit's remediation status recorded S9 as "already roadmap item 113". Item 113 is `migcore/incremental_delta_shape.go` — the incremental-backup delta, a different surface entirely. The 08-04 confirming pass caught it. **A finding marked as tracked by the wrong item is worse than one marked open**, because the status line reads as covered and nobody looks again.

**There is a second trap waiting for whoever takes this.** `internal/ir/diff/schema_drift.go` DOES have `ForeignKeysAdded` / `ForeignKeysDropped` / `ForeignKeysAltered`. A grep for "does diff know about foreign keys?" answers YES and is answering about a **different type on a different surface** (drift reports, not `schema diff`). Confirm which struct the command renders before concluding anything.

**Fix shape.** Add index-mismatch and FK entries to `TableDiff`, comparing the attributes that actually change semantics — the column list including `IndexColumn.Length`, `Unique`, the partial predicate, and the FK's columns/referenced table/actions. The drift-report structs are the model for the shape. **Pin it against the class it exists to catch:** the S8 matrix — prefix length, partial predicate, uniqueness — must each produce a diff entry, with a control that an identical schema still reports clean.

### 124. `information_schema.table_rows` on MariaDB undershot by 40%, so progress read as a count mismatch — *✅ SHIPPED in **v0.111.1** (2026-08-05)*

**The surface was narrower than the filing assumed, and finding that out was the work.** Both progress surfaces ALREADY labelled the number: the TTY panel renders `100%+` and annotates the count "est. exceeded", and the non-TTY `bulk copy progress` line has carried `total_rows_estimated=true` since roadmap #22. The one that did not was the **dry-run plan** — which is precisely the number an operator diffs against the final copied count, since it is printed once, up front, per table. Fixed by adding `row_count_estimated` to `PlanTable` (JSON and slog), mirroring the progress line's existing convention. `-1` (unavailable) is deliberately NOT labelled estimated: "unknown" and "an approximate zero" are different claims, and the sentinel exists so consumers cannot confuse unknown with empty.

The third finding from the same report, and the one the reporter themselves called "not anything sluice does wrong". They are right about the cause and it is still worth closing: on their source the estimate read 1,026,026 against 1,701,520 actual, so the copy sailed past 100% and the numbers "showed false mismatches".

**`verify` is NOT affected and that was checked, not assumed** — it calls `ExactRowCount` on both sides (`verify.go`; the MySQL implementation's own doc contrasts itself with `CountRows`, "which uses `information_schema.tables.table_rows` for ETA hints — that's approximate"). Their run agreed: they reported the data verified as matching. So this is a *presentation* defect confined to progress/ETA, not a correctness one.

The TTY panel already handles it (`model.go` renders `100%+` and annotates the count "est. exceeded", with a comment naming this exact InnoDB behaviour). What is left is everything that is not the live panel: the number is emitted elsewhere without the word "estimate" attached, so it reads as a target to be matched. **Fix shape:** label it at every surface that prints it — an ETA total is an estimate and should say so once, rather than being silently reinterpreted as an expectation. Cheap, and it removes a "did my migration lose rows?" moment at exactly the wrong time.

Note the class this belongs to: it is a *verification whose expected value is not independent* wearing UX clothes. The estimate and the true count come from different oracles, and the display implied they should agree.

### 123. The buffer-pool tier proxy mis-tiered a PS-160 to the tightest cap, and its own "operator-visible" provenance was never logged — *✅ SHIPPED in **v0.111.1** (2026-08-05, from the field report)*

ADR-0116 Part B caps copy parallelism from `@@innodb_buffer_pool_size`, on the premise that the value scales monotonically by PlanetScale plan tier (live-measured PS-10 0.125 GB → PS-160 9.80 GB) and is not masked by vtgate. **The premise failed in the field:** a PS-160 branch returned **32 MiB**, which bucketed to the smallest tier and capped table parallelism at **2 instead of 8** — a silent 4× throughput loss on a large instance. The reporter noticed only because they read the code.

**Two defects, one report.** (1) The heuristic had no plausibility check, so a reading that cannot be a tier answer was treated as evidence of a tiny instance — the *wrong* direction, because an absent cap merely falls back to the connection budget (a real slot bound) while a wrong tight cap throttles the copy and looks like sluice being slow. (2) `connectionBudget.tierCap`'s doc said it was "carried for the operator-facing log so the cap's provenance is visible" — **and nothing read the field**, which is why the operator could not tell whether parallelism 2 came from the cap, the connection budget, or a flag. A written invariant nobody checks, in the narrow form where the thing it promises is a log line.

**REPRODUCED against real PlanetScale 2026-08-05, and the premise's exception is now measured:** a PRODUCTION PS-10 branch returns exactly `134217728` (128 MiB), matching the ADR table; a DEV branch on the same database returns `33554432` (32 MiB) — the field report's value precisely. The two report different Vitess versions (8.4.6 vs 8.4.9), so they are demonstrably not the same infrastructure. Every measurement the heuristic was built from had been taken on a production branch, which is why the exception went unnoticed. Note how tight the boundary is: a real PS-10 returns EXACTLY the floor value and the check is strictly-below, so the smallest legitimate tier is still capped — one byte higher and the floor would have broken the tier it exists to protect.

**Fix.** A floor at PS-10's measured 128 MiB: below it, on the PlanetScale flavor only (the cap is already flavor-gated), the reading is treated as UNREADABLE rather than as a tiny tier — with a WARN naming the value and the floor. When the cap *is* applied it now emits an INFO carrying the observed pool size, the derived cap, and the pre-cap budget, which makes the tier decision auditable for the first time. Pinned by the extended change-detector plus `TestBufferPoolTierCap_ImplausibleReadingDoesNotThrottleTheCopy`, which drives the real `computeConnectionBudget` and carries the control that a genuine PS-10 reading still caps — mutation-confirmed by deleting the floor.

**Residual, stated because it is real:** sluice still has no credential-free way to read a PlanetScale branch's actual tier, so when the probe is masked there is now NO tier cap rather than a wrong one. The metrics-aware clamp (ADR-0115/0107) remains the robust path when telemetry is configured. What the fix buys is that the failure is loud and the fallback is the safe direction.

### 122. A vtgate transport loss was terminal in one wire framing and retriable in the other, so a cold copy died 5 times out of 5 — *✅ SHIPPED in **v0.111.1** (2026-08-05, from the field report)*

The blocking finding from the first production field report: `sluice migrate` completed a 2.64 GB / ~16M row MariaDB → PlanetScale move cleanly, and `sluice sync` failed **every** attempt during cold-start bulk copy — always on the widest table, always 90–130 s in, at a **varying** chunk index (so: not one bad row), with

```
Error 1105 (HY000): internal: vtgate connection error (read: connection reset by peer / unexpected EOF)
```

**Root cause, confirmed by probing the classifier rather than by reading it.** Under Error 1105, `classifyApplierError` consults `vtgateTransientSubstrings`, and that set carried vtgate's *availability* sentences only. Feeding it the observed text returns **not retriable**; feeding it the SAME underlying loss in vttablet's gRPC framing (`... vttablet: rpc error: code = Unavailable desc = connection reset by peer`) returns **retriable**. So one condition had two verdicts depending on which layer happened to report it, and the terminal one is the framing a cold copy actually meets.

**It is a sibling of a fix already in the file.** The Number-2013 branch was added for exactly this shape and its comment already names the trap — the transport cause is TEXT inside a `*MySQLError` message, so `errors.Is(err, io.EOF)` cannot see it, and under 1105 only the substring set is consulted. That fix stopped at one framing; the sweep did not ask which other framings carry the same loss.

**Fix.** `"vtgate connection error"` joins the set as category (3), transport loss. The anchor is vtgate's own product noun, not the generic tail: a 1105 message can carry an echoed statement, and a false positive is not merely a wasted retry — it arms the cold-copy tolerate-1062-on-retry wart on the next attempt. `TestVtgateTransportLoss_BothFramingsAgree` pins both framings to one verdict plus the echo-safety and client-cancel boundaries; mutation-confirmed both ways (removing the entry fails the vtgate cases; anchoring on `"connection reset by peer"` instead fails the echoed-statement case). Provenance is recorded as FIELD-DERIVED in both the slice and its pin, because unlike the rest of the set it was not read off an upstream constant.

**One classifier serves both consumers** — `flushWithReparentRetry` (cold copy, ADR-0108) and the CDC apply loop — so the fix reaches both; `TestVtgateTransportLoss_ReachesBothRetryConsumers` asserts that sharing by source so a future split cannot silently re-open half of it.

**What is NOT established, stated so nobody inherits it:** *why* the connection dropped. A storage-grow reparent on the downsized branch fits the timing, but their logs were not available and the classifier gap is provable without it. Their batch size is explained, though, and it rules one theory out: ~4,000 rows/statement is exactly `maxBulkInsertPlaceholders`(60000) ÷ 15 columns, i.e. the placeholder ceiling, which means the statement was under the ~1 MiB byte target and the failure was **not** an oversized write. Whether the retry now rides their specific drop out is unverified until they re-run.

### 121. `ir.Enum.TypeName` is dropped by every manifest round trip, so a restored PG enum is re-created under a synthesized name — *✅ SHIPPED in **v0.111.1** (2026-08-05)*

**Implementation notes.** The split Macaddr.Width needed, for a field that is non-zero far more often: `TypeName` now rides the type envelope (`enum_type_name`) so a restore re-creates the type under its real name, and `fingerprintType` strips it so no chain is repartitioned. The PG reader sets it for EVERY enum column, so folding it into the hash would have moved close to every Postgres chain in existence — a bigger blast radius than item 104 itself. Pinned by with-vs-without EQUALITY (which a self-consistent binary cannot satisfy by agreeing with itself), a byte-level assertion that the hashed bytes carry no `enum_type_name` key at all (the cross-version half), a no-mutation check, a rides-the-wire check at all three nesting sites (scalar, array element, domain base), and an anti-vacuity floor asserting an enum VALUE change still moves the hash. Mutation-confirmed both ways: removing the exclusion fails the fingerprint tests, dropping the decode half fails the envelope gate and the wire test.

**Named residual.** The schema DIFF does not see an enum type RENAME, because `ir.Enum.String` renders only the values — so a rename with identical values crosses a chain boundary unnoticed. That is the price of the exclusion and it is written at `fingerprintType`, not left implied. It changes no data and no column type.

**The `Char/Varchar/Text.Determinism` siblings are ADJUDICATED, not wired** — moved from `envelopeKnownGap` to `envelopeExempt` after running the three checks the gap entry demanded rather than inheriting `Enum.Collation`'s argument: (1) exactly one consumer, the `--where` string-equality resolver; (2) NO DDL-emit consumer on any of the three engines — the check that would have made it a must-wire, since an emitter rendering a non-deterministic collation from it would mean restore changed `=` semantics; (3) the predicate is compiled from a LIVE schema read on a path no decoded manifest schema reaches. `envelopeKnownGap` is now EMPTY, and its doc says so as a real state rather than a defaulted one.

The first finding from the reflective `schemaTypeEnvelope` gate built in item 117, and the reason that gate was worth more than the fix it shipped with. The Postgres reader sets `TypeName` for every PG enum column (`types.go`: `ir.Enum{Values: …, TypeName: c.EnumTypeName}`), and it is documented as the thing that stops a same-engine PG restore renaming `post_status` to `posts_status_enum`. It is not in the type envelope, so a manifest round trip drops it and **restore does exactly the renaming it was added to prevent**.

**Wiring it is NOT free, and this is the trap to plan for.** `TypeName` is non-zero on ordinary PG source data, so simply adding it to the envelope moves the schema fingerprint of every chain carrying a PG enum column and mints a new epoch — item 104 verbatim, and the same trap `Macaddr.Width` had to be threaded through. It needs the identical treatment: **ride the wire so restore is correct, exclude from the hash so no chain is repartitioned**, pinned by a with-vs-without EQUALITY test. `fingerprintType` in `internal/ir/backup/chain.go` is the hook, and it already recurses through `Array.Element` and `Domain.BaseType`.

**Sibling findings from the same sweep, filed together because they share a cause** (`Char/Varchar/Text.Determinism`): set by the PG reader from `collisdeterministic` and read back as `Unknown`. `ir.Enum.Collation`'s written rationale plausibly covers them, but nobody wrote it down for these, and `ir.Type` participates in `reflect.DeepEqual` via `SchemaSignature.Equal` and `diffRenameColumnIR` — so a lossy round trip is not obviously harmless. Decide and record: either wire them (same fingerprint treatment) or move them from `envelopeKnownGap` to `envelopeExempt` with the argument written out.

### 120. A MySQL `PRIMARY KEY (col(20), …)` is SILENTLY widened on a SQLite target — *✅ SHIPPED to `main` 2026-08-04; CI green. Released in **v0.111.0**.*

**Implementation notes.** The refusal sits in [`emitTableDef`](../../internal/engines/sqlite/ddl_emit.go) **ahead of the inline/table-level PK branch**, not inside `quoteIndexColumnList`. The rowid-alias path (`INTEGER PRIMARY KEY`, rendered on the column) never reaches that renderer, and the only argument that it is safe there is *MySQL rejects a prefix on an integer key (errno 1089)* — a premise about the SOURCE, which the emitter should not have to hold. Checking ahead of the branch costs one call and makes both renderings covered; `TestPreflightIndexesAgreesWithTheEmitterOnThePrimaryKey` carries the rowid-alias row that fails if it moves back.

`enforcesUniqueness` for a PK is passed as a **constant**, never `pk.Unique`: both CDC relation readers build `&ir.Index{Columns: pkCols}` with `Unique` unset, and a PRIMARY KEY constrains the data by definition. That is a matrix row too (mutation-confirmed: swapping in `indexKeyKind(pk.Unique)` fails exactly that row and nothing else). SQLite's `refuseUnrepresentablePrefix` was reshaped to take a column list plus a `keyKind` — Postgres's function of the same name already had that signature, for the same reason: two key-emitting sites and only one of them has an `ir.Index` to hand.

**The refusals are NOT the same message with a different subject.** A secondary index can be rebuilt over `substr(email, 1, 20)`; a SQLite `PRIMARY KEY` clause takes column names, so the prefix has to leave the key entirely. `keyKind.prefixRemedy` holds the two endings and `TestPrimaryKeyRefusalNamesAPrimaryKeyRemedy` fails if the PK inherits the index one.

**Sibling sweep — every engine that renders a PK column list, fixed-or-exempt:** `sqlite` FIXED (and that is the whole D1 story too — `d1` renders no DDL at all, being a migrate source only, so a D1-bound migration is reached by the `sqlite` fix because it writes a `.db` file); `postgres` EXEMPT, its inline PK goes through `emitIndexColumnList(…, enforcesUniqueness=true)` and is pinned by the `primary key refuses` case in `index_prefix_length_test.go`; `pgtrigger` EXEMPT, both `OpenSchemaWriter` and `PreflightIndexes` delegate to `postgres.Engine`; `mysql` EXEMPT because it carries prefixes natively — and since that exemption cites a fact about the target rather than about sluice, it is now pinned by `TestEmitCreateTablePrimaryKeyKeepsThePrefixLength` rather than asserted in a comment.

The end-to-end pin is a MySQL→SQLite pair in `migrate_index_preflight_cross_integration_test.go` (refusal + an unprefixed-composite-PK control). It also ground-truths the premise the whole item rests on — that a real MySQL accepts `PRIMARY KEY (email(20), id)` — and mutation-confirmed the old behaviour: with the refusal disabled the migrate **succeeds**, target table and all.

Found while implementing item 118, and deliberately not fixed there because it is a different defect wearing the same clothes: item 118 was about *when* a refusal fires, this is a refusal that **does not exist**.

SQLite's table-level `PRIMARY KEY` clause renders through `quoteIndexColumnList`, which has never consulted `ir.IndexColumn.Length`. A MySQL `PRIMARY KEY (email(20), id)` therefore becomes `PRIMARY KEY (email, id)` on a SQLite target — including one bound for D1, which is how D1-bound data is written, since there is no D1 target engine — with no warning. That is the **admits-rows-the-source-rejects** direction: the source forbids two rows sharing the first 20 bytes of `email`, the target permits them, and the divergence is visible nowhere. Same class as audit S8, opposite half — S8's first half was the secondary-index prefix (now refused), this is the primary key.

Postgres has no equivalent gap: its inline PK goes through `emitIndexColumnList` with `enforcesUniqueness=true`, so `checkIndexPrefixLength` already sees it. MySQL supports prefixes natively. **SQLite is the only affected target**, which is exactly the shape the item-118 sweep was built to surface.

**Why it needs its own change rather than a line in 118.** Closing it makes `PreflightIndexes` refuse a schema that migrates (wrongly) today, so it is a behaviour change with a compatibility note, not a timing fix. `TestPreflightIndexesDoesNotWalkThePrimaryKey` pinned the current behaviour and **failed the moment the emitter was fixed**, which is the signal that told that author to walk `table.PrimaryKey` in SQLite's preflight in the same pass — the two had to land together or the preflight and the emitter disagree. They did, and that test is now deleted in favour of a PRIMARY KEY matrix.

### 119. `--smart-compaction`'s per-row collapse is INERT on every MySQL-family source, and its own report says "no primary key" (Bug 223) — *✅ SHIPPED in **v0.111.1** (2026-08-05)*

**Implementation notes.** Fixed at the LOOKUP, not with the name-only fallback the item filed as the hazard. The rule reads the recorded schema for what it means: an exact (schema, name) match always wins, so a Postgres or multi-database manifest — where the qualifier is real — behaves exactly as before; only when no exact match exists does an UNQUALIFIED manifest table (`Schema == ""`) match by name, because an empty recorded schema means the reader had exactly one namespace and such a name is unique within one manifest by construction. Ambiguity REFUSES to pick and reports itself, which is belt-and-braces: the construction argument says it cannot happen, and this whole item exists because an argument of that shape was already wrong once. A wrong PK tuple means a wrong collapse, which is silent data loss on a BACKUP path — strictly worse than the inertness.

**The reporting half is fixed too, and it is the half that kept the first hidden.** `TablesWithoutPK` conflated "this table declares no PK" (expected, the operator's to act on) with "the qualifier matched nothing" (a sluice defect that makes the collapse silently inert). They are now separate buckets on both the top-level result and the per-group plan, and the defect bucket also emits a WARN — Bug 223 survived three releases precisely because its only symptom was a quiet line about tables that had a plain INT PRIMARY KEY.

**Non-vacuity, as the item demanded:** `TestSmartCompact_MySQLQualifierStillCollapses` asserts `rowsCollapsed > 0` and a shrinking stream, not merely a successful run — a MySQL leg that is byte-identical on two binaries scores a clean pass when nothing ever collapsed. Mutation-confirmed three ways: exact-match-only reproduces the inertness, picking-on-ambiguity fails the hazard test, and re-conflating the buckets fails the reporting tests.

**Root cause confirmed by reading, not inferred.** `smartCompactor.pkColumns` (`internal/pipeline/backup/chain_compact_smart.go:483`) matches a change event to its IR table with `if t.Schema != schema || t.Name != table { continue }`. A MySQL change event carries `Schema` = the database name; the manifest's IR records `Schema: ""`. The comparison can therefore never succeed on a MySQL source, every table falls through to the `return nil, false` tail, and every event passes through verbatim. Observed as `events_collapsed=0` with `tables_without_pk` listing two tables that both have `INT PRIMARY KEY`. Reproduced identically on v0.108.1, v0.110.0 and v0.110.1, so it is long-standing.

**Zero-loss** — the chain is correct, merely uncompacted — which plus the misleading report is why it survived: every prior exercise of smart compaction used a Postgres source (Bug 95's closure and Bug 139's control are both PG).

**The reporting half is the half that hid it, and is worth fixing even if the matching fix is deferred.** `TablesWithoutPK` conflates two conditions that need opposite responses: *the table declares no primary key* (expected, operator-visible, nothing to do) and *the schema qualifier did not match any table in the manifest* (a sluice bug). The message reads as the first while meaning the second. Split them; the second should probably be loud.

**The hazard, and why this must not be rushed.** The obvious fix — fall back to matching on table name alone — introduces a way to select the WRONG table's PK columns, and a wrong PK tuple means a wrong collapse, which is **silent data loss on a backup path**. That is strictly worse than the inertness being fixed. Any name-only fallback must refuse when more than one table in the schema shares the name, rather than picking one; and the ambiguous case needs its own report bucket, not `TablesWithoutPK`. Prefer fixing the mismatch at the source (make the recorded schema and the event's schema agree, or normalise both through one helper) over adding a fuzzy match in the consumer.

**Gate it with a MySQL-source cell that asserts `events_collapsed > 0`** — the v0.110.0 cycle's prescribed non-vacuity control was a MySQL leg that was byte-identical on both binaries and would have been scored a clean pass, because no collapse ever ran. An assertion that the collapse *happened* is what turns that from a green into a finding.

### 118. Every deferred-index refusal fires AFTER the bulk copy, and two shipped releases claimed otherwise (Bug 224 + its SQLite sibling) — *✅ SHIPPED to `main` 2026-08-04 (`6ec63868`); CI green. Released in **v0.111.0**.*

**Implementation notes.** `ir.IndexEmitPreflighter` (`PreflightIndexes(*ir.Schema) error`) is implemented by `mysql.Engine` (all four flavors), `postgres.Engine`, `sqlite.Engine`, and — the delegation that a compile-assert on `postgres.Engine` would have silently missed — `pgtrigger.Engine`, whose schema writer IS vanilla PG's. The orchestrator calls `migcore.PreflightIndexEmit` at **six** entry points, not the two the spec named: `migrate` (`phaseTranslateAndGateSchema`), `sync` cold-start single-database and multi-database, `add-table`, `restore`, and chain `restore` — every path that copies and then indexes. `TestIndexEmitPreflightReachesEveryCopyEntryPoint` is the fail-by-default roster over those six.

Each engine's refusal was split into a pure `refuseUnrepresentable*` core (`refuseUnrepresentablePredicate` on MySQL, `refuseUnrepresentablePrefix` on PG and SQLite) that the existing `check*` function still calls. The preflight calls the core, so the refusal TEXT lives in exactly one place while the advisory WARN-and-drop path (a partial non-unique index, a prefix on a non-unique index) stays where it belongs — at the emitter, fired once, describing what the emitter actually did. Running the whole emitter at preflight was rejected for a concrete reason: PG's `emitCreateIndex` takes an `emitOpts` carrying `EnabledExtensions`, and a preflight fabricating a zero value would have **over-refused** a pgvector/pg_trgm index the real writer accepts.

**What "correct" means here was pinned as verdict AGREEMENT, not as a refusal.** Each engine has a `TestPreflightIndexesAgreesWithTheEmitter` shape matrix that drives the REAL `Engine` value and compares its verdict against the real emitter's for the same index — so an over-refusal (breaks migrations that work today) fails just as loudly as an under-refusal. The end-to-end timing pin is `TestMigrate_IndexPreflight_*` (PG→MySQL partial unique, MySQL→PG prefix, MySQL→SQLite prefix, each with its non-unique control), which asserts the target table **does not exist** after the refusal — mutation-confirmed: removing the `migrate` call makes it fail with "the target table EXISTS after the refusal" while every message assertion still passes.

**One sibling found and deliberately NOT closed here.** SQLite's table-level `PRIMARY KEY` clause renders through `quoteIndexColumnList`, which has never consulted `IndexColumn.Length` — so a MySQL `PRIMARY KEY (email(20), id)` was **silently widened** on a SQLite target at emit time, with nothing warning — closed by item 120, which landed right after this. That is a silent constraint weakening in the emitter, not a timing defect, and closing it made this preflight refuse a shape the run accepted at the time. `TestPreflightIndexesDoesNotWalkThePrimaryKey` asserted the current behaviour and instructed whoever fixed the emitter to walk `table.PrimaryKey` in the preflight in the same pass — which is what item 120 did; that test is gone, replaced by the PRIMARY KEY rows of the same verdict-agreement matrix. Postgres has no equivalent gap (its inline PK goes through `emitIndexColumnList` with `enforcesUniqueness=true`); MySQL supports prefixes natively.

**The instance was filed as a timing bug; it is a class, and it has no preflight at all.** sluice's phase order is create tables (no constraints) → bulk-copy → create indexes → create constraints. Every "this index cannot be represented on the target" refusal lives in an engine's DDL emitter, and the emitters for secondary indexes are only reached in that third phase. So each refusal is loud, zero-loss and correct — and arrives after the entire table has been copied.

Known members, all confirmed by reading the call sites:

- **MySQL partial `UNIQUE`** (`checkIndexPredicate`, Bug 224). Reached early only from the two `CREATE TABLE` inline sites; the ordinary secondary-index path is `emitAddIndexClause`, in the deferred phase. v0.110.0's notes claimed "before any data moves" three times.
- **SQLite/D1 index prefix length** (`checkIndexPrefixLength`, sqlite `ddl_emit.go:477`) — its **only** call site is `emitCreateIndex`. SQLite renders no indexes inline, so there is no early path at all. v0.110.1's notes claimed "before any data moves"; corrected post-publish.
- **Postgres index prefix length** on the deferred `ADD CONSTRAINT … UNIQUE` path — v0.109.0's notes described this one accurately as deferred, so it is a member of the class but not a false claim.

**Why one fix rather than three.** Moving each check individually re-runs the sibling sweep every time a new target-unrepresentable index shape is added, and the two false claims above show that sweep is not reliably run. A single preflight that asks the target engine "can you emit every index in this schema?" before any data moves closes the present members and every future one.

**Fix shape.** An optional engine-level surface — `ir.IndexEmitPreflighter` or similar, `PreflightIndexes(*ir.Schema) error` — implemented by each engine by running its **existing** emit/check functions over every index, discarding the DDL and keeping the error. Engine knowledge stays in the engine package (IR-first tenet), and there is no second copy of the policy to drift, which is the trap a pipeline-side reimplementation would walk into. Needs no connection, so it can hang off `ir.Engine` and run inside `phaseTranslateAndGateSchema`, beside the existing cross-engine refusal.

**Two constraints that are easy to miss.** (1) The parity agreement applies — this touches a shared copy phase, so it belongs on **both** `migrate` and `sync` cold-start, not one. (2) Pin against **real engine types**, not a pipeline test stub; a stub satisfies the interface by construction and proves nothing about any engine, which is the v0.110.0 finding about the pipeline's other optional interfaces.

### 117. `ir.Macaddr` carries no WIDTH, which breaks a `macaddr8` migration outright and leaves a silent `--where` hole (Bug 225 + the audit 2026-08-04 C1 residual) — *✅ SHIPPED to `main` 2026-08-04 (`e1547e7c`). Released in **v0.111.0**. **`ir.Inet` was deliberately scoped OUT on evidence** (see below); the title said "and `ir.Inet`" while this was open, and leaving that on a DONE item would claim coverage the change does not have.*

*Full outcome:* `ir.Macaddr` carries a `Width`; both PG readers set it, the emitter picks `MACADDR`/`MACADDR8`, the width rides the wire and is EXCLUDED from the schema fingerprint, and the `--where` gate's four-row truth table is now decided rather than guessed. The `schemaTypeEnvelope` reflective codec gate was built alongside it and found four pre-existing holes (below).*

**Two corrections to the filing, both found by measuring rather than reading.**

**(a) The fix was not complete at the emitter — `macaddr8[]` still failed, for a different reason, and only a four-cell probe found it.** With the width plumbed and `MACADDR8` emitted, a PG→PG migrate of a `macaddr8[]` column still died: `ERROR: binary data has array element type 25 (text) instead of expected 774 (macaddr8)`. **pgx v5 registers a codec for the `macaddr8` scalar (774) and for `_macaddr` (1040) but NOT for `_macaddr8` (775)** — so the array got no `ArrayCodec` and pgx fell back to encoding the `pgtype.Text` leaves as text. This is the Bug-74 shape exactly: sluice's own path is byte-identical for the two widths, and the outcome differs because the pgx codec keyed on the TARGET OID differs. Measured {macaddr, macaddr8} × {scalar, array} against real PG 16 — three cells pass on stock pgx and the fourth does not. Fix: `registerPGMacaddr8ArrayCodec` (`macaddr8_codec.go`), an `ArrayCodec` wrapping the scalar codec pgx already has, registered per-conn in `copyFromOnSQLConn` beside the timetz one. Registering beat demoting the table to the batched-INSERT path (the `VerbatimType`/`Interval` precedent) because the element codec here is already correct and only the array wrapper was missing — demoting would cost every other column in the table its COPY throughput.

**(b) The write-path sibling enumeration, measured not asserted.** Binary COPY (monolithic + chunked, one seam) NEEDED the registration. The CDC `ChangeApplier` and `writeViaBatch` did NOT — they bind parameterised statements and PG's own input function parses the text, so the missing pgx array codec never comes into play. That is pinned rather than claimed: `TestApplier_MacaddrWidthMatrix` drives all four cells (INSERT and UPDATE arms) through the applier and fails if that ever stops being true.

**Implementation notes.**

- **The fingerprint exclusion is `fingerprintType` (chain.go), and it RECURSES.** `macaddr8[]` is a real column, so an exclusion reaching only the scalar would still have moved the fingerprint of every chain carrying the array form; `ir.Array.Element` and `ir.Domain.BaseType` are both walked. The `normalize` early-out was the trap the filing predicted — it short-circuits on a column with a non-nil Default, so the scan and the rewrite are now ONE predicate (`columnNeedsFingerprintNormalizing`) rather than two that can drift. Mutation-verified in three directions: removing the exclusion, removing the array recursion, and reverting the early-out predicate each make `TestSchemaHash_ExcludesMacaddrWidth` fail. The gate is the with-vs-without EQUALITY the filing asked for, at BOTH widths (6 is the one every existing chain carries), plus a byte-level assertion that the hashed bytes contain no `macaddr_width` key at all — which is what makes "the fingerprint did not move" a statement about older releases rather than about this binary agreeing with itself.
- **`String()` is width-aware and the diff paths do compare rendered strings** — verified, not trusted (`diff.typeString` / `diff.typeStringDrift`). `Width: 0` still renders `Macaddr`, so a legacy manifest does not read as a retype. That is where the retype detection the fingerprint gives up now lives, and the fingerprint gate asserts it rather than leaving it implied.
- **`ir.Inet` was re-checked and confirmed out of scope**, on the filing's own evidence.

**⚠ THE NEW REFLECTIVE GATE FOUND FOUR PRE-EXISTING HOLES, none fixed here.** `TestTypeEnvelopeRoundTripsEveryExportedField` (`internal/ir/type_codec_completeness_test.go`) drives `ir.AllTypes()`, fills every exported field non-zero, round-trips through the real `MarshalType`/`UnmarshalType`, and is BIDIRECTIONAL — a field in the exemption maps must NOT survive, so wiring one up later fails the gate and forces the entry out. It separates `envelopeExempt` (adjudicated decisions) from `envelopeKnownGap` (findings nobody has closed), because collapsing the two is how a gate certifies its own blind spot. The gaps it surfaced:

- **`Enum.TypeName` — the material one.** The PG reader sets it for every PG enum column, and it is documented as the thing that keeps a same-engine restore from renaming `post_status` to `posts_status_enum`. It does not ride the type envelope, so a manifest round-trip drops it and a restore re-creates the enum type under a synthesized name. Wiring it is NOT free — it is non-zero on ordinary PG data, so it needs exactly the ride-the-wire + exclude-from-the-hash treatment `Macaddr.Width` just got. Worth its own item.
- **`Char.Determinism` / `Varchar.Determinism` / `Text.Determinism`.** Set by the PG reader from `collisdeterministic`; a decoded schema reads back `Unknown`. The argument that makes `Enum.Collation` a considered decision (its only consumer, the `--where` evaluator, compiles from a fresh schema read) plausibly applies — but nobody wrote it down on these fields, and `ir.Type` participates in `reflect.DeepEqual` comparisons (`SchemaSignature.Equal`, `diffRenameColumnIR`) where a fresh-read column and a decoded one would disagree. Adjudicate; do not assume.

**The `--where` half.** `ColumnInfo.MACWidth` carries the width, and the zero value REFUSES rather than assuming 6 — the same adjudication as an unknown `NetworkRendering`, and reachable only if a new producer of `ir.Macaddr` appears without deciding (there are exactly two today, both PG readers). The 8-byte-literal-on-`macaddr8` over-refusal v0.110.1 shipped deliberately is lifted, and the 6-byte-literal-on-`macaddr8` silent hole closes by CANONICALISATION rather than a new refusal branch: the widened form is the canonical spelling, so the existing not-the-canonical-spelling error fires and NAMES `08:00:2b:ff:fe:01:02:03` as the literal to write. `TestMACLiteral_WidthTruthTable` is the full product, and it asserts the refusal REASON per cell, not just that something failed. **The widening is an environmental premise and is checked as one** (`TestMacaddr8WidensEUI48OnInput`, real PG 16): FF:FE insertion with no universal/local bit flip, with `macaddr8_set7bit` as the control that keeps the assertion pinning WHICH rule applies.

**Original filing follows.**

**One IR change closes two findings that were filed separately and look unrelated.** `internal/engines/postgres/types.go` maps both widths onto a single type — `case "macaddr", "macaddr8": return ir.Macaddr{}, nil` — and `ir.Macaddr` is an empty struct, so the eight-byte width is discarded at read time and cannot be recovered downstream.

**Half one — Bug 225, loud and total (found by the v0.110.1 regression cycle).** `ddl_emit.go` emits `MACADDR` for every `ir.Macaddr`, so a source `macaddr8` column is narrowed to six bytes on the target and the COPY fails. A Postgres `macaddr8` column cannot be migrated **or** synced to a Postgres target at all — rc=1, zero rows, on `migrate` and on `sync start`, and on the `macaddr8[]` array sibling. Identical on v0.108.1 through v0.110.1, so it is long-standing rather than a regression. There is no `--type-override` escape. Zero-loss (it refuses rather than truncating), which is why it went unnoticed: nobody with a `macaddr8` column ever got a successful migration to compare against.

**Half two — the C1 residual, silent.** Because the two widths are indistinguishable, `rowpredicate`'s canonical-spelling gate cannot know which it faces. Postgres widens EUI-48 to EUI-64 on input, so a six-byte literal on a `macaddr8` column never equals what the column delivers back, and a `--where` on it silently drops every CDC change to every matching row. v0.110.1 closed the opposite direction (an eight-byte literal is now refused) **deliberately too widely** — it is refused even on a `macaddr8` column where it would have worked — precisely because the width is unknown. See `checkMACLiteralWidth`'s doc, which carries the four-row truth table.

**Fix shape.** Add a width to `ir.Macaddr`. Then the DDL emitter picks `MACADDR` vs `MACADDR8`, and the literal gate stops guessing and can drop the over-wide refusal.

**SCOPED TO `Macaddr`, on evidence — `ir.Inet` is NOT part of this.** I checked the emitters rather than assuming symmetry: MySQL renders `ir.Macaddr` as `VARCHAR(30)` and `ir.Inet` as `VARCHAR(45)` (`mysql/ddl_emit.go:243`), both wide enough for either width, and Postgres's `INET` holds v4 and v6 alike. So `Inet` has **no total-failure sibling** — the only `inet4`/`inet6` exposure is the `--where` literal subtlety (MariaDB widens a v4 literal to `::ffff:` form), which is narrower and can be filed separately with its own evidence. Bug 225 is `macaddr`-only because `MACADDR` is the one emission that NARROWS.

**Surfaces already mapped (2026-08-04), so the implementer does not re-derive them:**

- **The fingerprint MUST exclude the width, and `omitempty` will not save you — this is item 104 verbatim.** `ComputeSchemaHash` marshals the canonical schema, which reaches `ir.Column.MarshalJSON` → `columnWire` → `MarshalType`, so a width emitted in the type envelope lands in the hash. `omitempty` drops only the ZERO value, and the reader sets **6** for an ordinary `macaddr` — so the field would be present on every real PG chain and the fingerprint would move, minting a new epoch. Exclude it in `canonicalSchemaForHash`/`canonicalColumnsForHash` (note the existing `normalize` early-out predicate must be extended, or it short-circuits before reaching the type). Pin with a **with-field-vs-without-field EQUALITY** test — a self-consistent binary cannot satisfy it, which is what makes it not item 104's self-referential frozen golden.
- **The width MUST still ride the wire.** If it does not, a manifest records a `macaddr8` column as bare `Macaddr` and restore rebuilds it as `MACADDR` — silent narrowing on the restore path. Ride the wire, exclude from the hash. (Forward-compat: an OLD binary reading a NEW manifest ignores the field and emits `MACADDR`, i.e. exactly what it does today — no regression, but say so.)
- **Both diff paths compare RENDERED STRINGS, not structs** — `schema_drift.go:382` uses `entry.Before.Type` (a string from `makeColumnDriftEntry`) and `column_shape.go:217` uses `typeString(c.Type)`. So making `String()` width-aware (`Macaddr8` only at width 8) makes `macaddr`↔`macaddr8` correctly VISIBLE as a type change without spuriously firing on legacy `Width: 0` manifests. Verify rather than trust this.
- **Zero value is the safe default.** `Width: 0` must emit `MACADDR` — today's behaviour — so every existing construction site (`cdc_relations.go:452`, `translate/`, tests) keeps working unchanged. This is the v0.99.51 zero-value trap; do not make 8 reachable by accident.
- **Two reader sites, not one:** the schema reader (`postgres/types.go:493`, text-keyed) AND the CDC relation reader (`postgres/cdc_relations.go:452`, OID-keyed — `pgtype.MacaddrOID` vs `Macaddr8OID`). These are the two registries that have drifted before (Bug 97). Both must set the width, and the `_macaddr8` array sibling (`macaddr8ArrayOID = 775`) needs checking too.

**⚠ THE TYPE CODEC HAS NO REFLECTIVE COMPLETENESS GATE.** `columnWire` got one (`TestColumnCodecCoversEveryField`); the `schemaTypeEnvelope` did not — `TestMarshalType_RoundTrip` is a curated list. So a `Width` added to `Macaddr` but not wired into **both** `MarshalType` and `UnmarshalType` is silently dropped and **nothing fails** — the exact S7 shape that motivated the columnWire gate. Build the sibling gate as part of this item: every exported field of every concrete `ir.Type` either appears in the envelope or is exempt with a reason. That gate is worth more than the fix.

**The trap this must not walk into is item 104's, and it is live here.** A new field on an IR type reaches the backup schema fingerprint and partitions every existing chain by release. `ir.Column` has a hand-written `MarshalJSON` over an enumerated `columnWire`, so the field must be added in three places to reach the wire at all — and the moment it does, it must be **excluded from the fingerprint** (`fingerprintIndex` / `computeSchemaHash`) or it mints a new epoch. Note the exclusion is not free: `canonicalManifestBytes` folds the fingerprint string, so signing does not backstop a flipped width. Pin the exclusion with a with-field-vs-without-field equality test, not a frozen golden built from post-change values.

### 116. The backup chunk writer rolls on ROW COUNT only, and the legacy manifest checkpoint re-PUTs the whole manifest per chunk (audit 2026-08-01 P3 + P4) — *P3 ✅ SHIPPED to `main` 2026-08-04; P4 still OPEN*

**P3 implementation notes.** `DefaultBackupChunkBytes = 64 << 20` — the same figure as `pgCopyChunkBytes`, chosen so the two answers to "how much may one in-flight chunk hold" agree. The roll is now `RowCount() >= chunkRows || BytesWritten() >= chunkBytes`; on narrow rows the byte arm never fires and boundaries are exactly where they have always been, which is the half that matters for compatibility and has its own control test.

**The ceiling counts UNCOMPRESSED bytes, and that is the load-bearing choice.** A compressed-size trigger would move every boundary the day the codec or its level changed, and since `flush`'s content-addressed same-path skip compares a chunk's SHA at its allocated path, every moved boundary re-uploads. `ChunkWriter.BytesWritten()` therefore counts the JSON Lines handed to the writer, before compression and encryption. Pinned by `TestChunkByteCeiling_BoundariesAreCodecIndependent` (same rows, `CodecNone` vs `CodecGzip`, identical boundaries) and `_RerunSkipsReuploadingIdenticalChunks` (same path AND same SHA across two runs).

**The resume half of the stated gotcha turned out not to exist, and saying so is the point.** Resume works at **TABLE** granularity (Bug 135): a partially written table is re-streamed from scratch and its prior chunks are never reused, because chunk contents already depended on scan order. Nothing keys on where a chunk ends. A test asserting otherwise would have asserted the absence of a coupling that was never there, so the file states the reasoning instead of carrying a vacuous pin.

`Backup.ChunkBytes` is zero-value-safe by construction (the v0.99.51 rule): zero resolves to the default via `chunkByteCeiling()`, never to "unlimited", because zero is what every test, broker path and future caller gets. Mutation-run three ways — dropping the byte arm fails the roll test, shrinking the default to 64 B fails the narrow-row control, and switching to `s.buf.Len()` fails the codec-independence pin — each failing exactly one test.

**No new CLI flag.** `--chunk-size` remains the operator knob; this is a ceiling that stops the row count from meaning gigabytes, not a second target to tune. `perf-parity-matrix.md` gap 16 is closed in the same pass.

**P4 (the cloud-store checkpoint amplification) is untouched and still OPEN** — it needs the numbered-sidecar design below, which is a real design decision rather than a ceiling.

Filed together because they are the same corpus shape seen from two sides, and because both were previously argued rather than measured. The numbers below are from `TestChunkRoll_MeasuresRowWidth` (renamed when the ceiling landed) and `TestLegacyCheckpointCost_*`, which are committed and stay as the regression floor.

**P3 — no byte ceiling on the chunk buffer.** `backupChunkStreamer.writeRow` ends with `if s.writer.RowCount() >= int64(s.chunkRows)`, and that is the only roll condition. The chunk accumulates in an in-memory `bytes.Buffer` until it fires, so the peak buffer is `chunkRows × average serialized row size` with the row size unbounded and unconsulted.

*Measured:* at a fixed 500 rows, widening rows from 64 B to 64 KiB grows the buffered chunk from 50 KB to **32.8 MB** — 644× the bytes for the same row count. Extrapolated to the shipped default of 100,000 rows/chunk at that width: **~6.1 GiB buffered for a single chunk**. The shape that reaches it is a wide `mediumtext`/`json` column, which is exactly what the v0.109.1 field report was about.

Every other buffering path in the tree already has a byte cap beside its row cap — `ir.MaxBufferBytesSetter` on the batched row writers, `ByteCap` in the applier batch loop, `pgCopyChunkBytes` on the PG chunked COPY. The backup chunk writer is the one that does not, which is what makes this a gap rather than a deliberate asymmetry.

**P4 — the legacy checkpoint re-PUTs the whole manifest per chunk.** `manifestCommitter.appendChunk` calls `commitLocked` (a full manifest rewrite) whenever the store is not an `irbackup.Appender`. `blobcodec.LocalStore` is the ONLY implementor in the tree, so every CLOUD store — S3, GCS, Azure — takes that path.

*Measured*, 50 tables × 8 chunks: legacy does **451 manifest Puts totalling 50.4 MB**; the sidecar path does the identical work in **1 Put of 74 KB**. That is **683×**. Cost scales with chunk count (4× the chunks → 4.0× the bytes) AND with table count (4× the tables → **15.7×** the bytes, because every checkpoint re-serialises every table entry), so a wide corpus with many chunks per table pays the product.

**Why the existing gate did not catch it, which is the transferable part.** `TestManifestCommitter_SidecarCheckpointCost_10kTables` pins the manifest to a single Put across 20,000 checkpoints — an excellent gate, on the path only a local store takes. The fast path was measured and the fallback that every remote backup uses was not. Same shape as the error-codes count check masking the text check: a green on the good case reads as coverage of the class.

**Fix shapes.** For P4, the promising one is emulating append on object stores with NUMBERED sidecar objects (`manifest.progress.00001.jsonl`, …) instead of one appended blob — object stores have no append primitive, which is why the capability is optional, but they do have cheap small PUTs and prefix listing. Replay already tolerates multiple lines; it would enumerate objects rather than read one. That makes checkpoints O(1) on every store. For P3, a byte ceiling beside the row ceiling, mirroring `pgCopyChunkBytes`.

**Gotcha for whoever takes P3.** Chunk boundaries are load-bearing beyond memory: resume keys on them, and the content-addressed same-path upload skip compares a chunk's SHA at its allocated path. Changing when a chunk rolls changes both, so the ceiling wants to land with a resume test and a re-run-skip test, not on its own.

### 115. A shared trigger-CDC change log is pruned against ONE stream's frontier, so a slower peer silently loses rows (audit 2026-08-01 S4) — *✅ SHIPPED in **v0.113.0** (fix shape (a): a source-side consumer registry)*

**What shipped.** ADR-0137 Phase C. `sluice trigger setup` now installs a third source-side table, `sluice_change_log_consumers`, and moves the change-log `schema_version` 1 → 2. Every trigger-CDC stream publishes its durably-applied frontier there on a one-minute cadence — **whether or not it opted into `--auto-prune-change-log`**, because the sync that loses rows is typically the one without the flag — and the prune cuts at `min(MIN(applied_id) across the registry, this stream's freshly-read frontier) - keep`.
