That is correct for every shape including two streams replicating the SAME table to different targets, which the scoped-prune option (b) could not close; option (b) was not implemented, and the `(schema_name, table_name, id)` index N-16 dropped was NOT re-added — the registry rides its own tiny PK and the change-log DELETE still rides the existing `id` PK range scan.

**The seam, and the fail-closed half.** A new OPTIONAL COMPANION `ir.ChangeLogConsumerRegistry` sits beside `ir.ChangeLogPruner` (the `ir.NetworkLiteralResolver` pattern). A source exposing the base pruner WITHOUT the companion is **not pruned at all** — the sidecar logs at ERROR and spawns nothing. The cut decision lives once, in `triggercdc.RegistryCut`, shared by all three engines. **Sibling sweep:** `pgtrigger` — FIXED (own PG SQL, integration-pinned); `sqlite-trigger` — FIXED (real-file unit pins); `d1-trigger` — FIXED by the same `CDCReader` over the D1 executor, with its HTTP decode separately pinned. The one sibling deliberately NOT gated is the operator-run `sluice trigger prune`, which is CLAMPED to the registry MIN and prints that it was, but does not refuse when there is no registry evidence — refusing an explicit operator action that has been safe for a single stream since Phase A would be a regression.

**The empty-registry hazard, handled explicitly.** An empty registry is indistinguishable from one nobody has written to yet, so `RegistryCut` REFUSES on it rather than reading it as "no consumers ⇒ prune everything", and refuses again when the calling stream's own `consumer_id` is absent (a cut derived from peers alone is not a safe bound for the caller). Both are unit- and integration-pinned, and mutation-run in both directions.

**What is NOT closed, in the flag help and a startup WARN.** A peer running a sluice OLDER than the registry never registers and leaves no trace on the source, so it cannot be detected; every sync on a shared source must be upgraded before enabling the flag. A peer that ran an old `trigger setup` IS caught — that rewrites `schema_version` below the floor and the engine refuses. A stopped-but-still-registered consumer holds the change log until an operator deletes its row (WARNed at 30 min, never auto-evicted — eviction would delete the rows a stream down for maintenance has not read).

<details>
<summary>Original filing</summary>

**The defect.** `runAutoPruneTick` reads THIS stream's durable position from its own target and hands the token to the source's `PruneConsumedChangeLog`, which deletes `id <= appliedLastID - keep`. The cut keys on `id` alone. A source change log is shared by every stream reading that database, so a second stream that is behind loses everything between the two frontiers — deleted before it reads it, with no way to discover it existed. This is precisely the staged-wave shape the docs recommend: several syncs off one source, disjoint table sets, necessarily different speeds.

**Mitigations that are real, and why this is not a Critical.** Auto-prune is OPT-IN (`--auto-prune-change-log`, off by default), so the silent path requires the operator to have asked for it. Since this was filed, starting the sidecar emits a loud WARN naming the hazard and telling the operator not to enable it on a staged/wave migration.

**What makes the fix non-trivial — the three constraints found while scoping it:**

1. **There is no consumer registry.** The source carries `sluice_change_log` plus `sluice_change_log_meta`, and the meta table is a singleton holding only `schema_version`. Each stream's frontier lives on its own TARGET, unreachable from the source-side pruner. Prune-to-MIN-across-consumers therefore needs a new source-side table and a change-log schema-version bump, with a migration path for existing installs.
2. **Table-scoped pruning is only a PARTIAL fix.** `DELETE ... WHERE id <= cut AND (schema_name, table_name) IN (<this stream's tables>)` fixes the disjoint-scope case (staged waves) and needs no new index — the PK range scan drives it and the table filter is applied per row. But two streams replicating the SAME table to different targets still cut each other, so scoping must not be described as closing the class.
3. **Do not re-add the (schema_name, table_name, id) index.** N-16 dropped it deliberately: it was maintained on every captured source DML for zero read benefit, pure write amplification on tiers where the operator pays IOPS. A scoped prune must ride the existing PK range scan.

**Fix shape, in preference order.** (a) A source-side consumer registry — each stream records its applied frontier there, prune cuts at the MIN. Correct for every shape including same-table peers; costs a schema bump. (b) Scoped prune per constraint 2 — cheaper, closes the documented staged-wave case only, and must be documented as partial. (c) Refuse auto-prune outright when the change log carries rows for tables outside this stream's scope — detects a peer without a registry, but false-positives when triggers are installed on tables nobody consumes.

**Gotcha for whoever takes it.** `ir.ChangeLogPruner` takes only the position token, so any of these needs the stream's table scope threaded through an interface implemented by three engines (pgtrigger, sqlite-trigger, d1-trigger). Prefer the optional-companion-surface pattern (`ir.NetworkLiteralResolver` is the recent precedent) over widening the existing method, so an engine that has not implemented it fails closed rather than silently pruning unscoped.

</details>

### 114. MySQL's `LOAD DATA` cold-copy is one monolithic statement per table, so a transient has NO resume point (audit 2026-08-01 Q2) — *✅ FIXED on `main`; shipped in **v0.113.0**. BEHAVIOUR CHANGE: a failed LOAD DATA table copy can now leave PARTIAL rows where it previously left none (each segment is its own transaction), which the resume/preflight paths already handle for the batched cores; and a keyless table whose copy hits a transient now REFUSES with `SLUICE-E-COPY-RETRY-AMBIGUOUS-KEYLESS` where it previously refused with a different message — the same disposition the batched cores took in the same situation. Needs a release note.*

**What shipped.** `writeLoadData` now loads a table as a SEQUENCE of bounded `LOAD DATA` statements (16 MiB of encoded TSV each, `defaultLoadDataSegmentBytes`, lowered by `--max-buffer-bytes`), each driven through the SAME `flushWithReparentRetry` the two batched write cores use. The segment's encoded bytes are retained for the length of the flush, which is exactly what the path lacked: the batched cores ride a transient by re-driving their buffered batch, and LOAD DATA had nothing buffered to re-drive. The retry policy, the ADR-0110 grow-gate Await/Trip, the wall-clock bound and the ADR-0108 keyless carve-out are all INHERITED from the shared helper rather than re-derived — `flushWithReparentRetry` now serves three cores, and the roster gate (`TestEveryMySQLBulkWriteLaneReachesTheGrowGate`) already recognised it.

**The premise the filing did not know about, and it makes the guarantee STRONGER than planned.** `LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE` downgrades a duplicate-key error to a WARNING and skips the row — the server cannot stop a transfer already in flight, so it behaves as if `IGNORE` were given. Verified against a real MySQL 8.0 (`TestLoadDataLocal_DuplicateKeyIsAWarningAndSkipsTheRow`), not assumed. That makes a byte-identical replay CONVERGENT on a keyed table whether the prior attempt rolled back, committed fully, or committed a prefix — so the resume is exactly-once without the batched path's tolerate-1062-on-retry wart, and without the recorded row cursor the filing assumed was necessary.

**The wart it costs, and the silent-corruption path that had to be closed.** A replay legitimately produces one 1062 warning per already-landed row, and the Bugs-102/103 post-load probe refuses on ANY warning under strict sql_mode. Tolerating them wholesale would let a real coercion hide among them — and it genuinely can hide: the server caps `SHOW WARNINGS` at `@@max_error_count` (1024), so on a large replay a single truncation warning sits entirely outside the visible window while every visible warning is a 1062. The tolerance is therefore bought with an INDEPENDENT number rather than asserted: duplicates-skipped = segment rows − the driver's affected-rows, total = the server's uncapped `@@warning_count`, and anything left over refuses. Pinned both as a pure decision matrix and end-to-end (`TestLoadDataSegments_ReplayRefusesWhenACoercionHidesAmongTheDuplicates`).

**Throughput — measured, and the model pinned rather than a ratio.** An extra segment costs exactly one extra TRANSACTION COMMIT and nothing else: on the development box a one-row LOAD DATA (53.4 ms) and a one-row INSERT (52.4 ms) cost the same, against a 0.6 ms round trip and the 0.35 ms added SHOW WARNINGS probe. End-to-end over a 7.2 MiB corpus the cost prices in linearly with the segment COUNT — 8 MiB budget 0.99x, 4 MiB 1.09x, 2 MiB 1.19x, 1 MiB 1.46x, 256 KiB 2.59x — so at the shipping 16 MiB budget the copy is within measurement noise of the old single-statement form. For scale, the batched-INSERT core this same writer falls back to commits every ~1 MiB, i.e. 16x more often. **The binding constraint turned out to be MEMORY, not throughput**: one segment's bytes are held per concurrent writer where the streaming form held 64 KiB, and a PG→MySQL cold copy can run `--table-parallelism` × `--bulk-parallelism` writers.

**Two measurement traps worth remembering** (both produced confident wrong numbers before being caught): successive tens-of-MiB loads hit a progressively dirtier InnoDB buffer pool, so the SAME form measured 2.59 s in load position 1 and 6.07 s in position 4 — a straight A-then-B comparison reported a fictitious 2.2x regression that was pure ordering. And the first version of the throughput test read the segment-budget package var inline for its second call, after the first call had already overwritten it — measuring one form against itself.

**What it deliberately does NOT do.** Segment boundaries are an IN-RUN replay point, not a durable cursor: a process that dies mid-table still restarts that table (or, on the chunked copy path, that chunk) next run. Cross-run resume is the pipeline's job and it already has one (ADR-0043/0096 per-(table, chunk) progress with an idempotent replay writer). Recording a row cursor here would need a stable source order the writer's input channel does not promise.

**Correction to this item's original premise.** It said the defect bites "a large table against an auto-grow target (the exact shape ADR-0110 exists for)". It cannot: the auto-grow/reparent shape is PlanetScale/Vitess, and those flavors declare `BulkLoadBatchedInsert` — `BulkLoadLoadDataInfile` is declared only by `FlavorVanilla` (incl. RDS / CloudSQL / Azure) and `FlavorMariaDB`. The defect is real on those flavors for the transient class they DO see (Multi-AZ/HA failover, connection reset, EOF, lock-wait), which is what the retry rides.

**The gotcha is now moot.** The filing offered "expose an operator flag to pick the retryable batched writer on a vanilla target" as the cheaper interim; the LOAD DATA core now has the retry itself, so there is nothing to opt into.


### 113. The incremental schema diff never compares CHECK constraints or foreign keys, so a mid-window `ADD CHECK` is not skipped — it is never recorded (found 2026-08-01 while fixing the retype-delta skip) — *✅ FIXED in **v0.113.0**. BEHAVIOUR CHANGE: a chain whose window carries an ADD CHECK or any FK DDL now REFUSES loudly at replay (SLUICE-E-BACKUP-SCHEMA-DELTA-UNSUPPORTED, remedy: fresh full) where it previously exited 0 having silently restored a target missing the constraint. Same posture column-dropped already took; needs a release note.*

**Why.** Item A5's fix (`9d373be6`) turned `tablesEqual` into a registry of structural aspects so no delta shape can reach a silent `continue`, and gated it so a new comparator forces a written disposition. That closes the *disposition* hole. It does not close a **coverage** hole one level up: `tablesEqual` never compared `CheckConstraints` or foreign keys at all, so those changes produce **no delta to dispose of**.

**Observed, not reasoned.** The item-60 integration ground truth printed during that chunk: `scenario="ADD CHECK CONSTRAINT only (no DML)" schemaDelta=0`. A source that adds a CHECK mid-window records nothing in the incremental, and a restore of that chain produces a target missing the constraint, exit 0. Same shape for a foreign key.

**Why it is a real silent divergence and not a documented scope limit.** The restore's whole contract is that the target matches the source at the window's end. A missing CHECK or FK means the target accepts rows the source would reject — the same class as the cross-engine index-uniqueness findings (audit-2026-08-01 S8), and the same class `sluice schema diff` cannot report either, since `TableDiff` carries no FK fields (S9). So there is no surface anywhere that would tell an operator.

**What.** Add `CheckConstraints` and foreign keys to the aspect registry in `internal/pipeline/migcore/incremental_delta_shape.go`, with a disposition each. Both are likely REFUSE rather than APPLY on first cut — a mid-window constraint tightening can fail against rows the replay has not caught up to yet, which is the same trade the column-dropped and narrowing-retype dispositions already record. The gate that already exists (`TestAlterAspectsAllClassified`) will force the decision the moment the comparators are added.

**Gotcha.** Check whether the *diff* is the right layer or whether the manifest simply does not carry enough to detect it — if the incremental's schema snapshot is itself lossy for constraints, adding a comparator is necessary but not sufficient, and the fix moves down to what the snapshot records. Establish that before designing.

### 112. The item-109 metadata-only FK add (fast, no re-validation) is `migrate`-only — a `sync` cold-start into a FK-enabled PlanetScale target runs a full validating `ALTER … ADD FOREIGN KEY` on every child row (observed live 2026-07-31) — *✅ SHIPPED + LIVE-VALIDATED 2026-08-01 (single-DB cold-start). CI green; end-to-end on a real 175M-row Metal migration.*

**Live validation (back-to-back, the definitive proof).** Same full sync (events 153M + orders 20M + customers 2M) into a FK-enabled PlanetScale-Metal target, run twice: **without item 112** (binary at `713f157e`) the `events` FK did an `ALTER … ADD FOREIGN KEY` that InnoDB executed as `copy to tmp table` — a full 153M-row table rebuild — which ran to exactly 3600s and was killed by the raised statement wall; the migration failed in the constraints phase and never reached CDC. **With item 112** (binary at `a5265d8d`) the identical FK became a metadata-only add + a bounded orphan scan (proven clean, no orphans), the whole FK phase took ~6 min (06:17→06:23), and the sync entered CDC and replicated a live source UPDATE to the Metal target in ~6 s. Item 112 is the difference between a failed migration and a working one on a real FK-bearing large table.

**ADR-0182 follow-up observed in the same run (item 110):** the raise's *revert* fires at the CDC handoff and does a rolling tablet restart; on the Metal cluster that restart ran long enough that sluice's revert-confirmation wait gave up and logged `FAILED to revert the keyspace query timeout` at ~20 min — even though the revert config change (timeout→900) had been submitted and was rolling out (the keyspace ended at 900). Two minor edges worth a look: (1) the revert's rolling restart briefly pauses the *initial* CDC stream until the tablets return (~20 min here); (2) the "FAILED to revert" WARN over-reports on a slow-restart tier — the change applied, only its confirmation timed out (the crash-safe record is preserved, so a re-run harmlessly re-confirms). Neither blocks correctness; both are ADR-0182 UX considerations for Metal/slow-restart tiers.

**Implemented.** (a) The unfiltered single-DB sync cold-start now arms the item-109 metadata-only FK path (`migcore.ArmForeignKeyConsistency(sw, len(RowFilters)==0)` in `coldStartOpenTargetWriters`), mirroring migrate; (b) — **the critical half** — the sync cold-start now runs the bounded orphan scan (`Streamer.verifyUnvalidatedForeignKeys`, mirror of the `*Migrator` method) after the copy, before `sw` closes and before the CDC anchor, abandoning the stream (Bug 177) on a `SLUICE-E-FK-SOURCE-ORPHAN` refusal. Filtered (`--where`) runs and the multi-DB cold-start are deliberately NOT armed (they keep full validation — safe, just not wall-optimized).

**The silent-loss CRITICAL caught during implementation (the whole point of the discipline).** `ValidateUnvalidatedForeignKeys` was called from exactly one place — the `*Migrator.verifyUnvalidatedForeignKeys` method — and NOWHERE on the sync path. Arming sync to add FKs metadata-only under `foreign_key_checks=0` *without* also wiring the orphan scan would have silently accepted a dirty source's orphans: the FK would exist in metadata while the data violated it. The arming and the scan are one indivisible change; either alone is wrong (the scan-less arm is silent-loss, the arm-less scan is a no-op). Pinned in `fk_consistency_sync_test.go`: `TestItem112_SyncColdStartOrphanScanFires` proves a dirty source refuses loudly (FK dropped first) and a clean source passes.

**Multi-DB follow-up:** wiring the orphan scan into `coldStartMultiDatabase` (so it too can arm the fast path) is deferred; until then multi-DB keeps the safe validating add.

**Observed.** A full sync cold-start of a 153M-row `events` table (referencing `customers`) into a FK-enabled PlanetScale-Metal target ran the copy, then a ~40-min direct index build (under `--planetscale-raise-query-timeout`, phase 3), then a **constraints phase that also ran for many minutes under the raise** — because sync did a *validating* FK add, not migrate's item-109 metadata-only path. Item 109's fast FK add (metadata-only under `foreign_key_checks=0` + a bounded chunked orphan scan, measured 0.082 s on the same 153M-row table) is gated to an *unfiltered migrate into a Vitess-flavor target*; `ForeignKeyConsistencyDeclarer`'s own doc says "sync cold-start / a pre-populated target never set it either." So on FK-enabled PlanetScale targets, sync cold-start pays a full 153M-row FK validation that migrate does not.

**Why it's the same shape as item 111.** The item-109 safety argument — "the child rows were just copied from a source where the constraint held, so re-validating them target-side is redundant, and the bounded orphan scan proves it rather than assuming it" — holds *identically* for a sync cold-start (its rows also come from a source that enforced the FK). So the metadata-only path is applicable to sync cold-start and was simply never wired, exactly like `--upfront-indexes`/`--planetscale-raise-query-timeout` were migrate-only until item 111.

**What.** Extend the item-109 metadata-only FK path (and its chunked orphan scan + the `SLUICE-E-FK-SOURCE-ORPHAN` loud refusal) to the sync cold-start's `CreateConstraints` on a Vitess-flavor target, gated the same way (unfiltered cold-start; a `--where`-filtered stream can legitimately orphan children, so it must keep the validating add / loud net). Verify the gating predicate the way item 111 did — check which path HAS the capability (`ForeignKeyConsistencyDeclarer` setter), don't reason from prose. Until then, `--planetscale-raise-query-timeout` on sync is what keeps the validating FK add from walling (as it did in this run), so the two compose — but the metadata-only path would remove the need for the raise on the FK phase entirely.

### 111. `--upfront-indexes` and `--planetscale-raise-query-timeout` exist on `migrate` but not `sync`, even though sync's cold-start runs the SAME copy path and needs them more (raised 2026-07-31) — *✅ DONE (phases 1–3). Phase 1 (`2d6a0958`): the parity GATE + CLAUDE.md working agreement. Phase 2 (`47c46acc`): `--upfront-indexes` wired to `sync` — a guarded upfront branch in `runBulkCopyWithOpts` (both cold-start callers) + the CLI flag + an ordering pin test; removed from `parityExempt` so the gate enforces it on both. Phase 3 (`580db05a`): `--planetscale-raise-query-timeout` wired to `sync` (option b) — a sync-side crash-safe recorder on the MySQL `ChangeApplier` in a dedicated `sluice_cdc_query_timeout_raise` table keyed by stream_id (the cold-start position row doesn't exist at raise time), the 3 raise/revert helpers extracted from `*Migrator` methods to shared funcs (migrate byte-identical), raise scoped inside `coldStart` + deferred-reverted right after the copy (not held for the stream's life), and the dangling-revert + refusals in `runOnce` every attempt (so warm-resume also cleans a crash-leak). Removed from `parityExempt` — the gate now enforces BOTH errno-3024 knobs on both structs. **Cleanup (`--analyze-after` wired to sync too):** the advisory post-copy ANALYZE — the third flag the gate surfaced, no architectural blocker — is now a guarded post-views branch in `runBulkCopyWithOpts` (both cold-start callers) + the sync CLI flag + an ordering pin test, and dropped from `parityExempt`. **`parityExempt` is now EMPTY — full parity on every copy-phase flag** (the gate + its enforcement stay live for the next flag that lands one-sided). **Two decisions recorded:** (a) multi-database sync LOUDLY REFUSES the raise (keyspace-scoped raise can't protect a fan-out cold-start; fully wiring `coldStartMultiDatabase` isn't worth the raise's narrow ROI — refuse, don't silently no-op); (b) `TestSyncSpecFlagParity` fleet-spec exclusion for both new flags, consistent with the sibling cold-start knobs (`skip-foreign-keys`, `bulk-batch-size`, `index-build-mem`) — exposing cold-start knobs on the fleet surface is a separate, larger decision. -race Integration gate must be green before any tag ships this (crash-recovery + cold-start ordering).*

**Phase 2 was INCOMPLETE, and the gate could not see it — closed 2026-08-01.** Phase 2 wired `--upfront-indexes` (and the `--analyze-after` cleanup) into `runBulkCopyWithOpts` and its two cold-start callers, and stopped there. The sync cold-start has a THIRD copy path: `Streamer.runColdStartParallel`, the ADR-0079 fast lane, which calls `runBulkCopyPhases` directly and was passing literal `false` for both arguments under a comment calling each "a migrate-path flag". That lane is the DEFAULT whenever the Postgres source exports a shareable snapshot, so `sync start --upfront-indexes` / `--analyze-after` against a Postgres source were silently ignored for the whole of this item's life while `TestCopyPhaseFlagParityMigratorStreamer` stayed green — the gate proves a field EXISTS on both structs and can say nothing about whether the value arrives. Both are now field-sourced, and the class is gated: `TestCopyPhaseKnobsReachTheOrchestratorFromAField` (internal/pipeline) fails the build if a curated `runBulkCopyPhases` copy-phase argument is a constant, and `TestBulkCopyOptsProductionSitesSetEveryKnob` does the same for the `bulkCopyOpts` literals — which is how `--copy-fanout-degree` turned out to be unset on the multi-database cold-copy too. This item's own claim that "**`parityExempt` is now EMPTY — full parity on every copy-phase flag**" was true of the struct fields and untrue of the wiring; this paragraph is the correction.

**Correction to this item's original premise (found during phase 1):** the "pure wiring" claim below was WRONG for the sync path. The upfront-index REORDERING lives in `runBulkCopyPhases`/`migrate_phases.go`, which the Streamer bypasses — it calls `runBulkCopyWithOpts` directly, and that entry point has no upfront branch and `bulkCopyOpts` no upfront field. So wiring `--upfront-indexes` to sync means adding a *mirrored upfront branch to `runBulkCopyWithOpts`* + a `bulkCopyOpts` field + the Streamer field + the CLI flag — modest and additive, but a new sync-copy code path, not field-threading. This is the "release notes / roadmap prose is a claim surface" lesson applied to a filing premise: the shape of the fix was assumed, the code said otherwise.

**Phase 1 (DONE).** `internal/pipeline/copy_phase_flag_parity_test.go` — a curated-list gate (no build tag, runs every CI) that fails the build if a copy-phase flag is on `Migrator` XOR `Streamer` without a reasoned `parityExempt` entry; the exempt check asserts XOR-presence so a stale exemption (wired-to-both, or renamed-away) also trips. Mutation-verified in both directions (independently, in the main session, not just the build agent's claim). Plus the CLAUDE.md working agreement making "applies to both unless a written reason says so" the rule. **The gate surfaced a THIRD migrate-only copy-phase flag nobody had noticed: `AnalyzeAfter`** (post-copy `ANALYZE`, migrate.go:596) — not a designed fork, no known architectural blocker, simply never wired to sync; a sync cold-start leaves stale planner stats exactly as migrate would. Exempted-with-reason and now durably visible; a good phase-2-adjacent cleanup.

**Phase 2/3 (OPEN) — the actual sync wiring:**

**Why.** `Migrator` (migrate) and `Streamer` (sync) share the schema-apply + bulk-copy phases via `runBulkCopy` and diverge only after (`streamer.go:184`). A sync cold-start does the identical large-table copy + index/FK build (`streamer_coldstart.go → runBulkCopyWithOpts → CreateConstraints`) before the CDC handoff — so it hits the exact same errno-3024 statement wall. Both errno-3024 headroom knobs are wired only at the Migrator layer: `UpfrontIndexes` is a `Migrator` field fed into the shared `runBulkCopyPhases` (migrate.go:904; the shared phase code at migrate_phases.go:510 already honors it), and `RaiseQueryTimeout`/`maybeRaiseQueryTimeout` is a `*Migrator` method wrapping the copy call (migrate.go:896). The `Streamer` has neither field. The tell that this is an accident and not a decision: `IndexBuildFallback` (the deploy-request path) IS wired to BOTH structs — sync got one of the three knobs and silently missed two. It matters *more* for sync: a walled cold-start strands a continuous-sync setup, not a one-shot job that can be rerun.

- **Phase 2 — `UpfrontIndexes` to sync.** Add a mirrored upfront branch to `runBulkCopyWithOpts` (build secondary indexes before the copy when set; skip the post-copy `CreateIndexes` but keep `verifyBuiltIndexes`), an `UpfrontIndexes` field on `bulkCopyOpts`, the `Streamer` field + its assignment in `streamer_coldstart.go`, and the `--upfront-indexes` flag on `sync start`. The sync serial path has no ADR-0077 budget-split overlap and no resume-state to thread, so it is additive. On landing, remove `UpfrontIndexes` from `parityExempt` — the gate then enforces it on both. (Consider `AnalyzeAfter` in the same pass: no architectural blocker, same shape.)
- **Phase 3 — `RaiseQueryTimeout` to sync (the design fork).** `maybeRaiseQueryTimeout` records the dangling raise crash-safely via `rc.store` (`ir.QueryTimeoutRaiseRecorder`, backed by `sluice_migrate_state`). The Streamer cold-start calls `runBulkCopyWithOpts` directly and has NO `resumeContext`/migrate-state store, so a sync that dies mid-copy could not auto-revert a keyspace-wide raise — the ADR-0182 "leave it as you found it" guarantee has no home. Wiring it needs a recorder-home decision first (give the Streamer cold-start a migrate-state store, or a sync-side recorder). Don't wire the raise without solving this; a half-measure that can't auto-revert is worse than the exemption. On landing, remove `RaiseQueryTimeout` from `parityExempt`.
- Both phases add the CLI flags with migrate's gating (PlanetScale target + `--planetscale-org` + service token; size gate; loud refusal off-target) and reuse the migrate flag help verbatim.

**Phase 1's durable enforcement (DONE).** The parity gate (`TestCopyPhaseFlagParityMigratorStreamer`) + the CLAUDE.md working agreement, described above — the flag/capability analogue of the perf-parity-matrix + `perf-parity-checker` machinery, and the Tier-1 ratchet that makes this class a build failure rather than a thing to re-notice.

### 110. Opt-in: raise PlanetScale's `queryserver-config-query-timeout` to its 3600s max for the migration, then revert — via the config-changes API (operator-requested 2026-07-31) — *✅ SHIPPED v0.106.0 (ADR-0182; `--planetscale-raise-query-timeout`, once-upfront/revert-once, size-gated ≥1M rows, crash-safe via `sluice_migrate_state`). See item 111: shipped migrate-only; sync parity is the open follow-up.*

**Why.** The ~900s statement wall is the root of the whole errno-3024 family (index builds, FK validation, and — measured 2026-07-31 — even a single `--upfront-indexes` bulk-copy insert on network-attached storage). The wall is a *configurable* keyspace setting, `queryserver-config-query-timeout` (default 900, max 3600). Measured head-to-head: on a Metal (local-NVMe) target the deferred 4-index build on 153M rows completes in ~35m — which fits 3600s but not 900s — so raising the timeout makes the *direct* path viable there without a deploy request. (On network-attached Scaler the same build exceeds even 3600s, so the raise does NOT help that case; value is tier-dependent.)

**API flow (fully reverse-engineered 2026-07-31 — NOT in the `update_keyspace` docs; the keyspace PATCH does nothing for these options):**
1. Read current: `GET …/branches/{branch}/keyspaces/{ks}` → `vttablet_options` (may be `{}` = default 900).
2. Stage: `POST …/branches/{branch}/keyspaces/{ks}/config-changes` with `{"change_type":"vttablet","options":{"queryserver-config-query-timeout":"3600"}}` — note the field is **`options`** (not `vttablet_options`) and the **value is a STRING** — → returns `{id, state:"draft", previous_options}`.
3. Submit: `POST …/branches/{branch}/config-changes/submit` with `{"ids":["<id>"]}` → `state:"applying"`.
4. Poll `GET …/keyspaces/{ks}/rollout-status` to `state:"complete"` + `config_change_in_progress:false` (the rollout is a rolling tablet restart, ~2–6m). Revert repeats 2–4 with the recorded previous value.

**What (design decided with the operator 2026-07-31):**
- **Opt-in flag, tightly gated** — a `--planetscale-raise-query-timeout` (name TBD). Fires ONLY on a PlanetScale/Vitess target with `--planetscale-org` + the service token already present (reuse the ADR-0148 plumbing, `internal/planetscale/api`), and never by default. Consider a size gate (skip on a migration with no large table) so a small run doesn't eat two rolling restarts for nothing.
- **Revert to the PREVIOUS value, not a hardcoded 900** — the API returns `previous_options`; record it and restore exactly that (an operator who set 1200 gets 1200 back). Empty `vttablet_options` ⇒ revert by clearing / setting the documented default.
- **Crash-safe, record-and-auto-revert** — persist "raised, previous=X" in `sluice_migrate_state` at raise time; revert on success AND on failure; a `--resume` or bare re-run detects a dangling raise and reverts it before anything else. This is the "leave it as you found it" guarantee and the bulk of the work.
- **Sequencing:** raise (+wait for rollout) BEFORE any copy — the rolling restart must not hit an in-flight copy. Revert AFTER all phases complete (or on abort).
- **Compose, don't replace:** orthogonal to `--upfront-indexes`, ADR-0148 deploy-request fallback, and item-109 metadata-only FK. It gives headroom so the direct path succeeds where it'd wall; the fallbacks remain.

**Gotchas.** The config change is KEYSPACE-WIDE and causes a rolling restart affecting anyone else on that keyspace — the flag's help must say so. Rollout adds ~5–12m total per migration. The `config-changes` create is keyspace-level (`change_type` accepts `vttablet`/`mysqld`); vtgate config is branch-level (`vtgate`). Keyspace name = database name for single-keyspace PlanetScale MySQL, but resolve it (list keyspaces) rather than assume. **Honest scope note for the ADR:** the measured evidence says `--upfront-indexes` on Metal is already the cleaner path needing no timeout tuning; this feature's real value is the deferred path on fast tiers and possibly rescuing the upfront-copy wall on Scaler (untested — the my5 insert walled at 900s; whether 3600s clears it is a hypothesis to verify). Frame it as a useful option, not a silver bullet. Wants ADR-0182.

### 109. The errno-3024 statement-wall handling stops at the INDEX phase — the CONSTRAINTS phase hits the same wall with no fallback, no hint, no code, and the resume loop spins on it forever (observed live 2026-07-30 at 153M rows) — *SHIPPED v0.105.0 (A metadata-only FK + chunked orphan scan, D loop guard; C rejected on evidence — Online DDL refuses FK tables)*

**RESOLUTION (2026-07-30).** Landed **A + B + D**; **C rejected** on evidence. Verdicts, each with the code/live proof that decided it.

**B keeps the loud-failure baseline (owner directive).** The bare metadata-only add would SILENTLY accept a source orphan on MySQL — inverting the documented `--allow-degraded-fks` baseline (loud-on-dirty-source, PG-target-only). So B keeps the metadata-only add (it dodges the wall) but then PROVES the child rows clean with a **bounded chunked orphan scan**: for every FK added metadata-only, the child PK range is split with the SAME machinery the parallel copy pins (`migcore.ComputeChunkBoundaries` / `ComputeKeysetChunkBoundaries`, over a target reader), and each chunk runs a PK-range-bounded `LEFT JOIN … WHERE parent IS NULL LIMIT 1` that cannot itself hit the wall. Clean ⇒ complete (proven, not assumed); a violation ⇒ **DROP the FK, then refuse** with the new refusal code `SLUICE-E-FK-SOURCE-ORPHAN` (exit 3) naming the child table, FK, and an example key — the loud signal the wall killed before a validating ADD could produce it. Engine surfaces `ir.UnvalidatedForeignKeyReporter` / `ForeignKeyOrphanScanner` / `ForeignKeyDropper` (`schema_writer_constraint_fk_wall.go`); orchestrator driver `migcore.ValidateUnvalidatedForeignKeys` (`foreign_key_orphan_scan.go`), run after the constraints phase in `runSingleDatabase` + multidb. Real-InnoDB pins: orphan → coded refusal + FK dropped; clean → FK stands; a bounded range that excludes the orphan reads clean while the one that includes it names id=3 (and a NULL-fk row is correctly NOT flagged — MySQL FKs are MATCH SIMPLE).

**Backing-index precondition (verified).** `foreign_key_checks=0` skips row validation but NOT the structural backing index `ADD FOREIGN KEY` builds when none covers the referencing columns — that build itself walls. In the normal migrate flow the source's FK-backing index is in the schema and built in the index phase (before constraints), so it holds and the add is O(1); the metadata shortcut is gated on `tableIndexCoversFKColumns` (IR left-prefix cover), and when absent it falls through to the validating ADD (which walls LOUDLY via A, never silently). **Known narrow limitation (flagged):** the orphan scan verifies FKs added THIS run; a crash in the seconds between a metadata add committing and the scan completing would leave an unvalidated FK a `--resume` then skips (idempotent prefetch). Closing that needs cross-run persistence of "which FKs are unvalidated" — a separate chunk; until then the remedy is a fresh run.

Verdicts, each with the code/live proof that decided it:

- **A — DONE (the floor).** Added `SLUICE-E-CONSTRAINT-STATEMENT-TIME-LIMIT` (`internal/sluicecode/sluicecode.go` + `docrows.go` + `docs/operator/error-codes.md`) and a `phase: PhaseConstraints` hint keyed on `"maximum statement execution time"` (`internal/pipeline/migcore/hints.go`) with an FK-appropriate remedy (`--skip-foreign-keys`, NOT `--resume` — a constraints 3024 is deterministic). It was already WIRED: all three `migrate.go` constraints sites and `migrate_multidb.go:396` wrap through `WrapWithHint(PhaseConstraints, …)`. Pinned through the real CLI (F6 lesson): `cmd/sluice/migrate_constraint_wall_hint_test.go` drives a walled FK ADD through kong and asserts the code + `--skip-foreign-keys` hint reach the operator.
- **B — DONE, and PROVED on real PlanetScale (the prize).** On the live 153M-row `scaletest-my4` failure case, `SET SESSION foreign_key_checks=0; ALTER TABLE events ADD CONSTRAINT … FOREIGN KEY …` returned in **0.082 s**, created a real FK (present in `information_schema.table_constraints` + `SHOW CREATE TABLE`), and was **NOT** routed to Online DDL. So on a VStream target whose copied rows are FK-consistent by construction, the wall-blocked O(153M-row) validation becomes an O(1) metadata change. Implemented as a wall-recovery mirroring the index fallback (`internal/engines/mysql/schema_writer_constraint_fk_wall.go`): a clearly-huge child skips the doomed validating attempt; otherwise the validating ADD runs and ONLY an errno-3024 wall triggers a metadata-only re-issue under session `foreign_key_checks=0` on a **dedicated `*sql.Conn`** (restored before the conn returns to the pool). **Safe by construction:** it arms ONLY for an UNFILTERED migrate (`len(RowFilters)==0`) from an FK-enforcing source, reconciled to that source before the constraints phase (ADR-0141 runs the re-derive *before* constraints, so the target matches the source at FK-add time), AND only on a VStream flavor — and it only ever substitutes for a validation that was WALLING anyway, so it removes no functioning loud net (a small table still validates; a genuine orphan still fails 1452; a `--where` run stays validated and surfaces A's coded refusal). Threaded engine-neutrally via `ir.ForeignKeyConsistencyDeclarer` / `migcore.ArmForeignKeyConsistency`. Real-InnoDB pins in `schema_writer_constraint_fk_wall_integration_test.go`: metadata-only ADD over an orphan succeeds + FK exists; a `SetMaxOpenConns(1)` no-leak pin proves the session var is restored (a later validating ADD on the shared conn fails 1452); same-engine vanilla no-op proven inert.
- **C — REJECTED (was "only if B fails"; B did not fail, and C is on shaky ground anyway).** Vitess Online DDL — which PlanetScale deploy requests use — **refuses FK-participating tables** unless the experimental `--unsafe-allow-foreign-keys` strategy is set (`vitess executor.go:565-575`), and whether PlanetScale accepts an FK-adding deploy request at all is UNVERIFIED. `--defer-secondary-keys` explicitly skips FK-backing indexes, so there is no MoveTables-native FK deferral either. B makes C unnecessary; the doubtful Online-DDL path is not built.
- **D — DELIVERED.** A constraints-phase 3024 is already classified TERMINAL (structured `*MySQLError` 3024 hits `classifyApplierError`'s terminal-code shield — not in the switch — so `RunDDLPhaseWithReparentRetry` does not retry it in-run). The field "loop" was across `--resume` runs. With B, an unfiltered migrate's `--resume` now SUCCEEDS metadata-only; with A, a filtered/non-migrate resume gets the coded refusal + converging `--skip-foreign-keys` remedy. Either way a second attempt no longer silently re-hits-and-dies.
- **Multidb gap FOLDED IN.** `migrate_multidb.go:395`'s bare `CreateConstraints` now runs through `RunDDLPhaseWithReparentRetry("constraints", …)` (ADR-0114 parity) and is armed the same as the per-database path.

**Deferred / not done:** the clearly-huge FK pre-skip reuses the index path's 64 GiB `DATA_LENGTH` probe; a walled sub-64GiB FK still burns the ~15-min attempt once before recovering (acceptable — it converges, unlike before). B was proven on PlanetScale by the coordinator's live probe, not re-run from this worktree (no live target touched here). **Concurrency note:** `addForeignKeyMetadataOnly` uses a dedicated pooled `*sql.Conn` with a session var + restore — no goroutines/shared state, so no `-race`-specific exposure, but it is a new pool-connection lifecycle path worth the CI `-race` Integration job confirming.

*Original analysis (kept for context):*

**Why.** Everything sluice built for PlanetScale-MySQL's ~900s statement-time wall is keyed to the *index* phase: the errno-3024 hint is `phase: PhaseIndexes` only (`internal/pipeline/migcore/hints.go:179,191`), and the ADR-0148 deploy-request fallback is reachable only from `CreateIndexes` via `buildTableIndexesWithDeployFallback`. `SchemaWriter.CreateConstraints` (`internal/engines/mysql/schema_writer.go:561`) runs a bare `w.db.ExecContext` per `ALTER … ADD FOREIGN KEY` — no fallback, no hint, no code. And `ADD FOREIGN KEY` is *heavier* than an index build, because InnoDB validates every child row against the parent as it adds the constraint.

**Field capture.** `--upfront-indexes` migrate of a 153M-row `events` table into a fresh PS-160: copy completed (522 min), all 4 indexes built inline, then `create constraints: add foreign key "events_customer_fk": Error 3024 … maximum statement execution time exceeded, elapsed time: 15m0.0006s`. The `--resume` loop hit the identical wall in exactly 15 minutes and died again — deterministic, so it cannot converge. This is the answer to "why is the PlanetScale-MySQL target the unreliable one at scale": the whole errno-3024 arc treated the wall as an index problem when it is a DDL-phase problem, and a schema with FKs (i.e. most real schemas) cannot complete a large migration.

**What (evaluate, don't assume — each has a real trade).**
1. **Extend the errno-3024 hint to `PhaseConstraints`** — the F6 wiring one phase over, with an FK-appropriate remedy. Cheapest, and it at least stops the operator getting a bare error.
2. **`SET foreign_key_checks=0` for the ADD, metadata-only.** In a *migrate* the child rows were just copied from a source where the FK held, so validation is provably redundant — this converts an O(rows) operation into an instant one and sidesteps the wall entirely. BUT: it trusts source integrity (a mid-copy reparent re-derive, ADR-0141, must have restored the table for this to hold), and it may not be permitted on Vitess/PlanetScale at all. Verify both before relying on it. This is the highest-leverage option *if* it holds.
3. **Route FK creation through the ADR-0148 deploy-request fallback**, as indexes do. Larger change: `CreateConstraints` needs the fallback plumbing `CreateIndexes` has. Composes with PR #308 (deploy-request wait, now sound) but inherits the F8 risk — an FK deploy request can hit the same vstreamer-throttle failure that wedged the index one and blocks the queue. Needs live validation, not just code.
4. **The resume loop must not spin on a deterministic 3024.** A constraints-phase 3024 is not transient; re-running reproduces it. Recognise it as non-retryable-in-place and route to the fallback or refuse with the remedy, rather than looping.

**Gotchas / related.** `migrate_multidb.go:395` already calls `CreateConstraints` directly, bypassing `RunDDLPhaseWithReparentRetry` — so even the grow-gate reparent retry doesn't cover one FK path; fold that in. The Postgres target has none of this (no statement wall, FKs added `NOT VALID` then validated per ADR — `migrate.go:950`), so this is MySQL/Vitess-family-only. Any fix must keep same-engine MySQL→MySQL (no wall) a clean no-op.

### 108. `--resume` refuses a dev branch whose deploy request is still healthily building, instead of adopting it — the operators the unbounded wait was written for are the ones it cannot rescue (observed live 2026-07-30) — *✅ SHIPPED v0.116.0*

**Why.** The ADR-0148 index fallback opens a PlanetScale deploy request on a dev branch and waits. Before the unbounded-wait change, that wait was capped at 1h while a real 106 GB / 4-index build takes ~3h25m throttled — so the common outcome was: sluice exits, the branch and its deploy request survive, and the build keeps going. On the next `--resume`, sluice hits `dev branch "sluice-index-<id>" already exists — a previous run left it behind` and refuses.

**Verified live**, not reasoned: against `scaletest-my3` with deploy request #1 at **78%, `deployment_state=in_progress`, `eta_seconds≈3099`**, a `--resume` with `--planetscale-deploy-timeout 0` refused. It behaved *safely* — still exactly 1 deploy request and 1 branch afterwards, nothing deleted, DR untouched — but it did not wait. The remedies it names are "inspect it yourself" or "delete the branch and re-run", and deleting would discard ~3h of completed index build.

**Why it matters despite the wait fix.** Going forward, an unbounded wait means a run no longer abandons a deploy mid-flight, so this state stops being *created*. It does nothing for anyone already holding a branch stranded by the old 1h default — which is precisely the population the change was written for. The fix prevents the disease without curing existing cases.

**What.** On encountering an existing sluice-owned dev branch, look up its open deploy request and **adopt it**: if the state is in-flight, hand off to the same poller the fresh path uses (progress narration, terminal-failure fast-fail, keep-the-branch rule all already exist). Only refuse when there is no deploy request, or when it is in a terminal-failure state — and in the latter case name the branch delete, which is then genuinely correct. The poller is already built and mutation-covered; this is a lookup plus a dispatch, not new machinery.

**Gotchas.**
- **Adopt only what sluice owns.** Match the `sluice-index-` prefix convention; never adopt an operator's own dev branch.
- **Verify the DDL matches** before adopting. A branch left by a run whose index set has since changed (a schema edit between attempts) must not be treated as satisfying the current set — compare the deployed DDL against what this run would emit, and refuse loudly on divergence rather than silently building the wrong indexes.
- The refusal currently carries **no `SLUICE-E-*` code**, so a DR automation cannot branch on it — the same machine-contract class as Bug 219. Code it as part of this work.
- Its remedy still suggests deleting a branch whose deployment may be live. That is the narrower survivor of the F8 advice bug: on the in-flight path the delete is not merely refused by the API, it would destroy work in progress.
- `--resume`'s index phase already "re-probes the target and rebuilds only what is still missing", so the post-adoption path needs no special-casing once the deploy completes.

**SHIPPED (`internal/planetscale/expandcontract/leg_adopt.go`).** The leftover branch is now looked up and, when its deploy request is already ISSUED, adopted onto the same `waitDeployed` poller the fresh path uses. It lands in the SHARED `legRunner`, so all three legs get it — the index-build fallback (the item's population), `expand-contract`'s expand/contract legs, and `sluice deploy-ddl` — rather than only the one that was reported.

**The adoptable-state enumeration is the deliverable, and it is derived rather than re-guessed.** `drStates` (deploy_state.go) already carries PlanetScale's full twenty-value `deployment_state` enum classified into in-flight / success / failure / human-gate; `classifyAdoption` reuses that classification instead of minting a second table, and `TestClassifyAdoption_CoversEveryDeploymentState` asserts its own graded set is EXACTLY `drStates`' key set in both directions, so a state added to the enum cannot ship unclassified. The verdicts: **adopt-and-wait** for the eight running states plus `pending_cutover` (the poller already owns that human gate); **adopt-and-finalize** for `complete` / `complete_pending_revert`; **refuse** for the six terminal-failure states, for `no_changes` (the DDL is already deployed), and for the not-yet-deployed ones.

**The line the design draws — and the one divergence from the entry above.** The item says to refuse only when there is no deploy request or it is in terminal failure. The implementation ALSO refuses a deploy request that exists and is healthy but was **never deployed** (`pending` / `ready`). The reason is that the fresh path makes two promises immediately before it calls `Deploy` — the dev branch's schema base still matches current production (`provisionFreshBranch` + `recheckProductionFreshness`) and the computed diff touches nothing outside the leg's intended tables (`assertDiffWithinExpected`) — and NEITHER can be re-established for a branch sluice did not provision in this run: production may have moved arbitrarily far since, and deploying from a base that has fallen behind silently reverts every newer production schema change (ADR-0162 finding 3, observed live). Refusing there costs a re-run and nothing else, because a deploy request that never deployed has no build to lose — which is exactly the property that made the OLD blanket refusal catastrophic and makes this narrow one free. The corollary worth stating explicitly: **adoption never reaches a `Deploy` call**, so the pre-deploy gates are absent from that path by construction rather than by omission (pinned — the adopt path fetches no diff and issues no deploy).

**Identity: three pieces of evidence, and the residual named.** (1) The branch NAME is `sluice-<kind>-<sha256(scope, ddl)[:10]>` (`legBranchName`), computed from the DDL *this run intends* — so a branch at that name was created by a run intending byte-identical DDL for the same scope. That is also the answer to the "verify the DDL matches" gotcha, and a better one than a DDL comparison: an index set that changed between attempts hashes to a DIFFERENT name, so the stale branch is never found and the fresh path runs. (2) The deploy request was opened FROM that branch and merges INTO this run's production branch; anything else refuses. (3) There is exactly ONE such request; two refuses. What this does NOT rule out, stated rather than implied: a person or another tool creating a branch at that exact name and opening a deploy request from it, and a collision in the 40-bit truncated hash. sluice does not read the DDL back off the branch — PlanetScale renders schema, not statements, and comparing rendered schema to intent would mean parsing DDL.

**Loud beats wrong on the lookup itself.** The new `api.ListDeployRequests` walks the paginated collection and returns `ErrDeployRequestListTruncated` rather than a short answer, because "no deploy request for this branch" carries the remedy *delete the branch*, and handing that to someone whose request was merely on page 21 would destroy a running deployment. The list is used ONLY to learn the request's number (`api.DeployRequestRef`, three fields, shape DERIVED); every field the verdict rides on comes from the live-captured GET-by-number response.

**Coded, and the message names only flags the running command has.** The refusal is `SLUICE-E-PS-DEV-BRANCH-NOT-ADOPTABLE` (registry + `docrows.go` + `docs/operator/error-codes.md`). Separately — the same surface, a pre-existing Bug 230 instance — all four of the index fallback's operator-guidance strings named `--resume` unconditionally, while the fallback is armed on FIVE entry points (`migrate`, `restore`, `sync start`, the fleet `sync run`, the `sync from-backup` broker) and only `migrate` has that flag. They now resolve through `migcore.RunningCommand()`, with the flagless text as the ZERO value, and `TestIndexFallbackRerunAdviceNamesOnlyRunnableFlags` grades the non-migrate text with `climsggate.BareFlags` — the same tokenizer the CLI-surface gate uses.

**Not adopted-into: a leftover branch whose deploy request the operator merely APPROVED without deploying.** It reads as `ready`, so it takes the never-deployed refusal. That is the intended outcome (the branch's base may be stale), but it is the one case where a re-run costs the operator a full re-provision after they did the thing sluice told them to do; if it shows up in the field, the fix is to re-run the pre-deploy gates on the adopted branch rather than to widen the verdict.

**CORRECTION — v0.116.0 shipped this refusing the exact case it was built for (Bug 231, fixed unreleased).** `classifyAdoption` ORed PlanetScale's `deployable` flag into the verdict as a second, "independent" refusal signal, on the premise that a request PlanetScale would still accept a `Deploy` call for cannot be one it is already deploying. **The premise is false**: the live API reports `deployable=true` throughout a running deployment. Measured by the v0.116.0 regression cycle — deploy request #3 read `deployment_state "in_progress", deployable=true` and was refused at `20:31:07`, strictly between PlanetScale's own `started_at 20:31:03.962Z` and `deployed_at 20:31:11.393Z`. Two fixes, deliberately separate:

- **The verdict.** For a `deployment_state` `drStates` documents, the state table is now the WHOLE answer; `deployable` is consulted only where the table has nothing to say (an undocumented state), and that case gets its own verdict rather than borrowing the never-deployed one.
- **The message, which was the worse half.** The refusal printed `deployment_state "in_progress"` and, in the same sentence, *"Nothing is deploying, so the branch is safe to delete"* — the advice this item shipped to remove, aimed at a branch with a live build on it. The delete-is-safe CLAIM now has one renderer (`legRunner.safeToDeleteAdvice`) and `TestAdoptRefusalNeverClaimsNothingIsDeployingAboutARunningState` greps for it across every state × every `deployable` shape × `open`/`closed`, failing if any refusal makes the claim from a state that does not establish it. The unrecognized-state refusal says it does not know and names no delete.

**Why the twenty-state matrix did not catch it, which is the transferable part.** `TestClassifyAdoption_CoversEveryDeploymentState` graded all twenty states with an anti-vacuity floor in both directions — and every row carried a hard-coded `deployable` value from the comment *"only the pre-deploy `ready` is deployable"*. That is an UNVERIFIED PREMISE about the live API standing in for a test axis, and the fake control plane encoded the same one (`Deployment.Deployable` left false for the entire post-deploy walk), so the end-to-end adopt pins were green against a shape PlanetScale never serves. The matrix was complete along the axis it enumerated and blind along the axis it assumed. `deployable` is now an enumerated SHAPE axis (absent / nested / top-level / both) and the verdict must be invariant across it for every documented state.

### 107. The preflight LIST was duplicated, so closing one instance left the class open — `verifyBackupIDs` was still restore-only (Bug 218) — *✅ SHIPPED v0.104.6*

**What.** Item 106 gave `backup verify` the schema-fingerprint check and shared the *predicate* deciding which lineage shapes get it. It left the *list* of preflights duplicated between the two commands — so a manifest whose recorded `BackupID` no longer matched its content still verified `all chunks OK` rc=0 while restore refused it with rc=3 and zero rows. Pre-existing back to v0.103.2 on all seven staged binaries; found by the v0.104.5 regression cycle, which did the thing a claim about a list invites: it enumerated the list.

**How it was found is the point.** v0.104.5's notes said the fingerprint was *"the only restore preflight it skipped"*. That sentence is a claim about a set, and the cycle checked it against the code rather than against the fix's shape: chain restore runs `preflightEncryption` + `verifySchemaHashes` + `verifyBackupIDs`, and the single-manifest path runs `verifySingleFullBackupID`. Verify had gained the second and not the third. The published claim has been corrected in place on the v0.104.5 notes and the live release body.

**Shape coverage runs the OPPOSITE way to item 106's**, which is why conflating them would have been a mistake: the BackupID check reaches a **bare full** as well as chain links, because restore checks it there (`verifySingleFullBackupID`). A bare full is exempt from the *fingerprint* check, not from every check.

**Fix — the class, not the instance.** `restoreManifestIntegrityPreflights(ctx, links, needsWalk)` is now the single definition of the list: fingerprint on the chain path, BackupID on both shapes. Three call sites use it — chain restore's step 2.7, `Restore.verifySingleFullBackupID` (needsWalk=false over the lone full), and `verifyBackupScan`. A preflight added there now reaches both commands or neither. Encryption preflight is deliberately excluded: it needs key material verify may not have, and folding it in would make verify refuse chains restore accepts whenever a key is absent.

**Pins, mutation-verified.** A tampered recorded id on a chain incremental and on a bare full each refuse under the restore code; stubbing `verifyBackupIDs` fails both deterministically. The existing bare-full-fingerprint-stays-green pin still passes, which is what proves the two shape rules did not get merged.


### 106. `backup verify` was green over chains `restore` refuses — the fingerprint preflight it never made (Bug 217) — *✅ SHIPPED v0.104.5 — but see item 107: the fix shared the predicate and not the LIST, leaving a second preflight behind*

**What.** `sluice backup verify` returned rc=0 `all chunks OK` over a chain `restore` refuses with rc=3 and zero rows. Found by the v0.104.4 regression cycle, which asked the question v0.104.3's own headline had turned into a house rule: does verify AGREE with restore? Pre-existing back to **v0.103.2** — every released binary has it.

**Why it is worse than a release-skew nit.** The cycle scoped it before filing, and the scoping is the interesting part: verify DOES catch a corrupted chunk, a deleted chunk, a severed lineage link, and (with `--verify-key`) signature failures. The manifest schema fingerprint was the **only** restore preflight it skipped — and changing **one hex digit** of a chain's own `schema_hash` was invisible to verify on all six staged binaries while all six refused to restore it. So this is not "verify cannot see across an epoch boundary", it is "verify cannot see a class of manifest damage restore refuses on". Signing was the only mitigation, and it works, but it is opt-in and the check it backstops is not.

**Fix.** `verifyBackupScan` now runs `verifySchemaHashes` over the built lineage chain — the same function, on the same links, that `chain_restore.go` runs — and reports the same `SLUICE-E-BACKUP-MANIFEST-INVALID` with the same two-cause wording, so a script branching on the code gets one answer from both commands.

**Scoped to what restore ACTUALLY does, which is the load-bearing half.** Restore runs this check on the CHAIN path only; a one-segment-no-incrementals lineage takes the single-manifest path, which never walks links and never fingerprints them. That is why a **bare full crosses an epoch fine** (item 102's blast-radius note), and a verify that refused it would report a chain broken that restores row-exact — the same defect inverted. The predicate is now shared: `Restore.lineageNeedsWalk` delegates to `verifyLineageNeedsWalk`, one function with two callers, so verify and restore cannot drift into disagreeing about which shape gets checked. Same reasoning as the nil comparator on the lineage walk above it: **verify must never refuse a chain restore would accept.**

**Pins, mutation-verified.** `verify_schema_fingerprint_test.go`: a one-hex-digit edit to the root full's fingerprint and to an incremental's each refuse under the restore code, an intact chain verifies clean, and — the honest one — a **bare full** with a mismatched fingerprint still verifies green. Disabling the check fails the two refusal cases deterministically. Real-binary half: cell 5 of the cross-version suite now asserts verify refuses the same epoch-crossing chain restore just refused, and names the schema fingerprint when it does.

**Behaviour change worth calling out in the notes:** an operator running `backup verify` on a schedule against chains written by an older release will see it start refusing what it used to pass. That refusal is the truth restore was already telling them.


### 105. The CDC-mode-per-source engine list is prose, and prose is where the engine-set claims go wrong — *DONE — the gate is live on `main`. It is a test, so it protects every subsequent release rather than shipping in one.*

**Why now.** Writing v0.104.4's release notes, the first draft said the MySQL close-vs-pump fix reached "MySQL, MariaDB, PlanetScale or Vitess". It does not: `Flavor.usesVStream()` (`internal/engines/mysql/flavor.go:89`) routes PlanetScale and Vitess to a different reader entirely, so the fix reaches `mysql` and `mariadb` and nothing else. Caught by reading the dispatch before publishing — which is the CLAUDE.md rule working, and also the reason the rule exists: this is the fourth release in a row where an engine-set sentence was the part that was wrong while the fix underneath it was right.

**What to build.** The `internal/docsync` pattern that already exists for filtered sync (`TestFilteredSyncEngineListMatchesTheCode`: capability pin → engine set → doc marker). Here the derivable fact is the CDC mode per source — binlog for `mysql`/`mariadb`, VStream for `planetscale`/`vitess`, logical replication for `postgres`, trigger for the pgtrigger/D1 variants — and the doc to hold to it is `docs/production-readiness.md`'s CDC-modes table, which is correct today and unguarded. ~80 lines, and it converts a recurring prose error into a build failure.

**Scope note.** Release notes and CHANGELOG entries stay prose and stay unguarded — they are archival and each names a moment. The gate belongs on the living doc; the discipline for the notes is to derive the sentence from the gated table rather than from the shape of the fix.

**BUILT (`internal/docsync/cdc_mode_engines_test.go`).** `TestCDCModeTableMatchesTheRegistry` iterates the real engine registry — the same blank-import set `cmd/sluice/main.go` links — reads each engine's `Capabilities().CDC`, and holds `docs/production-readiness.md`'s `<!-- cdc-modes: … -->` marker to the derived pairing. Today that is 14 engines: `mysql`/`mariadb` binlog, `planetscale`/`vitess` vstream, `postgres` logical-replication, the three trigger engines, and six with none.

Three properties worth keeping if it is ever edited. It checks the **mechanism**, not just presence — the sibling gate next door already asks "is this engine named in the CDC guide", and presence was never the thing going wrong. It includes the `none` engines, because "which sources have no CDC at all" is the same class of claim. And it carries a **non-vacuity floor** (a minimum registry size, three named engines whose mechanisms differ, and at least one non-`none`), so a dropped blank import fails the gate instead of quietly agreeing with the doc about a smaller world — the failure mode that made three of this session's gates pass against the defects they were named for.

Mutation-verified: flipping `planetscale=vstream` to `binlog` in the marker — the exact error in v0.104.4's first-draft notes — fails with `WRONG mechanism for planetscale: doc says binlog, registry says vstream`.


### 104. v0.104.3 added a FOURTH fingerprint epoch — the `omitempty` fix does not hold for the value a real Postgres source produces (Bug 216) — *✅ SHIPPED v0.104.4*

**What.** A backup chain written by v0.104.3 from a Postgres source whose tables have primary keys cannot be restored by v0.104.2 or any earlier release: schema-fingerprint mismatch, rc=3, zero rows. Confirmed against v0.104.2, v0.104.1, v0.104.0 and v0.103.2. This is item 102's class, one release later, in the release that shipped the fix for it.

**Why `omitempty` was not enough, which is the whole lesson.** Item 102's fix gave `ir.Index.ConstraintNamed` an `omitempty` tag so it would vanish from the marshalled schema and leave the fingerprint unchanged. It does vanish — **when the field is false.** The Postgres reader sets it **true** for every constraint-owned index (`schema_reader.go:1704`, from a `pg_constraint` join on `contype IN ('u','p')`), and Postgres auto-names both kinds, so on any real Postgres chain the field is present and the fingerprint moves. Controls narrow it: PG source with a PK → rc=3; PG source with an explicitly-named PK → rc=3; **PG source with NO primary key → rc=0, restores 103 rows**; **MySQL source with a PK → rc=0**.

**SCOPE CORRECTION (2026-07-29, v0.104.4 regression cycle).** The controls above read as "primary keys" and that is too narrow: a **named UNIQUE constraint carries the field too**, with no primary key required, so a PK-less table with a unique constraint also crosses the boundary. The rc=0 no-PK control did not catch it because that table had no unique constraint either — a control that confirms a narrow reading because it happens to lack the *other* trigger, which is the same shape of error as the self-referential golden this item exists for, one layer down. Every operator-facing statement of the scope (CHANGELOG for v0.104.3 and v0.104.4, both archived note files, both live GitHub bodies, `docs/operator/error-codes.md`) was corrected in place; the practical rule is "assume an ordinary Postgres schema is affected." The pre-release verification hashed a schema where the field was absent, which is exactly why it measured byte-identical.

**The gate shipped to prevent this cannot catch it, and that is the more important finding.** `internal/ir/backup/schema_hash_golden_test.go` freezes its constant over a `goldenSchema()` whose primary key carries `ConstraintNamed: true` — a value **no older binary could ever have written**. So the golden proves the current binary agrees with itself, which is the one thing that was never in doubt. A frozen-golden fixture that includes post-bump fields at their non-zero values is self-referential by construction.

**Fix shape.** Two candidates, and the first is better. (a) **Keep the field out of the fingerprint entirely** — the explicit-projection idea item 102 deferred, now with a concrete reason to build it: relying on a zero value is relying on a source rarely producing the interesting case. (b) Hold every post-bump field at its zero value in the frozen fixture, so the golden measures what an older binary would have hashed. (b) is a test-only patch that makes the gate honest; (a) is the design fix that makes the class stop recurring. Note that neither retroactively rescues a v0.104.3-written chain — that chain's manifest records a fingerprint computed WITH the field, so a future binary that excludes it will not reproduce that value either. Treat v0.104.3 as its own epoch for restore purposes and say so.

**Gate that would actually have caught it.** The cross-version CI cell (`internal/pipeline/backup_crossversion_integration_test.go`) already builds two real binaries against one store. Extend it to write a **named-PK Postgres** chain with the new binary and assert the PREVIOUS release restores it. That is a behavioural check across the boundary rather than a hash compared against itself, and it is the shape that found this — a regression cycle asking the boring question "does the new release's output still read on the old one?"

**Severity note.** It fails in the safe direction — loud refusal in preflight, never a silent partial restore — and with no production users there is no stranded chain in the field. It is HIGH because the published release notes asserted the opposite, and that assertion has been corrected in place rather than rewritten.

**SHIPPED (v0.104.4).** Fix shape (a), scoped down to the one field: `canonicalSchemaForHash` now drops `ir.Index.ConstraintNamed` before marshalling (`fingerprintIndex` in `internal/ir/backup/chain.go`), for a table's `PrimaryKey` and its secondary indexes alike, copying rather than mutating so the schema the manifest records still carries the name a restore re-emits. Scoping it to the field rather than rewriting the whole hash as an explicit projection is what makes it a *repair*: with the field gone the marshalled bytes are E3's exactly, so v0.104.4 chains restore on v0.103.0 – v0.104.2 and the epoch count goes back to three. A general projection would have been a fifth epoch for zero user benefit — the item-102 reasoning, unchanged.

Verified against a **real v0.104.2 build**, not against this one: a worktree at that tag, hashing the golden fixture with the `ConstraintNamed` line dropped (the field does not exist there), prints `07231daa…916868` — the constant now frozen in `schema_hash_golden_test.go`. That provenance is written into the constant's comment, because a golden verified against its own binary is what let this ship.

Three gates, in order of how much they would actually have caught:

1. **Cell 6 of the cross-version suite** — the working tree writes a primary-keyed Postgres chain, the newest release at the SAME `BackupFormatVersion` restores it, and it must PASS. This is the boring question the regression cycle asked, made permanent. Its peer binary is derived (`scripts/crossversion-build.sh`, newest same-format tag minus an orphan-epoch exclusion list that today holds exactly `v0.104.3`), so it advances on its own; equality of format is what keeps a refusal here attributable to the fingerprint rather than the version gate. Its non-vacuity guard asserts the chain it just wrote really carries a constraint-named index — the exact thing the pre-release verification of the `omitempty` fix failed to check.
2. **`TestComputeSchemaHash_ExcludesIndexConstraintNamed`** — flipping the field on a PK or a secondary index must not move the hash by a bit, plus a pin that hashing does not mutate the caller's schema.
3. **The frozen golden, made honest** — the constant is now a number an older binary demonstrably produced, and the block comment carries a third answer (exclude the field) alongside `omitempty` and a deliberate format bump, with the warning that `omitempty` is only worth what the zero value's frequency in real sources makes it.

**Not fixed, and deliberately.** A chain v0.104.3 wrote from a primary-keyed Postgres source stays unreadable by everything including v0.104.4 — its manifest records a fingerprint computed *with* the field, and nothing re-derives it. That is item 102's demand-gated shim, unchanged by this. `docs/operator/error-codes.md` now documents E4 as the one-release detour it is, including which v0.104.3 chains are affected (PG source with a PK) and which are ordinary E3 chains (MySQL sources, PG without a PK).


### 103. The MySQL CDC reader has the PG close-vs-pump race, unfixed — *✅ SHIPPED v0.104.4*

**Found while fixing the Postgres one (roadmap item covering the v0.104.3 CI data race), and deliberately NOT bundled with it.** `internal/engines/mysql/cdc_reader.go` (~415-430) nils `r.db` in `Close` with no join against its pump goroutine, and that pump reads `r.db` via `tableFor` (~1260) on the TABLE_MAP path. Same shape as the Postgres defect: `Close` tears down state the pump still owns.

**Why this is not a detector curiosity.** On the PG side the same shape was production-reachable and worse than a race warning: a pump that passes an `if r.db == nil` check and then reaches `r.db.QueryContext` dereferences a nil `*sql.DB` and **panics on a goroutine nothing recovers**, taking the process down. Two live call sites close a reader whose pump is running — `sync`'s per-attempt teardown (`streamer.go` deferred `stop()` → `CloseIf`) and `backup stream`'s transient-retry reopen (`stream.go`). Neither is MySQL-specific, so both reach this reader too.

**Not confirmed by CI, which is why it is filed rather than patched.** The PG instance surfaced from a real `-race` CI report; this one is a code-reading sibling with no failing run behind it. That is exactly the "pin the class, not the representative" situation — the class is *a reader whose Close races its own pump*, and the PG fix closed one instance of it. Do not assume the PG patch transplants: MySQL's pump has different lifecycle (go-mysql's streamer, not pgconn), and its cancellation path may or may not carry the second defect the PG fix uncovered (pgx returning an `*errTimeout` for an already-done context, which made a cancelled pump spin forever and leak a hot goroutine per torn-down stream).

**Fix shape, from the PG one.** Hand the pump a `done` channel as an ARGUMENT rather than reading it off the struct — so `Close` can clear fields without racing the channel itself — have the pump close it last, and make `Close` cancel-then-join before touching `r.db`. Pin it with a unit test whose stand-in pump re-reads `r.db` on exit so `-race` trips, plus a real-wire test asserting non-blockingly that the change channel is already closed when `Close` returns (no sleeps, no tolerance).

**Check for the cancellation-spin sibling while there.** The PG pump tested `pgconn.Timeout(err)` before `errors.Is(err, context.Canceled)`, so a cancelled pump never unwound. Whatever go-mysql returns on a cancelled read deserves the same question: does the error-classification order let a cancelled pump loop forever?

**Adjacent, small, PG-side, pre-existing — worth folding in whenever this file is next opened.** If cancellation lands exactly when a keepalive is due, `SendStandbyStatusUpdate` errors and `setErr` records that on what is otherwise a clean shutdown, so a healthy stop can surface a spurious error. Rare, and it fails in the noisy rather than the silent direction, which is why it is a note and not its own item — but it is the same "the reason we are stopping must not become the failure we report" shape the cold-start anchor fix (item 89) closed on the backup path, so it belongs with that family rather than being rediscovered as a mystery.

**SHIPPED (v0.104.4), and it is ONE half rather than the PG fix's two.** `StreamChanges` now hands the pump a `done` channel as an argument (never read off the struct, so `Close` can clear the field without racing the goroutine it waits for), closed as the pump's last act; `Close` cancels, joins, and only then closes the syncer and releases the pool. Joining before the syncer teardown, not after: the pump exits on ctx alone, so the join needs nothing from the syncer.

**The cancellation-spin sibling was checked, not assumed, and it is absent.** go-mysql v1.15.0's `BinlogStreamer.GetEvent` (`replication/binlogstreamer.go:29-36`) selects on `ctx.Done()` and returns `ctx.Err()` bare — no timeout dressing, so nothing for the pump's classification order to swallow, and no second half to write. That is a claim about a dependency rather than about sluice, which is why the integration pin exists at all: regress it and the test hangs at `Close` rather than failing an assertion.

**The adjacent note above, applied to this engine.** A cancelled dispatch used to be recorded through `setErr`: `tableFor` runs a live information_schema query and the channel send parks on `ctx.Done`, so an ordinary `Close` reached the dispatch-error branch with the teardown's own context error and `Err()` reported a deliberate stop as the stream's terminating failure. Both error branches now test `ctx.Err()` first.

**Pins, mutation-verified in both directions — and the integration one had to be rewritten to earn that.** Unit (`TestCDCReaderCloseJoinsPumpBeforeReleasingSchemaPool`): deleting the `<-r.pumpDone` wait fails it deterministically, and its stand-in pump re-reads `r.db` on the way out so `-race` trips too. Integration (`TestCDCReader_CloseJoinsLivePump`, real mysqld): parks the pump inside `tableFor`'s schema lookup through the existing `schemaLoader` seam, then asserts `Close` BLOCKS there and that the pool is still pingable from inside the parked lookup.

**The first draft of that integration test PASSED with the join deleted**, which is worth recording as its own data point. It did the obvious thing — close a live reader, assert the change channel is already closed — and a cancelled pump simply unwinds faster than `Close` returns, so the assertion held either way. Same family as item 104's self-referential golden: a gate whose green survives the defect it is named for. The parking is what converts it into a real gate; the ordering it asserts is now impossible to satisfy by luck.

**Still true of this reader, and deliberately not changed here:** `r.schemaCache` and the tableMap are pump-owned and untouched by `Close`, so the join is what makes them safe rather than a lock. If a future caller ever reads reader state from outside the pump, that is a new question, not one this fix answers.

**The third reader — VStream — was checked and is a MILDER shape, filed here rather than fixed.** `vstreamCDCReader.Close` (`cdc_vstream.go:827`) has the same outline: cancel, null the transport (`r.conn`), no join. But its pump never reads `r.conn` — it holds a `vtgateservice.VitessClient` built once at open — so there is no unsynchronised read of the field Close writes and no nil-deref, and closing a `grpc.ClientConn` under an in-flight stream is a supported operation that cancels the RPC rather than corrupting it. What remains is only that the pump can outlive `Close`'s return, which is the weakest third of the defect. **So PlanetScale and Vitess sources are NOT covered by the item-103 fix and did not need to be** (`Flavor.usesVStream()` routes them away from the binlog reader entirely — `flavor.go:89`); the fix reaches `mysql` and `mariadb`. If the join is ever wanted there too it is a small change, but it needs the cluster-gated suites to prove it, which is why it is not bundled here.


### 102. **CRITICAL, ALREADY SHIPPED** — adding a field to `ir.Index` partitions every backup chain by release, and v0.100.0 already did it: a pre-v0.100.0 chain cannot be restored by any v0.100.0+ binary, and it reports as *"your backup is corrupt"* — *open, CRITICAL / DR-availability. Fix shape needs its own scoping; deliberately NOT fixed in the chunk that found it.*

**What.** `irbackup.ComputeSchemaHash` (`internal/ir/backup/chain.go:46`) is a SHA-256 over `json.Marshal` of the IR schema, and the IR schema structs carry **no json tags** — every exported field marshals unconditionally under its Go name. So adding ANY field to `ir.Index` changes the marshalled bytes of every index of every table, and therefore changes the fingerprint of schemas that did not change. `verifySchemaHashes` (`internal/pipeline/backup/chain_restore.go:743`, called from step 2.7 at `:284`) recomputes that fingerprint on every link of a chain and REFUSES the whole chain on a mismatch.

Commit `89b89862` added `ConstraintDeferrable` / `ConstraintNullsNotDistinct` / `ConstraintWithoutOverlaps` to `ir.Index`, first released in **v0.100.0** (2026-07-23). `f5ab5ee1` then added `ConstraintInitiallyDeferred`, first released in **v0.103.0**. Each is an independent partition. There are three already-shipped hash epochs, and chains are restorable only *within* an epoch:

| epoch | releases | `ir.Index` shape | hash of the probe schema |
|---|---|---|---|
| E1 | ≤ v0.99.292 | (none of the `Constraint*` additions) | `4c20b032…08bef` |
| E2 | v0.100.0 – v0.102.2 | `+Deferrable +NullsNotDistinct +WithoutOverlaps` | `a75f53e0…4e164` |
| E3 | v0.103.0 – v0.104.2 | `+InitiallyDeferred` | `4bda0022…10f827` |

**⚠ The error messages quoted below are the PRE-FIX wording**, kept because they are what a v0.104.2-or-earlier binary still prints and what an operator hitting this today will actually see. The shipped refusal no longer says "corrupted" first — see the DECISION block above.

**Ground truth — reproduced on real released binaries, not inferred.** Built from tag worktrees and driven through the existing cross-version harness (`internal/pipeline/backup_crossversion_integration_test.go`, `integration && crossversion`) with the old tag pinned instead of derived, against a real Postgres container:
