- **v0.99.292 writes a chain → v0.104.2 restores → FAIL.** `code=SLUICE-E-BACKUP-MANIFEST-INVALID`, `hint="restore from an untampered copy, or sign the chain …"`, `err="chain restore: manifest manifest.json (backup 35c7d6c5986ae21a) schema hash mismatch: recorded 4c20b032f583a76660afdf88f0d5ec3c754433a5ece89d94b00fccc0ba108bef, recomputed 4bda0022832a1fb44e63ea8745038c3dc86439cf0d694274b556d5d18810f827 — the manifest's schema does not match the fingerprint written with it (corrupted or partially-rewritten manifest); refusing before any data lands"`.
- **v0.99.292 → v0.100.0 (the boundary itself) → FAIL,** identical shape, `recomputed a75f53e0…`.
- **v0.100.0 → v0.99.292 (reverse) → FAIL,** the exact mirror image (`recorded a75f53e0…, recomputed 4c20b032…`). This is a **partition, not a forward-compat gap**.
- **CONTROL: v0.100.0 writes → v0.102.2 restores → PASS,** rows asserted. Those two have byte-identical `ir.Index` structs, so the control proves the failures above are caused by the field additions and by nothing else in the harness.

**Which refusal fires, and why that is the whole point.** The schema-hash mismatch, every time — never a format-version refusal. `BackupFormatVersion` is **8** at v0.99.292, v0.100.0, v0.102.2 *and* v0.103.2, so the version check cannot preempt the hash check across either boundary by construction (the probe's roots stamped 7, under every reader's ceiling). The operator is therefore told their manifest is **"corrupted or partially-rewritten"** and advised to *"restore from an untampered copy"* — about a chain that is byte-for-byte intact. There is no version-gap wording anywhere in the message; the cross-version harness's own cell-2 assertion (*"refused but never said 'newer than this build supports' — the operator cannot tell a version gap from corruption"*) fires on it.

**Blast radius.**
- **Chains only.** `restore.go`'s lineage dispatch sends a one-segment-no-incrementals lineage down the single-manifest path, which never calls `verifySchemaHashes`. A **bare full** therefore crosses epochs fine; anything with ≥1 incremental or ≥2 segments does not.
- **Not DR-only.** `internal/pipeline/broker.go:1033` calls the exported `backup.VerifySchemaHashes` on the same chain — the broker live-apply path refuses identically.
- **Signed chains take a second, independent hit.** `deltaTableFingerprint` (`internal/ir/backup/signature.go:459-467`) folds `ComputeSchemaHash` into the signing bytes, so any manifest with a non-empty `SchemaDelta` also fails signature verification.
- Nothing lands on the target: the refusal is in `PhaseConnect` preflight, ahead of the BackupID check, the signature check, and all target work. (Code-ordering + logs; the harness does not independently assert it in these cells.)

**Remediation available to an operator holding such a chain today: none that is documented.** The recorded hash is never re-derived — `verifySchemaHashes` recomputes with the *running* binary's struct shape and compares against the recorded value; there is no "recompute at the version the artifact records" path for the schema hash, unlike the chunk-AAD dual-version rule. The one carve-out (`m.Schema.Sequences` non-empty && `FormatVersion < FormatVersionEncryptedChunkBinding` → WARN instead of refuse) is unrelated and does not cover this. There is no flag to skip the check. The practical escapes are all bad: run a binary from the chain's own epoch (works, but silently reintroduces every bug fixed since), or hand-edit `SchemaHash` in the manifest (which breaks signature verification and is exactly the tampering the check exists to detect). **Treat a pre-v0.100.0 or pre-v0.103.0 chain as unreadable by current binaries until this is fixed.**

**Fix shape — needs its own scoping, deliberately not attempted here.** Candidates: (a) re-derive the fingerprint at the version the artifact records, per ADR-0154's dual-version rule — requires a per-version canonical marshaller, which is real design work; (b) a compatibility shim that recomputes against each known historical `ir.Index` shape and accepts a match from any epoch ≤ the manifest's, downgrading to a WARN; (c) at minimum, distinguish the wording — a mismatch on a manifest written by an older release must not say "corrupted", because that sends an operator to look for a problem in their storage that is not there. (c) is cheap and independently valuable even if (a)/(b) are deferred.

**What has been done in the meantime (the forward half only).** The *next* instance of this class was caught before release: `ir.Index.ConstraintNamed` (item 84, unreleased) had the same defect and now carries `json:"ConstraintNamed,omitempty"`, which restores E3's hash byte-identically. The permanent gate is `TestComputeSchemaHash_FrozenGolden` in `internal/ir/backup/schema_hash_golden_test.go` — a frozen hex constant over a representative schema carrying one instance of every IR schema object, so any future untagged field addition to `ir.Schema`/`Table`/`Index`/`IndexColumn`/`ForeignKey`/`CheckConstraint`/`ExcludeConstraint`/`Policy`/`View`/`Sequence` fails CI. That stops the bleeding; it does **not** repair the three epochs already in the field, which is what this item is for. Note also that `ir.Column` was never exposed — it already carries lowercase `omitempty` json tags, which is why the class went unnoticed for two releases.

**DECISION 2026-07-28 (operator-confirmed: no production users).** The compatibility shim that would make stranded chains readable again — a registry of historical marshal shapes, retried on mismatch so an authentic old manifest is recognised rather than called corrupt — is **DEMAND-GATED, not built**. It is the only option that recovers data already on disk, and with no real install base it would be real complexity bought to rescue chains nobody holds. Revisit the moment that stops being true; the shape is recorded here so it does not need re-deriving.

**Shipped instead, in priority order.** (a) The refusal no longer accuses the operator of tampering — a schema-fingerprint mismatch now names BOTH causes, a manifest from a different release epoch and genuine corruption, because telling someone mid-recovery that their backup store has been tampered with when they merely upgraded is the actual harm here. (b) An epoch-CROSSING cell in the cross-version gate, pinning the partition as known-and-accepted; it fails loudly if the shim is ever built, which is the right trigger to update it. (c) `TestComputeSchemaHash_FrozenGolden` (landed with the `omitempty` fix) is the recurrence prevention: any future field addition that moves the hash fails CI instead of silently minting a fourth epoch.

**Deliberately NOT done: hashing an explicit projection** instead of the live struct — the ADR-0181 lesson applied here. It is the better long-term design and it is the wrong move today: done carelessly it changes the hash once more and creates a fourth epoch, for zero user benefit, and the frozen-golden gate already prevents recurrence. It buys ergonomics (never having to think about `omitempty` again), not safety. Worth doing the next time this file is opened for a field addition, when the hash is changing anyway.

**RE-AFFIRMED 2026-07-28, and a fourth epoch shipped anyway — see item 104.** v0.104.3 minted E4 through the `omitempty` this section called the containment, and the v0.104.4 fix opened this file again with the hash already moving, which is exactly the moment named above for the general projection. It was still NOT taken: a projection reproducing E3's bytes by construction is delicate, and one that does not reproduce them is a fifth epoch. What shipped is the narrow form — a named exclusion set for the one field (`fingerprintIndex`) — which returns the bytes to E3 exactly. The epoch table below is therefore E1/E2/E3 plus a one-release E4 that only v0.104.3-written primary-keyed Postgres chains sit in; `docs/operator/error-codes.md` carries the operator-facing version.

**It fails in the SAFE direction, and that is why it is not a stop-everything.** A loud refusal before any data lands, not silent corruption — the opposite of the class this project fears most. What made it serious was the message and the absence of any escape, and (a) closes the half that was actively misleading.

**Why no existing test could have caught it.** Every other test in this repo runs ONE binary against its own output, and one binary always agrees with itself about what `Index` marshals to. Only the two-binary cross-version harness (built for the unrelated Bug 212 / item 90) can observe this class at all — and it derives its old tag as *"the newest tag whose `BackupFormatVersion` is strictly lower"*, which is v0.103.2 for the current tree: an E3→E3 pair, in-epoch, green. The tag-derivation rule that makes the item-90 gate non-vacuous is exactly what made it blind here. Worth folding into the fix: the crossversion gate should ALSO pin a pair that straddles a known hash epoch.

### 101. `backup compact --smart-compaction` left a chain restore REFUSES, on the most ordinary shape it exists for — *✅ SHIPPED v0.104.3 — found while fixing item 98, pre-existing and NOT caused by it*

**What.** Smart compaction rewrites each merged incremental's change chunks: it buffers row events into per-PK accumulators and flushes them at end-of-incremental. `finalize` called `flushAll` *after* the stream's closing `TxCommit`, so the rewritten stream's last position-bearing event was a collapsed row event — and a collapsed event deliberately carries its chain's **FIRST** position (`rowAccumulator.flush`: `Position: prev.Position`, with its own comment saying so). Any incremental that touched **one row in more than one transaction** therefore ended BELOW its own recorded `EndPosition`, and `chain_restore.go`'s F1 tail-truncation backstop reads exactly that as a truncated change-list and refuses the chain with `SLUICE-E-BACKUP-INCOMPLETE`. Loud, not silent — but it is a **compacted backup that will not restore**, which is the DR-availability class of items 94/95/97.

**Two comments in the same file contradicted each other, and the code followed the wrong one.** `finalize`'s doc says it "does NOT emit accumulator events at the very end if a TxCommit has already been emitted — that would put row events AFTER the closing TxCommit"; its body did precisely that. Its reasoning (b) claims the policy table "uses the LATEST event's position for the net event"; `flush()` uses the first. The invariant was documented, believed, and unenforced.

**How it surfaced, which is the interesting part.** `TestADR0087_Bug139_ResumeHeals_WholeChainCompacts_PG` went red under item 98's fix. It was **green before only because the item-92/98 defect was masking this one**: the incremental in question was a replay-only window with `start == end`, and the F1 guard skips a manifest that claims no advance (`claimsAdvance` false). Fixing the window so it honestly advanced is what let the guard see the compacted chunk stream at all. One silent-ish defect standing in front of another is worth noting as a pattern — the masking test was passing for a reason that had nothing to do with what it asserts.

**Proven pre-existing, not inferred:** the unit probe was run against the BASE tree with item 98's change stashed, and failed there (`kinds=BCBCU`, last event at the first transaction's position while the incremental closes at the second's). The trigger needs no rotation, no resume, no encryption and no stream — two transactions touching one row inside a single incremental, then `backup compact --smart-compaction`.

**Fix.** `finalize` calls `flushCollapsedInsideClosingTx`, which holds the closing `TxCommit` back, flushes the accumulators, and re-appends it — so the collapsed rows land INSIDE the last transaction (a tighter envelope than before, not a looser one) and the closing position is once again the stream's last event. Positions and collapse semantics are untouched, deliberately: raising a collapsed event's position to its chain's last would ALSO not guarantee reaching the end, because accumulator insertion order is not position order. A stream with no transactional envelope keeps the previous shape.

**Gate.** `internal/pipeline/backup/chain_compact_smart_closing_position_test.go` — the property the restore path actually needs, stated directly (last position-bearing event == the closing position), across {one row in two transactions, two rows whose insertion order is not position order, INSERT-then-UPDATE where the policy keeps the INSERT's position, a chain that collapses to nothing} plus the no-envelope non-vacuity half. Mutation-verified: restoring the bare `flushAll` turns three of the four cells red and leaves the no-envelope pin green.

**Scope note.** This landed as a SEPARATE commit on the item-98 branch because item 98's fix cannot be green without it. It is an independent defect in an independent orchestrator and can be reviewed — or split — on its own.

### 100. `backup prune`'s within-segment incremental trim produces a chain that cannot be restored — *✅ SHIPPED v0.104.3 — contract decided: SEGMENT-GRANULAR retention*

**Found while implementing item 95's readability gate; ground-truthed, not inferred.** Prune has two retention shapes. Dropping leading WHOLE segments is restore-safe (the next segment's full is a self-contained base) and is what item 95 fixed. The other shape — dropping leading incrementals INSIDE the floor segment — leaves that segment's full anchored at S with its first surviving incremental starting at S′ > S. The events in (S, S′] are simply gone, so restoring gives you a snapshot at S with changes from S′ forward and a hole in between. The restore path refuses it, correctly and twice: first on the severed parent link (`build lineage: … does not chain off preceding link … — branching/mis-stitched lineage`), then — with a real position comparator — on the forward gap `ValidateFirstIncrementalBoundary` exists to catch.

**Reproduced on a REAL rotated Postgres chain, in PLAINTEXT, on the pre-fix binary:** prune dropped exactly one incremental, exited 0, and the subsequent `ChainRestore` failed. Also reproduced on the synthetic single-segment fixture. Encryption is not involved.

**Reach (of the defect, before the fix).** Every `--keep-incrementals` prune of a NON-rotated (single-segment) chain was a within-segment trim, since no `KeepIncrementals > 0` can retire a segment's incrementals entirely; so was any keep/duration that landed mid-segment on a rotated chain. `--keep-duration` past every incremental in the floor segment is safe (the segment keeps only its full — no first-incremental boundary to violate), as is any prune that only retires whole segments.

**Why the package doc did not catch it.** `chain_prune.go` claims the trim leaves "the segment full + the remaining incrementals still form a contiguous chain (the boundary invariant prune always preserved)". That claim is about POSITIONS and it is false in both senses — the trim breaks the position boundary AND the parent-link chain. The re-stitch that would have preserved the parent link was deliberately removed in the segment-list reframe ("Reframed (zero users) from the grafted parent-link re-stitch…"), and nothing replaced it; the CLI's own `BackupPruneCmd` doc still described the removed re-stitch as current behaviour until item 95 rewrote it.

**Behaviour after item 95, before the contract decision (interim, deliberate — kept as history).** The readability gate refused these prunes at the PRE-COMMIT leg under `SLUICE-E-BACKUP-CHAIN-UNREADABLE`, exit 3, with nothing deleted and the catalog untouched. That is strictly better than the pre-fix behaviour (destroy, exit 0, discover at restore time) and it is the loud-failure tenet applied — but the refusal's prose is the generic "the chain does not walk", which gives an operator no remedy, and it makes `--keep-incrementals` unusable on a single-segment chain.

**The release-blocking interim (RESOLVED, kept for the history).** Item 95's gate made `--keep-incrementals` on a single-segment chain refuse *every time* under the generic "the chain does not walk" prose. The first fix made that refusal purpose-built — it names the shape, names the severed link concretely, promises inertness ("NOTHING WAS DELETED: this is the pre-commit leg"), and **computes the retention that IS safe on that particular chain** — but it was explicitly the third option below only, with the contract still open.

**The decision this needed** (a contract call, which is why it was filed rather than patched): make retention segment-granular for incrementals (retain more than asked, never less); or re-anchor the floor segment's full so the trimmed chain is genuinely contiguous; or keep refusing with a purpose-built, remedy-bearing refusal.

**Decided and shipped: SEGMENT-GRANULAR retention — the first option.** `--keep-incrementals` and `--keep-duration` are rounded **UP** to the nearest segment boundary (`segmentAlignedKeep`, built on the `segmentBoundaryKeepCounts` the refusal already quotes to the operator, so the counts prune ACCEPTS and the counts it NAMES cannot drift apart). Prune therefore only ever retires whole leading segments — the shape whose restore safety is unconditional. The operator's number becomes approximate in the safe direction, never fewer incrementals than asked; the run reports `incrementals_requested` and `incrementals_retained` on every prune and logs an explicit rounding line with the reason when they differ, because silent over-retention is how "my disk did not shrink" starts. `PruneResult` carries both numbers so `--dry-run` reports the ROUNDED plan rather than the requested one.

The other two options were weighed and rejected in the doc comment: re-anchoring the floor full would make retention exact but turns a maintenance command into one that reads the SOURCE, and refusing is honest but leaves the headline retention flag unable to succeed on the most common chain shape.

**What still refuses, and why that is not a hedge.** Rounding UP can only reach a boundary that EXISTS at or above the request. When none does — always the case on a never-rotated chain, which has no boundary at all — honouring the request segment-granularly means retaining the whole chain and deleting nothing, and reporting *that* as a successful prune is the silent no-op the contract exists to prevent. So that one case keeps item 100's purpose-built refusal verbatim (`SLUICE-E-BACKUP-CHAIN-UNREADABLE` / exit 3, the same prose, the same computed boundary list), now raised from the retention arithmetic **before** any gate rather than as a decoration on the readability gate's structural leg. Two consequences worth stating: the refusal is unconditional where it used to fall through to the generic prose when it could not prove the sever (there is no second refusal behind it now), and it fires for `--dry-run` too — a dry run that promises a prune the real run refuses is worse than no dry run.

**The condition is two questions, not one.** `dropN == 0` alone would be wrong: a rotated chain whose LEADING segment holds no incrementals of its own contributes no boundary, so a keep-count rounds up to "retain everything" while a whole segment is still droppable. The refusal therefore also requires that the restore floor has not moved. Pinned by `TestPruneLineage_LeadingIncrementalLessSegmentStillDrops`.

**The invariant is asserted, not assumed.** After rounding, the committed plan can no longer trim inside the floor segment — but `PruneChain` checks it anyway and refuses before writing, because the failure that would follow is an unrestorable DR archive discovered at restore time. The dead ADR-0067 `IncrementalCoverageStart` re-sync branch for the trimmed case went with it; a kept floor segment's recorded coverage is correct because its incrementals are untouched.

**Detection was specific and stayed that way.** The readability gate still catches the other unreadable-chain conditions — a missing chain-root manifest, an identity/key mismatch, a structural break prune did not cause — and those keep the generic decoration, whose recovery is a `cp` of a surviving header rather than a retention change. Prune no longer matches on `errChainDoesNotWalk` (its shape cannot reach the gate); the sentinel stays for the next caller that can explain a structural refusal in its own terms. Pinned by `TestPruneLineage_UnreadableChainKeepsTheGenericRefusal`.

**Gates.** `TestSegmentAlignedKeep_RoundsUpAcrossEveryChainShape` — the rounding as a TABLE over chain shapes rather than one representative chain (never-rotated, 2-segment, 3-segment, ragged 3/1/2, leading-incremental-less, one-per-segment, × requests below / on / above a boundary, plus the two aligned counts that do not appear in the boundary list: retire-everything and retain-everything), with `TestSegmentAlignedKeep_NeverRetainsFewerThanAsked` checking the round-UP and boundary-alignment invariants exhaustively over every request each shape admits. Unit pins in `internal/pipeline`: the round-up succeeds and leaves the floor segment whole; a request above every boundary refuses and names the counts; `--dry-run` reports the rounded plan and refuses byte-identically to the real run on the shape that refuses; and the must-NOT-change directions (a keep-count already on a boundary is not rounded; `--keep-duration` past every incremental is still the no-op; a cutoff newer than all of them still retires them all). Integration: the `prune` cell of `backup_chain_shaping_encrypted_matrix_integration_test.go` is PROMOTED from a refusal cell to a full round trip — it asks for a keep-count that does not land on a boundary, asserts the rounding was reported, that whole segments went, that **no surviving segment lost an incremental in place**, and the harness then restores the pruned chain and compares rows to the source oracle in all three encryption modes; `TestItem100_SingleSegmentKeepIncrementals_RefusesActionably` keeps the never-rotated refusal on a real PG chain, now also asserting dry-run/real-run agreement.

**A PRE-EXISTING defect this uncovered and fixed in passing — `backup verify` read the chain's encryption identity from `records[0]`, not from the chain root.** Promoting the matrix's `prune` cell to a real prune was the first time anything in the suite ran `backup verify` over a chain whose ROOT segment had been retired. It failed: `verify: 2 of 4 chunk(s) failed verification`, both CHANGE chunks, `aes-gcm open: message authentication failed`, on a chain that restored **row-exact** in the same test — the Bug-215 verify/restore disagreement inverted (a red verify on a healthy chain). Ground-truthed, not inferred: the two failing chunks were named in the log.

Root cause is exactly item 95(a) on the verify path. Every rotation-born segment full mints its OWN chain CEK, while every CHANGE chunk stays sealed under the stream's original CEK — the one wrapped on the chain-root `manifest.json`. `chain_restore.go` was fixed for this (`ChainRestore.chainIdentityManifest` resolves the root by absolute path); `verifyBackupScan` still unwrapped `records[0].Manifest`, which is the chain's identity only while segment 0 is catalogued. After a whole-segment prune it is a later segment full whose CEK never sealed a change chunk. Fixed with the verify-side twin, `verifyChainIdentityManifest`, with the same fallbacks (no root manifest → a pre-fix-compacted chain; root records no encryption → a plaintext chain) so nothing that verified before stops verifying. It also feeds the kek-mode check, the per-chunk `RebindEnvelopeKEK`, and the plaintext-splice flag, which had the same latent skew.

Mutation evidence is the strongest kind here — the cell was observed RED with the old resolution and GREEN with the new one, in the same run configuration, per-chain only (per-chunk carries its own wraps; the plaintext control has no key). Worth noting as a class: this is the FOURTH member of "correctness established against a chain shape the read path is later asked to read differently", and it was invisible precisely because the cell that would have reached it was parked on a refusal. **A refused cell does not exercise the code behind the refusal** — worth remembering the next time a KNOWN-BROKEN cell is filed. The main session may want to promote this to its own roadmap item; it is recorded here because it was found and fixed in this chunk.

**Assertions deliberately inverted (the "do not let a cell quietly stop testing what it was built for" rule).** Three, each with the reason recorded at the site: the matrix `prune` cell's KNOWN-BROKEN refusal assertions → the round trip its own failure message instructed (it said "promote the cell to a normal round trip" and that is exactly what happened); `TestPruneLineage_WithinSegmentTrimNamesTheBoundaryKeepCounts` → `TestPruneLineage_KeepCountRoundsUpToTheSegmentBoundary`, with its boundary-naming half preserved in a new sibling that asks for a count above every boundary; and both `--dry-run` non-vacuity assertions (unit + integration), which established non-vacuity by asserting the dry run SUCCEEDED where the real run refused — defensible only while the refusal came from a gate `--dry-run` skipped by design.

**The gate that generalises it, because this is the third instance.** Items 91 (wrong code + exit status), 96 (no code at all) and this (both, no remedy) are one class: an operator-facing refusal whose human-readable half is right and whose actionable half is missing. `TestRefusalCodesCarryAnActionableRemedy` (internal/sluicecode) now holds every `ClassRefusal` code to a non-empty, actionable remedy in the `docRows` mirror — which `TestRegistryDocSync_ContentEquality` already holds equal to `docs/operator/error-codes.md`, so one gate covers both homes. "Actionable" is a deliberate FLOOR, mechanically: at least a sentence, and either a backticked artifact (flag/command/statement — how 46 of the 50 rows say it) or an imperative opener from a closed verb vocabulary (how the other four do). Lifted refusals are exempt via the registry's existing `RETAINED-BUT-UNEMITTED` marker rather than a suppression, and `TestRemedyActionablePredicateHasTeeth` pins the predicate against synthetic negatives so it cannot decay into "returns true". It found **zero pre-existing violations** — it is a ratchet, not a cleanup. Its known boundary: it gates the CATALOG's remedy column, not the runtime `CodedError.Hint` at each construction site (no empty-literal hint exists today; a static check for one is a possible follow-up).

### 99. `assertDataWindowEndPositionInvariant` is close to vacuous on the Postgres path — *open, medium*

**Found while root-causing item 92, and deliberately not acted on there.** That invariant is a load-bearing part of the Bug-184 completeness net: on an engine whose CDC positions do not commit after their rows, a data-bearing window's `EndPosition` must never coincide with a schema-history anchor, because the restore side uses exactly that to tell a genuine DDL-only window from an emptied-data one.

On the PG path it can essentially never fire. Postgres stamps schema anchors at LSN `0/0` — `maybeSnapshotSchema` takes the relation message's `xld.WALStart`, which pgoutput reports as zero — so `SchemaHistoryAnchors(EndPosition)` is false for any real `EndPosition`. The assertion runs, costs nothing, and cannot catch the class it exists for on the engine most likely to hit it.

Worth confirming against MySQL/VStream before deciding the fix: if the anchor LSN is genuinely unavailable at that point, the invariant may need a different discriminator entirely rather than a repaired comparison. Note this is the same *shape* as the class in item 97 — a guard whose local logic is right and which never reaches the state it guards.

### 98. `BackupStream`'s rollover shares item 92's replay defect on its first rollover after a resume — *✅ SHIPPED v0.104.3 — and the exposure is WIDER than filed, in two ways*

`BackupStream.captureWindow`'s `changeChunkBuffer.processChange` carries the same `maxChanges > 0 && … && !*inTransaction` cutoff that item 92 fixed in `IncrementalBackup`, and the same exposure: a resumed stream's **first** rollover re-receives the parent's boundary transaction, so a tight `--max-changes` can be satisfied by the replay alone and close a rollover that captured nothing new. Subsequent rollovers ride one open stream and cannot replay, which is why the exposure is first-rollover-only.

It already carries a related concept — ADR-0067's `skipThrough` floor using `PrecedesOrEqual` — but only for the rotation-boundary case, not for this one. The fix is item 92's `advanced` latch applied to the same cutoff; the reason it was not done in the same pass is that it is a different orchestrator with its own resume semantics and deserves its own pin rather than an assumed-identical patch.

**Correction 1 — the byte cap has the identical defect, and the filing named only the change cap.** `RolloverMaxBytes` sits two lines below `RolloverMaxChanges` in the same `processChange`, guarded by the same `!*inTransaction`, and it counts the bytes the *replayed* events buffer. This is a class/representative split of exactly the Bug-74 shape: two bounds dispatching on one window-closing decision, where fixing and pinning the named one proves nothing about its sibling. Both are guarded, and both are pinned separately — the mutation runs confirm the split is real (dropping one guard leaves the other bound's subtests green).

**Correction 2 — `skipThrough` is genuinely a different question, and reusing it would have been wrong.** It is set only by the in-process rotation FSM (`b.skipThrough = &res.priorEnd`), never on a resume, and it *drops* events ≤ P_N. It can drop safely precisely because the pump never restarted there and the dropped events are provably already committed in the prior segment. The resume case must **keep** its replay, for item 92's reason — and more strongly here: this orchestrator has two documented exits that end a window mid-transaction (the eager stop-signal exit, and the ctx-cancel drain, which skips its flush while `inTransaction`), so the parent's tail really can be severed and the replay is then the only thing carrying it. Filtering would convert a benign duplicate into silent loss. Same file, opposite disposition; the `captureWindow` doc comment now says so explicitly so the next reader does not unify them.

**Two things the filing got right, confirmed rather than assumed.** The replay *is* one transaction, and both caps only close on a transaction boundary, so exactly one rollover per resume can be replay-only — "first rollover only" holds in the count sense too. And an in-process rotation is not a resume (`stream_rotation.go` keeps the same CDC handle), so it introduces no replay of its own.

**One more resume door than "process restart".** The GitHub-#22 transient-retry path re-opens the pump mid-stream (`StreamChanges(currentParent.EndPosition)` after a retriable rollover error), which is a resume and replays like any other. The fix covers it for free because the latch is per-window against the rollover's own `StartPosition` rather than a once-per-process flag — worth stating, because a fix keyed on "the first rollover of the process" would have missed it silently.

**Also corrected in passing:** the ADR-0087 resume-heal comment claimed `StreamChanges(P_N)` "resumes strictly-after P_N like any normal resume". That premise is the one item 92 disproved. The heal itself is unaffected (it *wants* the (P_N, S] window), but the sentence was teaching the wrong engine behaviour.

**Shipped shape.** `captureOutcome` gains a sticky `Advanced`, latched in `processChange` the first time an event arrives at a position strictly after the rollover's `StartPosition`, via item 92's `windowAdvancedPast` (engine `ir.PositionMonotonicChecker`, position-inequality fallback; neither wrong answer loses data). Both caps gain `&& out.Advanced`. **The wall-clock deadline is deliberately exempt** — a window that expires over a quiet source must still close, or the stream would lose its cadence and its heartbeat — so the worst the condition can cost is a rollover that runs to `--rollover-window`. A rollover that still ends replay-only logs `warnReplayOnlyRollover`, the streaming twin of the incremental path's WARN.

**Gates.** `internal/pipeline/stream_rollover_bound_replay_test.go` — the scripted pins, {change cap, byte cap} × {comparator, no-comparator}, plus the no-replay non-vacuity half for each cap and a pin that a replay-only rollover closed by an *exempt* exit still commits honestly at `start == end`; `…_pg_integration_test.go` — the real-wire pin, chaining three stream runs so each resumes at a commit LSN PostgreSQL itself produced, each stopped after exactly one committed rollover through the ADR-0156 readout hook (a stream left running would pick the missed delta up on its next rollover, so stopping on the replay-only rollover is what makes it a DATA pin), ending in a chain restore that must carry every row. Mutation-verified three ways, each confirmed to compile: dropping the change-cap guard turns its subtests + the restore red (`dave` missing) while the byte-cap subtests stay green; dropping the byte-cap guard does the mirror image; forcing the latch to `false` turns both non-vacuity pins AND the pre-existing `TestBackupStream_RolloverOnMaxChanges` red.

**Deferred, now DONE (2026-07-28, the v0.104.3 docs pass):** the `--rollover-max-changes` CLI help in `cmd/sluice/backup.go` got the one-line clarification item 92 gave `--max-changes` (it counts change EVENTS including transaction framing, and cannot close a rollover before the window has advanced past its own start position). `--rollover-max-bytes` got the advancement half too — `stream.go`'s `RolloverMaxBytes` doc says it carries the same condition for the same reason, and the flag help did not. `docs/value-types.md`'s sizing section was corrected in the same pass: it carved Postgres out of the framing arithmetic entirely, on a claim the PG CDC reader disproves.

### 97. `backup verify` reports a rotation-born encrypted chain healthy that `restore` cannot decrypt (Bug 215, v0.104.2 cycle) — *✅ SHIPPED v0.104.3 — and BOTH halves were worse than filed*

**Root cause, from the operator's actual failing chain.** Every rotation-born segment full runs the ordinary `backup full` orchestrator against an EMPTY provisional dir, so `setupChainEncryption` takes its `prior == nil` arm and mints a FRESH chain CEK per segment. Unwrapping every manifest's CEK and trying each against every chunk showed the chain root and all four segments holding four different keys, and the failing chunk decrypting only under the last segment's. **The AAD was byte-correct in every case** — v9 injective, right file, right ordinal. The binding was never the defect; the key was. `alignEncryption` resolved the CEK owner through `b.segStore`, so anything extending the chain after a rotation sealed under the segment's key while the read path used the root's.

**The filed framing was too narrow, and the real trigger is more common.** "Rotation-born resume" was incidental. The trigger is only *"the open segment is not the lineage root"* — so an ordinary **`backup stream` restart** on a rotated encrypted chain hits it too, more often and just as silently, and broker replay (`SyncFromBackup`) was equally affected. `backup stream` matched the read path only by accident: it resolves the key once at startup, when the open segment IS the root, and carries it across rotations.

**Why verify passed, which is the more valuable half.** `decrypt_probe=true` meant *"an envelope was supplied"* and nothing more. The probe unwrapped each chunk's OWN `WrappedCEK` — a field only per-chunk mode populates — so on a default per-chain chain it returned nil for every chunk **without touching a byte of ciphertext**. The only decryption in an entire `backup verify --encrypt` run was one chain-root CEK unwrap. Even in per-chunk mode it proved the wrap opened, never that the ciphertext authenticated under it. So `backup verify` on an encrypted chain was not meaningfully verifying decryptability at all — the trust signal was hollow, which is why it could report green over an unrestorable chain.

**Fixed:** the CEK owner resolves at the lineage root (parent header kept only as the no-root fallback), and verify now performs a real authenticated open of every encrypted chunk under the key AND binding restore would use, reporting `decrypted=N`. It also walks `BuildLineageChain` first, because restore refuses a mis-stitched chain before anything else. `docs/operator/encryption.md` and the `SLUICE-E-BACKUP-CHUNK-AUTH-FAILED` row both claimed verify could not catch this class; corrected, and the `docsync` gate held them to it.

**The gate — `backup_chain_shaping_encrypted_matrix_integration_test.go`:** {rotate, rotate-then-resume, rotate-then-stream-resume, compact, compact-after-rotate, prune} × {per-chain, per-chunk, plaintext}, each cell writing an encrypted chain, applying the operation, then **restoring and comparing rows** against a source oracle — plus a verify/restore agreement assertion on every cell. 18/18 green. The three `prune` cells get there through a REFUSAL rather than a prune: the keep-count they ask for is item 100's within-segment trim, which item 95's readability gate refuses at the pre-commit leg, so each cell asserts the coded class (`SLUICE-E-BACKUP-CHAIN-UNREADABLE` / exit 3), the defect's shape (the severed parent link, at the `pre-commit` stage — not the destructive `post-sweep` one), and the refusal's INERTNESS (catalog unchanged, chain-root manifest intact, chain still restores row-exact), failing if item 100 changes shape or silently disappears. Mutation-verified three ways for the encrypted half, including short-circuiting the authenticated open to confirm the verify/restore disagreement gate actually fires, and three more for the prune cells (move the gate to post-sweep, strip the `sluicecode` wrap, ask for a whole-segment-only prune — each turns the cell red with the assertion that names it).

**What.** An ENCRYPTED chain that `backup stream` rotated and one `backup incremental` then resumed (the ADR-0087 / Bug-139 rotation-born resume path) restores everything up to the last rollover and then exits 3 at `chunk failed authenticated decryption` on that incremental's own chunk. Pre-existing: identical on v0.104.1 and v0.104.0. Plaintext is unaffected.

**The part that makes it HIGH is not the failed restore — it is that `backup verify` says the chain is fine.** `verify` returns rc=0, `all chunks OK chunks=10 decrypt_probe=true`, on a chain `restore` cannot read. Verify is the trust signal this project tells operators to rely on before they need a backup; a green verify over an unrestorable chain is worse than no verify, because it converts "I should check this" into "I checked this". That disagreement is the finding, more than the decryption failure itself.

**Controls that scope it.** No rotation → clean. No stream → clean. The chain is healthy immediately before the resume. Plaintext unaffected. So it is specific to a rotation-born resume writing chunks whose AAD or CEK derivation does not match what the read path later recomputes for them.

**This is the THIRD instance of one class, and the class is now the finding.** Bug 214 (compaction deleting the chain-root manifest), item 95 (`backup prune` doing the same), and this. Every one is a chain-SHAPING operation — compact, prune, rotate-then-resume — whose correctness was established against PLAINTEXT chains and never round-tripped through the encrypted read path. Bug 139's closure verified this exact resume path entirely on plaintext, exactly as compaction's Bugs 95/139 were closed on plaintext. Encryption changes what a "redundant" file is (the root manifest carries the KDF salt) and what a chunk's identity is (the AAD binds it), so a plaintext round-trip is not evidence for an encrypted one — and three separate operations have now shipped on that assumption.

**The gate this class needs, and it is bigger than any one fix.** Every chain-shaping operation needs an encrypted round-trip cell — write encrypted, apply the operation, **restore and compare rows** — in the same matrix, not per-bug as each is found. The v0.104.2 compaction fix added exactly one such cell; the right move is to generalise it into a table of {compact, prune, rotate, rotate-then-resume, compact-after-rotate} × {per-chain, per-chunk, plaintext control} rather than wait for the fourth instance. A second gate worth having alongside it: **`verify` and `restore` must agree** — a fixture where verify passes and restore fails should itself be a test failure, since that disagreement is what turned this from a bug into a trap.

### 96. The compaction readability refusal has no `SLUICE-E-*` code — *✅ IMPLEMENTED (`SLUICE-E-BACKUP-CHAIN-UNREADABLE`); SHIPPED v0.104.3*

`verifyChainReadable`'s refusal (item 94) is a bare `fmt.Errorf`, so `internal/pipeline/backup/chain_readable_gate.go` contains no `sluicecode` reference at all. The prose and the `cp` recovery are good, but a script or agent branching on `SLUICE-E-*` — which is exactly what `docs/operator/error-codes.md` instructs operators to do — cannot detect it, and it exits 1 rather than the refusal status 3.

Worth doing precisely because it is the thin version of the defect v0.104.2 spent three fixes on: an operator-facing refusal whose human-readable half is right and whose machine-readable half is missing, which is item 91 (Bug 213) restated. It also lands the same release-note claim twice — v0.104.2 tells operators a chain can be refused up front, without giving them a code to match on.

Add the code alongside `CodeTargetDeferrableKey`'s declaration, class `ClassRefusal` so `ExitCode()` yields 3, mirror it into `docrows.go` and `docs/operator/error-codes.md` (both gated by `sluicecode_test.go`, so the in-repo table cannot drift), and port the row to the site. Reuse `verifyChainReadable`'s existing `op string` parameter so the same code serves prune when item 95 is decided.

**Shipped shape.** `SLUICE-E-BACKUP-CHAIN-UNREADABLE`, `ClassRefusal` (exit 3), wrapped INSIDE `verifyChainReadable` rather than at its call sites — the guard's body moved to an unexported `checkChainReadable` and `verifyChainReadable` became the coding wrapper, so a future caller cannot acquire the guard without acquiring its refusal class. One code serves both operations, with the existing `op` naming which refused (`backup compact` / `backup prune`) and `stage` naming which leg (`pre-swap`/`pre-commit` = nothing deleted; `post-sweep` = already deleted, recovery named). The row still needs porting to the sluicesync.com mirror, whose build hard-fails on a count mismatch.

### 95. `backup prune` has Bug 214's defect too, on a path that runs far more often — *✅ IMPLEMENTED (keep the root manifest + the shared readability gate); SHIPPED v0.104.3*

**Found while fixing item 94, in the same read path, and deliberately left unfixed there because it needs a decision rather than a patch.** `pruneWholeSegments` (`internal/pipeline/backup/chain_prune.go`) deletes `seg.FullManifestPath` through `seg.Store(store)`. For the ROOT segment that store is the lineage root and that path is `manifest.json` — so prune destroys the chain's identity header exactly the way compaction did, and a passphrase-encrypted chain then fails to restore at `unwrap chain cek` while the operator holds the correct passphrase.

**This is worse than item 94 in reach.** Compaction is occasional maintenance; prune is ordinary retention and runs on a schedule. It fires whenever prune drops segment 0.

**Not a code-reading guess.** `TestPruneLineage_MultiSegmentDropsLeadingWholeSegment` **asserts the deletion as intended behaviour**, so the current shape is deliberate and tested — which is precisely why this needs a decision. Item 94's mutation testing independently proved the consequence: a passphrase chain with no root manifest fails the restore at `unwrap chain cek`.

**Recoverable, and for a reassuring reason.** Every rotation-born segment full carries the same chain salt (`stream_rotation.go` runs `backup.Backup` with the aligned envelope), so copying any surviving segment's header to the chain root restores readability.

**The decision this needs.** Compaction was easy: the deleted data provably still exists in the merged segment, so keeping the root header costs nothing. Prune is genuinely different — should a chain whose root segment has been legitimately retired keep a dangling identity header forever? Probably yes (it is small, and it is the chain's identity rather than segment 0's data), but that is a contract call, not a bug fix. Whatever is decided, `verifyChainReadable` already takes an `op string` so prune can reuse it verbatim; the implementation is the guard plus two call sites.

**Shipped shape — decided: KEEP the root manifest, unconditionally.** `pruneWholeSegments` skips exactly one delete, behind the named `keepsChainIdentity(seg)` (`seg.Dir == "" && seg.FullManifestPath == lineage.ManifestFileName`); everything else about a retired root segment — its incrementals, its change chunks, its data chunks — still goes. Not gated on encryption: a keep-it-when rule is one future encryption mode or one future reader away from the same outage, and nobody notices until a restore. `verifyChainReadable` is reused verbatim at two prune call sites, wired the way compaction wires it — pre-commit (prune's deletes all run after the catalog commit, so a refusal there has written nothing and removed nothing) and post-sweep (so a retention run can never report success over a chain it just made unreadable). `PruneOpts.Envelope` mirrors `CompactOpts.Envelope`, and the CLI builds it from the chain-root manifest exactly as `backup compact` does. The pre-fix reproduction was exact on a real 8-segment rotated PG chain: per-chain died at `unwrap chain cek`, per-chunk at `resolve chunk cek: unwrap chunk cek`, plaintext restored fine.

**Two further defects the round trip uncovered — the first is FIXED here, the second is NOT and needs its own item.**

**(a) FIXED — `chain_restore.go` read the chain's encryption identity from `links[0]`, not from the chain root.** Keeping the root manifest was necessary but not sufficient: with it kept, the per-chain leg got past the CEK unwrap and then died at `chunk failed authenticated decryption` on a surviving incremental. Ground truth (real 8-segment chain): **every rotation-born segment full mints its OWN chain CEK**, while every CHANGE chunk in the whole chain stays sealed under the stream's ORIGINAL CEK — the one wrapped on the chain-root manifest. A segment full is restored through its own nested `Restore` against its own segment root, so the divergence is invisible until `links[0]` stops being segment 0 — which is exactly what a whole-segment prune does. Fix: `ChainRestore.chainIdentityManifest` resolves the root `manifest.json` by absolute path and uses it for the encryption preflight whenever it records chain encryption, falling back to `links[0]` otherwise (a pre-fix-compacted chain has no root manifest; a plaintext chain's root records no encryption — both must keep restoring). This is the other half of "the root manifest is the chain's IDENTITY": it carries the CEK the change chunks are bound to, not just the Argon2id salt.

**(b) FILED AS ITEM 100, now FIXED (segment-granular retention) — prune's within-segment incremental trim produced a chain that could not be restored, and always had.** Prune's other retention shape drops LEADING incrementals inside the floor segment, leaving that segment's full anchored at S with its first survivor starting at S′ > S. The events in (S, S′] are gone, so the restore path refuses it — first on the severed parent link (`does not chain off preceding link … — branching/mis-stitched lineage`), then on the forward position gap. **Ground-truthed on a real rotated PG chain, in PLAINTEXT, on the pre-fix binary: prune exited 0 and the subsequent `ChainRestore` failed.** This is unrelated to encryption and is not caused by the gate — the gate SURFACES it, refusing pre-commit with nothing deleted, which is strictly better than destroying first and finding out at restore time. But it means `--keep-incrementals` on a NON-rotated (single-segment) chain now always refuses, because every such prune is a within-segment trim. The package doc's claim that "the segment full + the remaining incrementals still form a contiguous chain" is false; that claim is about positions and the trim breaks both the position boundary and the parent link. Deciding the shape — segment-granular retention only, re-anchoring the floor full, or an explicit "this narrows the window and drops the base" refusal with a remedy — is a contract call, filed rather than papered over.

### 94. `backup compact` on an ENCRYPTED chain exits 0 and leaves the chain UNRESTORABLE (Bug 214, v0.104.1 regression cycle) — *✅ SHIPPED v0.104.2*

**What.** `backup compact` against an encrypted chain reports success — `groups_merged=1 segments_removed=3`, exit 0 — and the chain is then unrestorable. `verify` and `restore` both refuse at `unwrap chain cek`, zero rows, minutes after that same chain restored 230/230 md5-exact. Pre-existing, NOT a v0.104.1 regression: v0.104.0 and v0.103.2 do the same thing.

**Root cause, confirmed by reading.** `sweepRootSegmentArtifacts` (`internal/pipeline/backup/chain_compact.go`) deletes the chain-root `manifest.json`, on the stated reasoning that after compaction "the root manifest + root incrementals + root chunks are orphans". That reasoning holds for a PLAINTEXT chain, where the file is genuinely redundant once the merged segment owns its own copy. It is false for an encrypted one: ADR-0152 binds the chain CEK wrap to the ROOT MANIFEST'S IDENTITY, and `chain_restore.go` unwraps via `lineage.UnwrapChainCEK(envelope, enc.WrappedCEK, rootManifest)`. The root manifest is the chain's identity, not a spare copy of segment 0's — deleting it revokes readability for **every** segment, including ones compaction never touched.

**The tell that it was never round-tripped.** Compaction's history in the bug catalog (Bugs 95, 139) is entirely about refusals to merge, and both were closed against plaintext chains. Encrypted compaction has apparently never had a compact→restore cell.

**Recovery for anyone hit by it:** `cp <chain>/seg-merged-*/manifest.json <chain>/manifest.json` restores the chain byte-exactly — compaction copies the oldest full's manifest into the merged segment dir before deleting the root, so the identity still exists on disk. Verified in both per-chain and per-chunk modes.

**The precise mechanism is narrower than "ADR-0152 binds the CEK to the root manifest", and the narrower version is what the gate keys on.** The killer is `cmd/sluice/backup.go`'s `buildReadEnvelope`: for `kek_mode=passphrase-argon2id` it reads the **Argon2id salt off the chain-root manifest, and silently falls back to a fresh-salt default when that file is absent**. The restore then builds a wrong-KEK envelope and fails while holding a perfectly good passphrase. That silent fallback is why the symptom is `unwrap chain cek` — i.e. "wrong passphrase" — rather than an honest missing-file error, and it is why the same deletion is harmless on a KMS chain, where no key material comes from the root.

**Modes differ in symptom, not severity.** Per-chain fails at `unwrap chain cek`; `--encrypt-mode=per-chunk` fails on the first chunk at `resolve chunk cek: unwrap chunk cek: crypto: chain CEK unwrap failed`. (An earlier version of this entry said per-chunk surfaced as `SLUICE-E-BACKUP-CHUNK-AUTH-FAILED` on 6/6 chunks — same root cause, wrong code; corrected before it reached release notes.) `--dry-run` is inert and the plaintext control is unaffected — both good, and both part of why this stayed hidden.

**Fix shape.** Stop deleting the root manifest — it is small, and on an encrypted chain it is load-bearing forever. Then add the gate the class actually needs: **compaction must prove the chain still restores before it deletes anything.** A compact that reports success on a chain it has made unreadable is the same shape as the format-floor bug (an operation whose local reasoning is right and whose whole-chain consequence is unimplemented), and the durable answer is the same — a post-compaction readability check, not a more careful sweep. Pin the round trip: encrypted compact → restore, per-chain AND per-chunk, with the plaintext control.

### 93. A PG source table whose only key is a DEFERRABLE PK has no usable replica identity, and adding it to a publication breaks the SOURCE APPLICATION's own writes — silently, from sluice's side (reproduced on v0.103.0/1/2) — *✅ IMPLEMENTED (`SLUICE-E-SOURCE-REPLICA-IDENTITY`); SHIPPED v0.104.2*

**What.** Postgres will not use a deferrable primary key's index as a replica identity (`pg_index.indimmediate = false`), so a table whose only key is a deferrable PK has **no usable replica identity**. `sluice sync start` adds it to `sluice_pub` with `pubupdate=t pubdelete=t`, and from that moment Postgres refuses the **source application's own** `UPDATE` and `DELETE` on that table:

```
ERROR: cannot update table "dpk" because it does not have a replica identity and publishes updates
ERROR: cannot delete from table "dpk" because it does not have a replica identity and publishes deletes
```

`INSERT` keeps working, which is what makes it insidious — the table looks healthy until the first update.

**Why this ranks above an ordinary preflight gap.** The breakage lands in the operator's *own application*, not in sluice's output, and it is sluice's publication that triggers Postgres's check. So the symptom appears somewhere the operator has no reason to connect to sluice, while sluice logs **nothing** — zero lines mentioning replica identity at cold start on any of three binaries tested. A plain-PK table in the same run is unaffected, so it also looks table-specific rather than tool-caused. Both recoveries are verified: dropping the publication, or `ALTER TABLE … REPLICA IDENTITY FULL`.

**Same catalog bit as Bug 211, opposite side of the pipeline.** `indimmediate=false` is exactly what makes a deferrable key illegal as an `ON CONFLICT` arbiter on the TARGET (Bug 211, fixed v0.104.0). This is the SOURCE-side consequence of the same bit, and it is pre-existing rather than a regression — reproduced identically on v0.103.0, v0.103.1 and v0.103.2. It was recorded in Bug 211's companion section and never promoted to a roadmap item; the v0.104.1 learnings sweep caught that it was still unfiled.

**Verified still open at HEAD (v0.104.1).** The only `relreplident` read anywhere in `internal/` is the `--where` full-before-image preflight (`internal/engines/postgres/where_cdc_preflight.go`); there is no general replica-identity-usability check. sluice's only other handling is REACTIVE — `cdc_reader.go` errors when an UPDATE arrives with no identity — and that never fires here, because the operator's write fails first, upstream of sluice ever seeing a change.

**Fix shape.** One preflight at PG-source cold start: every in-scope table's replica-identity index must be unique **and** `indimmediate`. That single catalog read covers three cases at once — this one, Bug 211's target side, and the keyless case (which today produces only an INFO about copy strategy). Refuse loudly, naming the table, the reason, and both remedies (make the constraint immediate, or `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL`). Prefer refusing at start over letting sluice put the source into a state where the operator's writes fail.

**Evidence.** `sluice-testing` BUG-CATALOG, Bug 211 companion section; repro script `workspace/v1032/focus1c_replicaidentity.sh`.

**Shipped shape.** `ir.ReplicaIdentityPreflighter` (optional SOURCE-engine surface on the `SchemaReader`), implemented by `postgres.SchemaReader.PreflightReplicaIdentity` (`internal/engines/postgres/replica_identity_preflight.go`) and driven from **both doors into a publication**, ahead of each: `coldStartReadSourceSchema` (alongside the other source-side preflights, i.e. before cold start's `EnsurePublication`) and `AddTable.Run` (before `extendPublicationScope`'s `ALTER PUBLICATION … ADD TABLE`). The add-table door was covered too because, unlike the target-side sibling, there is no defence-in-depth floor behind it — the source's refusal fires in the operator's application and never reaches sluice, so a missed door is a permanently silent gap. A refusal leaves the publication and the source untouched. Capability-gated on `ir.CDCLogicalReplication` (excludes `postgres-trigger`, whose delegated SchemaReader satisfies the interface but creates no publication; excludes MySQL and every non-CDC path). One catalog read per cold start, classified by a pure `replicaIdentityUsable` that re-implements PG's own relcache rule (an index counts only if valid + unique + **immediate** + non-partial), covering `relreplident` ∈ {`d`, `i`, `f`, `n`} plus an unknown-letter refusal. New coded refusal `SLUICE-E-SOURCE-REPLICA-IDENTITY`, naming every offending table, its reason, and — when the table carries one — the concrete `REPLICA IDENTITY USING INDEX <idx>` fix.

**One correction to the filed fix shape, ground-truthed on PG 16 before implementing.** The entry's phrasing ("replica-identity index must be unique **and** `indimmediate`") reads as if a deferrable PK plus a usable immediate UNIQUE index were fine — the way it IS fine on the target side (Bug 211: `ON CONFLICT` arbitrates on any immediate unique index). It is **not** fine on the source: `REPLICA IDENTITY DEFAULT` resolves to the *primary key* and nothing else, so `CREATE TABLE t (… PRIMARY KEY DEFERRABLE, UNIQUE (k))` still has no replica identity and PG still refuses the application's UPDATE. The two checks are therefore deliberately asymmetric, with separate codes; the source-side refusal names the `USING INDEX` remedy that makes exactly that shape work. The asymmetry is oracled — `TestReplicaIdentityPreflight_OracleMatrix` puts every fixture shape into a real publication, attempts a real `UPDATE` in a rolled-back transaction, and requires sluice's refusal set to equal PG's rejection set in both directions.

**Gates (Tier 1).** `internal/engines/postgres/replica_identity_preflight_test.go` (the pure classification family, every `relreplident` × index state), `…_integration_test.go` (the PG oracle + the scope/over-refusal guard), and `internal/pipeline/replica_identity_pg_integration_test.go` — the PATH pin, driving `Streamer.Run`: three refusal shapes each asserting **no publication exists afterwards and the source's own `UPDATE` still works**, the deferrable-PK-plus-UNIQUE asymmetry cell, an all-publishable stream that must cold-copy + take live CDC, the `--exclude-table` escape, and the add-table door (a live `AddTable.Run` of a deferrable-PK table, asserting the table did NOT join `pg_publication_rel`, the source stayed writable, and the running stream did not wedge). Mutation-verified: deleting the call site turns all four refusal pins red (they run to the context deadline — the pre-fix shape) while both must-not-refuse pins stay green; moving the preflight to after `EnsurePublication` turns them red on the timing assertion specifically; inverting the classifier's deferrable branch or its FULL branch fails the oracle as UNDER- and OVER-refusal respectively.

**Knock-on.** `deferrable_key_pg_integration_test.go`'s fixture now sets `ALTER TABLE dpk REPLICA IDENTITY FULL` — the source-side gate runs first and would otherwise refuse before the Bug-211 target-side gate under test could be reached. `relreplident` is not part of the IR and is not carried to the target, so the target's key stays deferrable and that pin still tests exactly what it did.

### 92. A tightly-bounded `--max-changes` incremental can write a chain segment that captured nothing (observed 2026-07-27) — *✅ SHIPPED v0.104.3*

**Observed.** Building the item-90 cross-version gate, an incremental run with `--max-changes 2` immediately after a prior one wrote a real, chain-linked, correctly-stamped, correctly-parented manifest with `start_position == end_position` and **none of the committed delta in it** — while logging `changes=6`. The identical run with `--max-changes 0` and a time bound picked the delta up. Surfaced as two restore cells returning 3 rows instead of 4; the harness works around it by dropping the bound, documented in the test.

**Not silent loss, on current evidence.** The replication slot did not advance past the missed delta, so a later time-bounded window caught it — a soundness-preserving miss rather than data destruction. That is what keeps this off the critical path. What it costs an operator is subtler: someone building a chain with tight `--max-changes` bounds can accumulate empty segments while believing each captured their writes, and the summary line reports a non-zero change count while doing it.

**One hypothesis already falsified — do not re-derive it.** The obvious story is that `--max-changes` counts every `ir.Change` including `TxBegin`/`TxCommit` framing, so a low bound truncates mid-transaction before any commit lands. **Reading `captureWindow` disproves this:** the cutoff is `totalChanges >= maxChanges && !inTransaction`, which already refuses to close inside a transaction, and the doc comment on `MaxChanges` states that contract explicitly. The framing events *are* counted toward the bound (so `--max-changes 100` is nearer 33 single-row transactions than 100 rows, which is worth documenting on its own), but that alone does not produce an EMPTY window. `changes=6` against a delta this small is itself unexplained and is the thread to pull.

**Second unexplained signal.** `assertDataWindowEndPositionInvariant` exists precisely for the "emptied-data window" class on engines whose positions do not commit after their rows — and it did not fire here. Either the window was not classified as data-bearing, or the invariant does not cover this shape. Whichever it is, it is worth knowing, because that assertion is a load-bearing part of the Bug-184 completeness net.

**How to approach it.** Three-phase protocol, Phase A first: this is exactly the "multiple plausible hypotheses, first guess already wrong" shape the protocol exists for. Instrument `captureWindow` to log each `ir.Change` kind, `totalChanges`, `inTransaction`, `lastPos`, and the flush/return branch taken, then reproduce with `--max-changes 2` against a committed two-transaction delta. Do not write a fix off the counting story above — it has already been checked and does not explain the observation.

**Root cause (ground-truthed on real PG 16, instrumented `captureWindow`).** The window was not empty of events — it was full of *the parent's*. A resumed CDC stream opens by RE-DELIVERING the transaction the parent segment ends on: PostgreSQL's logical decoding begins at `max(requested_lsn, confirmed_flush_lsn)` and skips only transactions whose commit record is STRICTLY BEFORE that point, so restarting at a parent `EndPosition` — which is exactly a commit LSN — replays that whole transaction. Every pgoutput event of a transaction carries that transaction's commit LSN, so the replay's `lastPos` *is* `StartPosition`. The instrumented run, resuming at `0/25CC498` with `--max-changes 2`: `TxBegin@0/25CC498` (total 1, in_tx) → `SchemaSnapshot@0/0` (2, in_tx) → `Insert@0/25CC498` (3, in_tx — the row the parent already captured) → `TxCommit@0/25CC498` (4, `!in_tx`) → `maxChanges close total=4 max=2` → manifest `start == end == 0/25CC498`, `chunks=1`, `changes=4`. The operator's `changes=6` is the same shape with a larger boundary transaction. The `--max-changes 0` run picked the delta up because it kept streaming past the replay. A useful side finding from the same run: the slot's `confirmed_flush_lsn` trailed the request by *two* committed transactions and PostgreSQL still replayed only the boundary one — the requested LSN is the floor, so delivered positions never regress below `StartPosition`.

**Why `assertDataWindowEndPositionInvariant` stayed silent.** Neither of the two guesses in the filing: the window WAS classified as data-bearing (one chunk, `CDCPositionCommitsAfterRows` false). The invariant simply does not cover this shape — it asserts `EndPosition` does not coincide with a *schema-history anchor*, and this window's `EndPosition` coincides with its own `StartPosition`. Adjacent finding worth its own item: on the Postgres path the schema anchors are stamped at LSN `0/0` (`maybeSnapshotSchema` is handed the relation message's `xld.WALStart`, which pgoutput reports as zero), so `SchemaHistoryAnchors(EndPosition)` can essentially never be true there and the assertion is close to vacuous for PG. That is a separate defect from this one and was left untouched.

**Shipped shape.** `captureWindow` learns its `startPos` and latches an `advanced` flag the first time a change arrives at a position strictly after it; the `MaxChanges` cutoff gains `&& advanced`. Ordering comes from the engine's `ir.PositionMonotonicChecker` (POSTGRES ONLY — an earlier version of this entry said MySQL implemented it too; it does not, and takes the position-inequality fallback, which is why the guard is engine-neutral in effect even though the comparator is not) so a parent anchor in an older token representation still compares by LSN, falling back to position inequality otherwise; neither wrong answer loses data (`windowAdvancedPast` documents both directions). The replayed events are deliberately KEPT rather than filtered: they are duplicates in the ordinary case, but when the parent's own window ended mid-transaction — the channel-close and ctx-cancel exits can do that — the replay is the only thing carrying the severed tail, so dropping it would convert a benign duplicate into silent loss. A run that still ends data-bearing without advancing (a wall-clock window that expires before the source commits anything new — legitimate, and no longer reachable via the bound) now logs a WARN naming the shape, because `changes=N` alone reads as "N of your writes are in here". `MaxChanges`'s doc comment and the `--max-changes` help now say it bounds change EVENTS including transaction framing (a one-row transaction is three).

**Gates.** `internal/pipeline/incremental_maxchanges_replay_test.go` — the scripted pin (both the comparator and no-comparator engine shapes) plus its non-vacuity half (a stream with no replay must close exactly where it did before) plus the `windowAdvancedPast` family; `internal/pipeline/incremental_maxchanges_replay_pg_integration_test.go` — the real-wire pin, chaining two incrementals so the second resumes at a position PostgreSQL itself produced, asserting the bounded window's `EndPosition` moves past its `StartPosition` and that a chain restore carries the row committed after the parent. Mutation-verified in both directions: dropping `&& advanced` turns the replay pins red while the non-vacuity pin stays green; forcing `windowAdvancedPast` to `false` turns the non-vacuity pin red too.

### 89. `refuseSignedChain` reports a cancelled context as a probe failure (observed 2026-07-27 on the v0.104.0 tag) — *✅ SHIPPED v0.104.1*

**What.** `BackupStream.refuseSignedChain` (`internal/pipeline/stream.go`) wraps every error from `lineage.ChainIsSigned` as `"backup stream: probe signed chain: %w"`. That includes `context.Canceled`. When a caller cancels during a rollover, the probe is interrupted and `stream.Run` returns an error naming the probe, instead of exiting cleanly — `TestBackupStream_ContextCancel_DuringRollover_CleanExit` asserts the clean exit and caught it.

A caller's own cancellation is not a probe failure. This is the same distinction the MySQL and Postgres `setErr` allowlists already draw for their `ctx.Err()` sites, and it is stated there in as many words: *the caller's own cancellation, never a source fault.*

**Why it is filed rather than fixed on the spot.** It surfaced as an intermittent CI failure on a release tag, and it did not reproduce in 25 consecutive local runs on the same OS. The right fix is probably one `errors.Is(err, context.Canceled)` arm, but "probably" is doing work in that sentence — whether the clean exit wants a bare `ctx.Err()`, a `nil`, or a sentinel depends on how `Run` classifies its exit, and getting that wrong converts a rare wrong-error into a swallowed real one. It deserves reading the exit path properly rather than a guessed one-liner.

**Provenance, so the next person does not re-derive it.** The error path predates the v0.104.0 delta — `git log -S "probe signed chain"` attributes it to `ac9a80ca`, the ADR-0154 signing wiring. The delta *did* touch this file (the rollover stamp moved from FormatVersion 5 to 9), so it was a plausible suspect and was checked: the stamp does not gate the signed-chain probe, and the failure is a context race, not a version branch.

**Why it had never been seen.** The Windows matrix only joins on tag pushes; routine PR and branch runs are Linux-only. So this test's Windows timing had been exercised far less than its run count suggests.

**Shipped, with one correction to the filing above and one adjacent leak.** The disposition is `nil`, chosen because that is what `Run`'s own ctx-cancel arm already does (the rollover drain-commit at the top of the loop returns `nil`), and because it *has* to be `nil` for the non-pretty CLI path to read it as a clean stop: `backup stream` returns `Run`'s error straight to kong, so a bare `ctx.Err()` would exit 1. The live panel already normalises both (`live_panel.go` treats nil-or-`context.Canceled` as "stopped"), which is why only the non-TTY path was exposed.

The correction: **the probe is not the defect, it is one of eight equally reachable wordings.** Every step of `newRolloverLoop` reads the store, and every `irbackup.Store` implementation returns `ctx.Err()` from its entry guard — so the same cancel landing one call earlier reports `stream: read existing stream_state: …` or `stream: resolve parent: …`. Fixing the probe alone would have left the class open. The fix is therefore one classifier, `cleanExitOnCallerCancel`, applied at both of `Run`'s setup-phase error returns rather than inside the probe. Its two guards are separately mutation-tested: `ctx.Err() != nil` keeps a *foreign* `context.Canceled` (a store's own per-call context) loud, and the `errors.Is` arm keeps an unrelated failure that merely races the cancel loud. It is deliberately NOT extended past setup — `commitRollover`'s errors carry an in-flight manifest, where returning nil would silently drop a committed window, which is the opposite disposition; that path already has `drainCommitInFlightRollover`. The one-shot `probe signed chain` siblings (`chain_compact.go`, `chain_prune.go`, `incremental.go`) are left alone: they have no long-running clean-exit contract, and a Ctrl-C exiting 1 there is ordinary CLI behaviour.

The adjacent leak: `Run` armed its `CloseIf(cdc)` and `deregisterStopCh` defers *after* the signed-chain probe, so the refusal path — and now the cancel path — returned with the source replication connection still open. The defers moved above the probe.

**The flake is now a gate.** `TestBackupStream_ContextCancel_DuringSetup_CleanExit` injects a store that cancels the run context from inside a named setup read, so the cancellation lands in the step deterministically rather than racing a `time.Sleep`; it runs both the reported instance (the signed-chain probe) and a sibling (the concurrent-writer preflight), and each subtest fails only for its own call site's mutation. `TestBackupStream_SetupError_StaysLoud` is the non-vacuity half — three cases proving the classifier does not swallow a real failure. The original rollover test was de-flaked at the root: its cancel now waits on the `Readout` callback, which fires at the top of the rollover loop, so the cancel can no longer land in setup at all (200 consecutive local runs green).
